metadata.title: EAU Guidelines on Management of Non-Neurogenic Female Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the evaluation and management of non-neurogenic lower urinary tract symptoms in women. It covers urinary incontinence, overactive and underactive bladder, bladder outlet obstruction, nocturia, pelvic organ prolapse with urinary symptoms, urinary fistulae and urethral diverticula. It presents diagnostic recommendations and evidence on conservative, pharmacological and surgical treatments, as well as follow-up.

conditions_covered: Non-neurogenic Female Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms
Pelvic organ prolapse and lower urinary tract symptoms
target_population: Women with non-neurogenic lower urinary tract symptoms
therapeutic_areas: bladder wall injection of botulinum toxin A

toxicities.event: Dry mouth
recognition: Dry mouth is the most frequently reported adverse effect of anticholinergic treatment.
ER formulations have lower dry-mouth rates than IR formulations. Transdermal oxybutynin has a lower rate than oxybutynin IR and tolterodine ER.
prevention: Consider ER anticholinergic formulations whenever possible.

toxicities.event: Cognitive dysfunction and cumulative anticholinergic effects
recognition: Anticholinergics produced significantly more cognitive impairment than placebo in the Panel's systematic review.
Oxybutynin IR may cause or aggravate cognitive dysfunction. Evidence about the long-term effects of OAB-specific anticholinergics remains limited.

In older women, cognitive effects from drugs with anticholinergic properties are cumulative and increase with exposure duration. Whether medication-related cognitive dysfunction directly predicts later dementia remains unclear.
prevention: Use long-term anticholinergic treatment cautiously in older women, particularly those with existing cognitive dysfunction or at risk of it.
Assess mental function when starting anticholinergics in older patients and monitor it during treatment.
Assess cumulative anticholinergic burden and associated co-morbidity when considering anticholinergic treatment for OAB.

toxicities.event: Constipation and other anticholinergic adverse effects
recognition: The Panel's systematic review found significantly more constipation and UTI with antimuscarinics than with placebo.
IR preparations generally produce more adverse effects than ER preparations; higher anticholinergic doses improve OAB symptoms but increase adverse-effect risk.
prevention: Counsel patients about potential adverse effects and review efficacy and adverse effects early after treatment begins.

toxicities.event: Adverse-event-related discontinuation of anticholinergic treatment
toxicities.incidence: In the RCT summary, relative risks of discontinuation due to adverse events were Darifenacin: 1.2 (0.8–1.8); Fesoterodine: 2.0 (1.3–3.1); Oxybutynin (includes IR): 1.7 (1.1–2.5); Propiverine (includes IR): 2.6 (1.4–5); Solifenacin: 1.3 (1.1–1.7); Tolterodine (includes IR): 1.0 (0.6–1.7); and Trospium (includes IR): 1.5 (1.1–1.9).
recognition: Reported reasons for poor adherence included adverse events (22.4%), inadequate efficacy (41.3%) and cost (18.7%).
prevention: Review patients early for treatment efficacy and adverse effects.

toxicities.event: Skin reactions leading to treatment withdrawal
recognition: Withdrawal because of skin reactions is more frequent with transdermal oxybutynin despite its lower dry-mouth rate than oxybutynin IR and tolterodine ER.

toxicities.event: Hypertension and other reported adverse events
toxicities.incidence: Among mirabegron recipients, hypertension occurred in 7.3%, nasopharyngitis in 3.4% and UTI in 3%; the overall adverse-event rate was similar to placebo.
recognition: Trials assessing cardiac and ocular outcomes excluded patients with uncontrolled hypertension or cardiac arrhythmia.

toxicities.event: Voiding dysfunction, increased PVR volume and possible need for CISC
toxicities.incidence: Compared with placebo, voiding dysfunction was significantly more frequent after both the 100 unit dose and the 200 unit dose; compared with antimuscarinics, voiding dysfunction was also significantly more frequent. A numerical incidence was not provided.
recognition: PVR volume may rise after bladder-wall injection, and some patients may require CISC.
In elderly and frail elderly patients, success may be lower and PVR volume (> 150 mL) higher.

management.actions: CISC may be required, potentially for a prolonged period.

prevention: Before treatment, explain the possibility of prolonged CISC.

toxicities.event: UTI and bacteriuria after bladder-wall injection
toxicities.incidence: UTI rates were significantly higher than placebo at both the 100-unit dose and the 200-unit dose and significantly higher than with antimuscarinics; no numerical rate was given. Bacteriuria risk after onabotA (100 U) was described as high, with uncertain clinical significance.
recognition: UTI is among the principal adverse events reported after onabotA 100 U injection.
prevention: Explain the risk of UTI before offering treatment.

toxicities.event: Implant complications and surgical revision
toxicities.incidence: In the ROSETTA trial, SNS had a 9% removal rate and a 3% revision rate at two-years follow-up. In the INSITE trial, adverse events affected 30% of the SNS arm at six months; implant-site infection and lead migration each affected 3.4% of cases. A separate review reported adverse events in 50% of implanted cases and surgical revision in 33–41%.
recognition: Potential implant problems include lead displacement, malfunction, battery wear and implant-site infection.
In a series of women treated for obstruction-associated retention, more serious events were associated with one-stage than two-stage implantation.
prevention: Provide lifelong surveillance of women with an SNS implant for lead displacement, malfunction and battery wear.

toxicities.event: Short- and long-term complications of augmentation cystoplasty
toxicities.incidence: A review with five to seventeen years of follow-up reported short-term bowel obstruction (2%), infection (1.5%), thromboembolism (1%), bleeding (0.75%) and fistula (0.4%). Long-term findings included need for CISC (38%), asymptomatic bacteriuria (70%), changed bowel symptoms (25%), UTI (20%), metabolic disturbances (16%), urinary tract stones (13%), deteriorating renal function (2%) and bladder perforation (0.75%). Malignant transformation was reported in other series, with almost all reported cases arising beyond ten years after surgery.
recognition: Bladder emptying may remain inadequate after surgery.
A small long-term risk of malignancy requires surveillance.
prevention: Explain potential complications and the high likelihood of needing CISC before surgery; establish that the patient is willing and able to perform it.
Arrange lifelong surveillance, including cystoscopic surveillance because of malignancy risk.
Provide specialist stoma or continence-nurse support before and after major surgery.

toxicities.event: Gastrointestinal, central nervous system and mental-health adverse effects
toxicities.incidence: Two open-label studies reported nausea and vomiting in > 40% of patients. A meta-analysis of four RCTs involving 1,910 women with SUI suggested adverse-event-related discontinuation in around one in seven. In an RCT of women with MUI, treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 61.3% of the duloxetine group and discontinuation in 15.7%.
recognition: Reported effects include nausea, vomiting, dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, insomnia, somnolence and fatigue.
Mental-health problems and suicidal ideation are identified as potential harms. The cited meta-analysis of four SUI trials reported no suicidality, violence or akathisia events.
Adverse-event rates were higher among participants also taking other antidepressant agents.
prevention: Carefully counsel selected patients about adverse-event risks before prescribing.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Initiate and withdraw duloxetine using dose titration because of the high risk of adverse events.

toxicities.event: Hyponatraemia
recognition: Risk increases with age and with a lower baseline serum sodium concentration.
A pooled analysis of three RCTs reported that most patients tolerated treatment without clinically significant hyponatraemia.
prevention: Monitor serum sodium carefully in older patients receiving desmopressin.
Avoid desmopressin when baseline serum sodium is below the normal range.
Counsel patients about hyponatraemia before treatment.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Avoid prescribing desmopressin when baseline serum sodium is below the normal range.

toxicities.event: Gastrointestinal upset, blurred vision, bronchospasm and bradycardia
recognition: The cited review described potentially frequent or serious adverse effects alongside a lack of supportive evidence for UAB treatment.
prevention: Do not routinely recommend parasympathomimetics for women with UAB.

toxicities.event: Adverse effects of urinary catheterisation
recognition: Indwelling catheters can be associated with UTI, stones and urethral injury.
Catheter-related bladder discomfort may be substantial in women.
In the reviewed non-randomised studies, suprapubic and urethral drainage did not differ in UTI or UUT outcomes, but urethral complications were less likely with suprapubic catheters.

management.severity: Need for drainage when CISC cannot be performed or other drainage approaches have failed or are unsuitable
management.actions: An indwelling catheter may be considered; suprapubic catheterisation may reduce urethral trauma and pain compared with urethral catheterisation.

prevention: Teach prospective CISC users its technique, frequency, equipment and potential harms.
Individualise catheterisation frequency to avoid repeated or chronic bladder overfilling.

toxicities.event: Complications of synthetic mid-urethral slings
toxicities.incidence: The ESTER review reported bladder perforation of 5% with retropubic MUS versus 0.2% with transobturator MUS. Groin pain was reported as 6.3% versus 1.3% for transobturator versus retropubic MUS. Tape or mesh exposure or extrusion was 2.1% versus 2.4% for retropubic versus transobturator MUS. A UK study following > 92,000 patients reported complications in 9.8% using a broader definition and longer follow-up.
recognition: Reported complications include bladder perforation, voiding dysfunction, groin or suprapubic pain, mesh exposure or erosion, recurrent infection and sexual difficulties.
The guideline notes limited detail about long-term complications and that their frequency may exceed that suggested by the published medical literature.
prevention: Discuss procedure-specific harms and alternatives as part of informed, shared decision-making.
Follow applicable national or local rules governing mesh surgery.

toxicities.event: Complications of single-incision slings
toxicities.incidence: In a comparative RCT at 36 months, groin or thigh pain occurred in 14.1% with single-incision slings and 14.9% with MUS. During 36-month follow-up, tape or mesh exposure occurred in 3.3% versus 1.9%, and further SUI surgery in 2.5% versus 1.1%, respectively. Among 290 questionnaire respondents, dyspareunia was reported by 11.7% in the single-incision group and 4.8% in the MUS group.
recognition: Mesh exposure, repeat SUI surgery and dyspareunia were more frequent at 3 years with the single-incision devices evaluated.
Long-term efficacy remains uncertain, and different single-incision devices should not be assumed to have identical safety profiles.
prevention: Explain the uncertainty about long-term efficacy when offering a single-incision sling.

toxicities.event: Voiding dysfunction and prolapse after SUI surgery
toxicities.incidence: The ESTER review reported voiding difficulties of 7.5% after laparoscopic colposuspension versus 5.1% after retropubic MUS. In another comparison, voiding difficulties were 15.4% after autologous sling versus 10.2% after retropubic MUS. At five years, enterocoele/vault/cervical prolapse occurred in 42% after Burch colposuspension versus 23% after TVT, and rectocele in 49% versus 32%.
recognition: Autologous sling may cause postoperative outlet obstruction.
Colposuspension has a greater long-term POP risk than MUS; postoperative voiding dysfunction is an important complication of sling surgery.
prevention: Discuss relative benefits and complications of the available SUI operations before surgery.

toxicities.event: Embolism and local abscess associated with urethral bulking materials
recognition: Autologous fat is linked to a risk of fatal embolism; hyaluronic acid is linked to local abscess formation.
prevention: Do not offer autologous fat or hyaluronic acid as urethral bulking agents.

toxicities.event: Urinary retention and UTI after urethral bulking
toxicities.incidence: In one small trial, retention followed peri-urethral injection in 30% (six out of 20) versus 5% (one out of 20) after transurethral injection.
recognition: UTI is described as the most frequent adverse event after bulking-agent injection.
The peri-urethral route may carry a greater retention risk than the transurethral route.
prevention: Discuss lower efficacy, likely need for repeat injection and uncertain long-term safety before treatment.

toxicities.event: Complications of external urethral compression devices
toxicities.incidence: In a review of ACT® studies, explantation occurred in 19–31%. AUS case series reported mechanical failure requiring revision in < 42% at ten years and explantation in 5.9–15%. A separate AUS review reported explantation of 0–45%, erosion of 0–22% and mechanical failure of 0–44%.
recognition: Complications, mechanical failure and explantation can occur even in expert centres.
Older age, previous Burch colposuspension and pelvic radiotherapy were reported as risk factors for AUS failure.
prevention: Tell patients considering AUS or ACT® that cure is possible but complications, mechanical failure and device removal remain substantial risks.

toxicities.event: Complications after combined POP and anti-incontinence surgery
toxicities.incidence: Across pooled RCTs, surgical adverse events occurred in 28% after combined surgery versus 15% after POP surgery alone (RR: 1.8). Serious adverse events, including bladder perforation, urethral injury and tape exposure, occurred in 14% versus 8% (RR: 1.7).
recognition: Combined treatment may increase voiding difficulties despite reducing postoperative SUI.
prevention: Offer simultaneous POP and SUI surgery only after discussing its benefits and risks relative to POP surgery alone.
Explain the increased adverse-event risk of combined surgery.

toxicities.event: Complications of procedures for female BOO
associated_therapies: transurethral incision of the bladder neck
toxicities.incidence: In a series of 84 bladder-neck-incision patients, VVF occurred in 3.6%, SUI in 4.7% and urethral stricture in 3.6%; another review reported postoperative SUI in 3– 33%. In a study of transurethral bladder-neck incision for refractory DU, SUI developed in five (6.1%) patients and vesico-vaginal fistula in two (2.4%). One urethrolysis study reported de novo SUI in 39%.
recognition: Urethral dilatation may be followed by new or worsened SUI, urgency or frequency.
Urethroplasty can be followed by recurrent stricture; urethrolysis and sling revision can be followed by recurrent SUI.
Persistent postoperative bladder symptoms were associated with a longer delay before urethrolysis in one study.
prevention: Explain the potential need for repeated intervention after urethral dilatation.
Warn patients undergoing bladder neck incision about postoperative SUI, vesico-vaginal fistula and urethral stricture.
Monitor for recurrent stricture after urethral dilatation, urethrotomy or urethroplasty.

toxicities.event: Complications of intraurethral inserts
toxicities.incidence: In a study of 92 women, the device was removed within seven days in 60% because of discomfort, peri-catheter leakage or technical problems; an additional 20% discontinued later. Migration into the bladder occurred in six cases and symptomatic UTI in four cases.
recognition: Discomfort, leakage around the device, technical difficulty, migration and symptomatic UTI were reported.
prevention: Do not offer an intraurethral device to women with BOO.

toxicities.event: Complications following urinary fistula repair
recognition: Potential outcomes include persistent or recurrent fistula or UI; new or continuing LUTS; wound infection, UTI or urosepsis; ureteric obstruction; BOO; bladder contracture; vaginal stenosis; sexual dysfunction; neurological or psychological complications; and infertility.
prevention: Maintain continuous bladder drainage after repair until healing is confirmed.
Provide appropriate skin care, nutrition, rehabilitation, counselling and support before and after repair.

toxicities.event: Complications after urethral diverticulectomy
toxicities.incidence: Reported early complications included UTI (0–39%), de novo SUI (3.8–33%) and de novo urinary retention (0–9%). Delayed urethral stricture occurred in 0–5.2%, and urethro-vaginal fistula in 0.9–8.3%.
recognition: Persistent or newly developed urgency, UUI or other LUTS may indicate persistent or recurrent diverticulum, de novo OAB or urethral obstruction.
A distal fistula beyond the sphincter may cause a split stream or vaginal voiding; a fistula between the mid-urethra and bladder neck may cause UI.

management.actions: Repair may be undertaken with consideration of an additional tissue flap, such as a Martius flap; timing is not established, although the guideline describes a delay of three to six months as a balance between discomfort and tissue quality.

prevention: Before diverticulectomy, counsel patients about recurrence and persistent or de novo LUTS, including UI.

Do not use a concomitant synthetic MUS at diverticulectomy because synthetic material beside a fresh suture line and potentially infected urine may increase erosion, extrusion, fistula and granuloma risks.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Offer prophylactic antibiotics only after discussing the risk of increasing antimicrobial resistance; the cited trials reported fewer symptomatic UTIs, while possible harms were not assessed in the Cochrane review.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients using CISC or an indwelling catheter who have recurrent UTI.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not routinely place ureteric stents to prevent injury during routine gynaecological surgery; the cited RCT did not show a reduction in ureteric injury.
Do not offer concomitant anti-incontinence surgery during abdominal prolapse surgery when neither symptomatic nor occult SUI is present.
prophylaxis.target_population: Women requiring surgery for bothersome POP without symptomatic or occult SUI.

prophylaxis.recommendation: During the period between fistula diagnosis and repair, UI pads may be provided to help prevent skin complications from ongoing leakage; barrier cream or local oestrogen may also be considered.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients awaiting urinary fistula repair who have persistent urinary leakage.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Keep the bladder continuously drained until healing is confirmed.
prophylaxis.duration: Expert opinion suggests ten to fourteen days for simple and/or post-surgical fistulae and fourteen to 21 days for complex and/or post-radiation fistulae.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Individualise CISC frequency according to need and ability so that chronic or repeated bladder overfilling is avoided.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients performing CISC for incomplete bladder emptying or urinary retention.

infection_management.management: When UTI accompanies LUTS, reassess the patient after treatment. Urinalysis is part of initial LUTS assessment, with urine culture when necessary.
Do not routinely treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in older patients to improve UI. In nursing-home residents, eradication did not change UI frequency or severity.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Recurrent UTI during CISC or indwelling catheterisation
infection_management.prevention: Prophylactic antibiotics may reduce symptomatic UTI, but increasing antimicrobial resistance is a concern; offer them only after discussion of that risk in patients with recurrent UTI.
Explain the increased UTI risk before offering injection.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: UTI associated with indwelling urinary catheterisation
infection_management.prevention: Reserve indwelling transurethral catheterisation or suprapubic cystostomy for situations in which other drainage approaches have failed or are unsuitable.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Wound infection, UTI or urosepsis following fistula repair
infection_management.prevention: Maintain continuous postoperative bladder drainage until healing is confirmed.

conditions.name: Overactive bladder
conditions.description: A chronic, symptom-defined condition involving urinary urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia, with or without UUI, when UTI or another evident pathology is absent. DO is a characteristic urodynamic finding but is not required for diagnosis.
conditions.epidemiology: The EPidemiology of InContinence (EPIC) study reported OAB symptoms in 11.8% of adults overall, including 12.8% of women and 10.8% of men.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Urgency, frequency and nocturia may occur with or without UUI. Symptoms can substantially affect QoL.

subtypes.name: OAB wet
subtypes.distinguishing_features: OAB accompanied by UI.

subtypes.name: OAB dry
subtypes.distinguishing_features: OAB without associated UI.

diagnostic_workup.test: Clinical history and focused physical examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise LUTS, associated conditions and medication use, and assess for alternative explanations.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Diagnosis rests on symptoms rather than a urodynamic demonstration of DO.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure frequency, urgency and UI and document changes over time.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial evaluation and assessment of treatment response.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The OAB-specific recommendation calls for at least a three-day diary; the general LUTS recommendation specifies a duration of > 3 days.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess for UTI and other urinary abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Absence of nitrite and leukocyte esterase may exclude bacteriuria in women with LUTS.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish whether DO is present or obtain findings that might alter an invasive treatment decision.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Not routine before first-line treatment of uncomplicated OAB; considered when results could change invasive treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Failure to demonstrate DO does not exclude OAB, and a urodynamic diagnosis of DO does not predict treatment response.

diagnostic_workup.test: Urinary biomarkers and urinary microbiota assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigated as potential diagnostic measures.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Not recommended for routine diagnosis or management.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Evidence is insufficient or conflicting; studies of uNGF, BDNF to creatinine ratio and uNGF to creatinine ratio found increases in women with OAB compared with healthy controls, whereas PGE2/ Cr and ATP/Cr ratios did not differ.

follow_up.schedule: Follow-up depends on the treatment and local service capacity. Arrange early review after starting anticholinergic or beta-3 agonist therapy; further schedules depend on the intervention.
recommended_tests: Review efficacy and adverse effects early after starting anticholinergic medication.
Monitor PVR volume during treatments that may produce or worsen voiding dysfunction.
For an SNS implant, maintain life-long surveillance for lead displacement, malfunction and battery wear.
After augmentation cystoplasty, provide lifelong follow-up, including cystoscopic surveillance because of the small malignancy risk.
long_term_effects: Repeated onabotulinumtoxinA injections may remain effective, although treatment discontinuation can occur.
Long-term anticholinergic exposure in older women is associated with concern about cumulative cognitive effects.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Further onabotulinumtoxinA injections may be offered when previous injections were effective, subject to the manufacturer's minimum interval guidance.

conditions.name: OAB wet
conditions.description: The form of Overactive bladder accompanied by UI.
conditions.clinical_presentation: OAB symptoms occur together with urine leakage.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Quantify urgency, frequency and UI episodes.

diagnostic_workup.test: Clinical history and focused physical examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the pattern of leakage and distinguish associated or alternative causes of LUTS.

conditions.name: OAB dry
conditions.description: The form of Overactive bladder without associated UI.
conditions.clinical_presentation: OAB symptoms occur without urinary incontinence.

diagnostic_workup.test: Clinical history and focused physical examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise urgency and accompanying LUTS and assess for other causes.
Quantify frequency and urgency.

conditions.name: Stress urinary incontinence
conditions.description: Involuntary urine loss during effort or physical exertion. Urethral hypermobility and intrinsic sphincter deficiency are described as common, sometimes overlapping mechanisms.
conditions.epidemiology: SUI prevalence appears highest at ages 45–59 years. A meta-analysis of six studies comprising 3,678 cases reported a threefold SUI risk in women with metabolic syndrome compared with women without it. Reported associations include parity, obesity, previous hysterectomy or pelvic surgery, diabetes mellitus and pulmonary disease; findings concerning ethnicity conflict.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Leakage accompanies exertion and can be demonstrated with a cough stress test. Associated voiding symptoms, POP, substantial OAB/UUI or prior pelvic treatment affect whether the presentation is classified as complicated.

subtypes.name: Women with uncomplicated SUI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: No previous SUI operation, extensive pelvic surgery or pelvic radiotherapy; no neurogenic LUT dysfunction, bothersome genitourinary prolapse, voiding symptoms or medical condition affecting the LUT.

subtypes.name: Women with complicated SUI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Includes previous incontinence or extensive pelvic surgery, pelvic irradiation, anterior or apical POP, voiding symptoms, neurogenic LUT dysfunction, substantial OAB/UUI or congenital abnormalities such as bladder exstrophy.

subtypes.name: urethral hypermobility
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Loss of bladder-neck and urethral support permits displacement of the urethra during increased intra-abdominal pressure.

subtypes.name: intrinsic sphincter deficiency
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Weakness of the urinary sphincter itself, potentially following trauma, radiotherapy, pelvic surgery, neurological disease or ageing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish probable SUI, identify complicated features and determine whether specialist referral is needed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Substantial additional storage symptoms, particularly OAB, warrant consideration of MUI.

diagnostic_workup.test: Abdominal, vaginal, perineal and neuro-urological examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess associated POP, PFM strength and other relevant findings.
Demonstrate stress-related leakage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of women presenting with SUI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A standing test is more sensitive than a supine test. The ICS standardisation describes a supine/lithotomy test with 200–400 mL in the bladder and one to four coughs.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess symptoms, severity, associated bother or treatment-related change.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Questionnaires do not replace the clinical consultation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess bladder emptying, especially when voiding symptoms or complicated SUI are present.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment and before treatments that might impair voiding, including SUI surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Most women with SUI do not have significant PVR volume; ultrasound and catheter measurements correlate well in the cited cohort of > 900 women.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify diagnosis or findings that could influence invasive treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider when storage symptoms coexist, incontinence type is uncertain, voiding dysfunction is suspected, POP is present, previous SUI surgery has occurred or findings could change treatment; not routine for uncomplicated, clinically demonstrable SUI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Preoperative testing has not improved surgical outcomes in uncomplicated, clinically demonstrable SUI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Quantify urine loss or assess response to treatment when quantification is required.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Use a standardised activity and duration protocol; a 1-hour exercise test threshold of 1.4 g has good specificity but lower sensitivity for SUI and MUI symptoms, whereas a 24-hour threshold of 4.4 g is more reproducible but harder to standardise.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate selected anatomical questions rather than routinely diagnose SUI.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Not part of routine SUI assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: No imaging test has been shown to predict SUI treatment outcome.

follow_up.schedule: Allow sufficient time to assess conservative or physical therapy; review pharmacological treatment early and arrange short-term postoperative review after most operations.
recommended_tests: Assess treatment efficacy and early postoperative complications.
Monitor PVR volume if treatment may cause or aggravate voiding dysfunction.
long_term_effects: Late surgical complications and recurrence warrant assessment; the guideline notes limited high-quality long-term complication data.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The Panel supports long-term outcome assessment through registries.

conditions.name: Women with uncomplicated SUI
conditions.description: A clinical category of SUI without previous SUI surgery, extensive pelvic surgery or pelvic radiotherapy, neurogenic LUT dysfunction, bothersome genitourinary prolapse, voiding symptoms or another medical condition affecting the LUT.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Stress-related leakage can be elicited on examination without the listed complicating features. Significant accompanying storage symptoms, especially OAB, raise the possibility of MUI.

diagnostic_workup.test: Clinical history, physical examination and standardised cough stress test
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish clinically demonstrable SUI and exclude complicated features.
Investigate only when findings could change invasive treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Not routinely required before surgery for uncomplicated, clinically demonstrable SUI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The cited trials did not show improved surgical outcomes from routine preoperative testing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess emptying and establish a baseline before treatment that could worsen voiding.

follow_up.schedule: Postoperative short-term follow-up assesses benefit and early complications; subsequent follow-up depends on treatment.
recommended_tests: Assess continence and postoperative voiding problems.
long_term_effects: Recurrence and procedure-related complications may emerge later.

conditions.name: Women with complicated SUI
conditions.description: A category of SUI with features such as previous incontinence or extensive pelvic surgery, pelvic irradiation, anterior or apical POP, voiding symptoms, neurogenic LUT dysfunction, significant OAB/UUI or congenital abnormalities.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Stress-related leakage occurs alongside at least one complicating clinical feature; after prior SUI surgery, leakage can reflect persistent or recurrent SUI, newly developed UUI, or both.

subtypes.name: recurrent SUI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Stress-related incontinence recurring after an earlier SUI procedure; second-line procedures are generally less effective than primary procedures.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise prior treatment, symptoms, POP and patient-specific factors.

diagnostic_workup.test: Urodynamics, including multichannel urodynamics where appropriate
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify persistent or recurrent SUI, de novo UUI, voiding dysfunction and factors relevant to further invasive treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider with associated storage symptoms, uncertain incontinence type, suspected voiding dysfunction, POP or previous SUI surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The preferred operation for recurrent SUI cannot be established firmly from the available comparative evidence.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide further investigation when selecting surgery for recurrent SUI.
Identify impaired emptying and monitor interventions that could worsen it.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly relevant in complicated SUI or when voiding symptoms are present.

follow_up.schedule: Follow-up depends on the intervention; early postoperative assessment is needed after most surgical procedures.
recommended_tests: Assess continence, voiding function and complications after surgery.
long_term_effects: Repeat procedures may have lower efficacy and greater complication risk than first-line surgery.

conditions.name: Mixed urinary incontinence
conditions.description: An incontinence category encompassing combinations of stress and urgency symptoms. Presentations may have equal components, a predominant component, or differing relationships between clinical symptoms and DO.
conditions.epidemiology: Most cited studies report MUI prevalence of 7.5–25%, making it apparently the second most common UI form after SUI; approximately one-third of women with UI may have MUI. In a secondary analysis involving 655 women, questionnaire-based categorisation identified MUI in 50−90%, whereas objective criteria identified it in only 8%. Population estimates are limited by differing definitions and study methods.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Stress leakage and urgency-related symptoms coexist in varying proportions. Women with MUI generally have more severe symptoms and respond less well to treatment than women with only SUI or UUI.

subtypes.name: stress-predominant MUI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Stress symptoms predominate over urgency symptoms.

subtypes.name: urgency-predominant MUI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Urgency symptoms predominate over stress symptoms.

subtypes.name: USUI with DO
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Urodynamic stress urinary incontinence occurs together with DO.

subtypes.name: USUI with clinical urgency symptoms, but no DO
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Urodynamic stress urinary incontinence coexists with reported urgency without demonstrated DO.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise both symptom components and identify the most bothersome one.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Classify the presentation as stress-predominant or urgency-predominant when possible.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document frequency and patterns of leakage and support management decisions.
Characterise demonstrable SUI and DO to assist counselling and treatment selection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As part of multimodal MUI assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: There is no evidence that urodynamic assessment changes MUI treatment outcomes.

recommended_tests: Assess both stress and urgency symptom components after treatment.
long_term_effects: The response of pre-existing urgency to SUI surgery is unpredictable.
SUI surgery is less likely to cure overall UI in women with MUI than in women with SUI alone.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: One treatment may not resolve every component of MUI.

conditions.name: Underactive bladder
conditions.description: A symptom-defined condition involving a slow stream, hesitancy and straining, with possible incomplete emptying or storage symptoms. It differs from the urodynamic diagnosis of DU.
conditions.epidemiology: Reported prevalence in women ranges from 12-45%, varies with diagnostic definitions and increases with age. In a survey of 15,861 women aged > 40 years, 20.1% reported weak flow, 27.4% incomplete emptying and 38.3% terminal dribbling; these are symptom estimates rather than a confirmed UAB prevalence.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Slow or interrupted stream, hesitancy, straining, incomplete emptying and post-micturition dribble may accompany nocturia, daytime frequency and urgency.

subtypes.name: idiopathic DU
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Reduced detrusor contractility without another identifiable cause; it may be partly age-dependent but can also occur in younger women.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify voiding and accompanying storage symptoms.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: No single symptom or symptom combination reliably identifies DU.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Capture patient-reported UAB symptoms for research.
Identify reduced urinary flow that may indicate impaired emptying.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Flow findings alone cannot reliably distinguish DU from BOO.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess residual urine and voiding efficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Evaluation of incomplete emptying and monitoring when relevant.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: No agreed threshold for abnormal PVR volume in women is established. BVE = voided volume (VV)/(VV+PVR) × 100.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish DU from BOO and identify their possible coexistence.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When the cause of voiding dysfunction needs clarification.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: No consensus exists on Qmax, PdetQmax, PVR volume or BVE thresholds for DU.

staging.additional_rules: The guideline identifies no established UAB classification system or sufficiently supported prognostic stratification.

follow_up.schedule: The interval depends on patient characteristics, treatment and frequency of urinary complications; long-term natural history is not well established.
recommended_tests: Assess bladder emptying and urinary complications according to clinical circumstances.
long_term_effects: High PVR volume and incomplete emptying can be associated with UTI, UUT deterioration, bladder stones and overflow UI.

conditions.name: Detrusor underactivity
conditions.description: A urodynamic finding of a detrusor contraction with insufficient strength and/or duration, producing prolonged or incomplete bladder emptying within the usual time.
conditions.epidemiology: Ambulatory studies reported DU prevalence of around 12–19% in women. Estimates depend on the diagnostic criteria used; one study of 1,015 women identified DU in 14.9%, 9.6% or 6.4% under three different definitions.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Reduced or interrupted stream, hesitancy, incomplete emptying, a palpable bladder and reduced sensation may occur, but symptoms overlap with BOO and cannot establish DU on their own.

subtypes.name: Acontractile detrusor
subtypes.distinguishing_features: No detrusor contraction can be measured.

subtypes.name: detrusor hyperactivity with impaired contractility
subtypes.distinguishing_features: DO during filling coexists with DU during voiding; a study reported this finding in over 30% of elderly women.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen for poor emptying and possible DU.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Similar findings can occur in BOO. One study defined a DU group using PdetQmax < 20 cm H2O, Qmax < 15 mL/s and BVE < 90%, with no obstruction on video-urodynamics; these are study criteria, not a consensus definition.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish DU from BOO and assess detrusor contraction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a reliable distinction between these causes is needed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: DU and BOO may coexist. Women may void by relaxing the pelvic floor without a detectable detrusor contraction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate detrusor power per unit of bladder surface.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: WFmax varies during voiding; the table reports WFmax 11-24 W/m2 for ideal voiding and WFmax 5−10 W/m2 for non-ideal voiding in eight asymptomatic female volunteers, and WFmax > 7 W/m2 as expert opinion for an unspecified population.

diagnostic_workup.test: Projected isovolumetric pressure (PIP) and bladder contractility index (BCI)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate isovolumetric detrusor pressure or express it as an index.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The reported formula is PdetQmax + 5xQmax; these measures were developed mainly in men and lack agreed female diagnostic thresholds.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate isovolumetric detrusor pressure using a measure developed in women.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The reported formula is pdetQmax + Qmax. In 100 women with UUI, the 5th-95th percentile was 29–78 cm H2O, with proposed typical values of 30-75 cm H2O.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure isovolumetric voiding contraction directly.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The reported Mean ± SD was 48.7 ± 24.4 cm H2O in 70 women with UUI.

staging.additional_rules: No consensus defines normal or abnormal contraction-strength values for diagnosing DU.

prognostic_tools.name: BCI
prognostic_tools.interpretation: These expert-opinion contraction categories come from a population described as mainly men with BPO; they are not a validated female prognostic system.

follow_up.schedule: Individualise visits according to clinical characteristics, treatment and urinary complications; longitudinal natural-history data are lacking.
recommended_tests: Monitor emptying and complications according to clinical need.
long_term_effects: Persistently poor emptying may contribute to UTI, UUT deterioration, bladder stones and overflow UI.

conditions.name: Bladder outlet obstruction
conditions.description: Obstruction during voiding characterised by raised detrusor pressure and reduced urine flow. Female BOO requires pressure–flow evaluation for precise diagnosis and is distinct from the broader category of voiding dysfunction.
conditions.epidemiology: Estimates among women range from 2.7-29% because definitions and study populations differ. A large LUTS referral series reported BOO in ~20% of women. In a series of 1,142 women referred for LUTS assessment, excess daytime frequency was reported by 69% of those with BOO.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Storage as well as voiding symptoms may occur. Presentation can include recurrent UTI, chronic retention or acute/chronic kidney disease.

subtypes.name: Anatomical BOO
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A physical or mechanical impediment to urinary outflow, such as urethral stricture, anti-incontinence surgery, POP, diverticulum, caruncle, malignancy or a paraurethral mass.

subtypes.name: Functional BOO
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Non-anatomical, non-neurogenic outflow obstruction associated with failure of relaxation or increased tone of the bladder neck, sphincter or PFMs.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify symptoms, complications and possible mechanical or functional causes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: History and examination alone do not establish the diagnosis accurately.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess flow and incomplete bladder emptying.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Flow studies alone cannot accurately diagnose female BOO because DU can produce similar findings.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Look for complications such as UUT dilatation or hydronephrosis and assess anatomical features.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When complications or relevant anatomy require assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Ultrasound alone cannot accurately diagnose BOO in women.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess peri-urethral fibrosis associated with pathological urethral stricture.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The clinical and prognostic value of detected fibrosis is not established.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess sphincter or PFM activity and help differentiate anatomical from functional obstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected cases, in conjunction with pressure–flow testing.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: EMG alone cannot diagnose BOO accurately; abnormal urethral activity may also be seen in asymptomatic volunteers.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Visualise an anatomical obstruction and establish its site and calibre.
Confirm BOO and distinguish it from DU.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Low flow accompanied by high detrusor pressure supports obstruction, but there is no universally accepted female threshold.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Localise obstruction and examine its anatomical or functional pattern.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When localisation or additional diagnostic clarification is needed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Imaging may show a tight bladder neck, urethral narrowing with proximal dilatation, or obstruction during sustained detrusor contraction.

definitions.description: Urinary outflow is physically or mechanically impeded, rather than obstructed by urethral or pelvic muscle tone.
Outflow is obstructed without an anatomical or neurogenic cause through failure of relaxation or increased tone in the bladder neck, sphincter complex or PFMs.

staging.additional_rules: These are classification categories rather than severity stages. Neurological causes of functional obstruction are outside this guideline's scope.

prognostic_tools.name: Solomon–Greenwell nomogram
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The document reports these probability categories without specifying an interpretation for values between 0 and 5 or at the stated boundaries.

prognostic_tools.name: Blaivas-Groutz nomogram
prognostic_tools.interpretation: A commonly used female BOO nomogram; it may overestimate obstruction, and evidence supporting clinical validity is limited.

follow_up.schedule: Monitor regularly for worsening voiding or renal function and, after treatment, for recurrent obstruction.
recommended_tests: Monitor for stricture recurrence after urethral dilatation, urethrotomy or urethroplasty.
long_term_effects: Persistent or progressive obstruction can worsen voiding or renal function.

conditions.name: Anatomical BOO
conditions.description: Female BOO caused by a physical or mechanical barrier to urine outflow rather than by abnormal muscle tone.
conditions.epidemiology: A retrospective series of 192 women with BOO found mechanical obstruction in 64%. Another study reported a substantially different anatomical-to-functional distribution, illustrating inconsistency across study populations.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Voiding and storage symptoms may accompany obstruction caused by urethral disease, prior continence surgery, POP or a mass.

subtypes.name: urethral stricture
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Pathological urethral narrowing, potentially involving fibrosis.

subtypes.name: BOO due to POP
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Prolapse may kink or compress the urethra.

subtypes.name: BOO after mid-urethral sling
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Obstructed voiding follows placement of an anti-incontinence tape or sling.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inspect the urethra and vagina for a mechanical cause.
Inspect the obstruction and define its nature, location and calibre.
Assess calibre in suspected pathological urethral stricture.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Published calibre thresholds vary from 14-20 Fr.

diagnostic_workup.test: Pressure–flow studies with video-urodynamics where needed
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm obstruction and define its site.
Characterise peri-urethral fibrosis in pathological stricture.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The prognostic significance of the fibrosis finding is uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess consequences such as hydronephrosis.

staging.additional_rules: Anatomical BOO is one of the guideline's two principal female BOO categories.

follow_up.schedule: Regular follow-up; specifically monitor recurrence after treatment of urethral stricture.
recommended_tests: Assess voiding and possible stricture recurrence after dilatation, urethrotomy or urethroplasty.
long_term_effects: Strictures can recur after treatment; persistent obstruction may impair renal function.

conditions.name: Functional BOO
conditions.description: Non-anatomical, non-neurogenic obstruction due to failure of relaxation or increased tone of the bladder neck, urethral sphincter complex or PFMs during voiding.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Voiding difficulty or retention may occur, sometimes with storage symptoms.

subtypes.name: primary bladder neck obstruction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The bladder neck fails to open adequately during voiding without a physical obstruction; an estimated 4.6–16% of women presenting with voiding symptoms have this condition.

subtypes.name: dysfunctional voiding
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Involuntary intermittent contraction of peri-urethral striated or levator muscles during voiding in neurologically normal women produces an intermittent or fluctuating flow.

subtypes.name: idiopathic urinary retention (Fowler’s syndrome)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A high-tone external urethral sphincter fails to relax; retention occurs most often, but not exclusively, in young women.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the pelvic floor as a potential source of functional obstruction.
Demonstrate obstruction and evaluate detrusor and outlet activity.
Locate the functional obstruction and assess bladder-neck opening.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When further anatomical localisation is useful.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An inadequately opening bladder neck may support primary bladder neck obstruction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess failure of sphincter relaxation or abnormal PFM activation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected cases, including suspected Fowler’s syndrome or dysfunctional voiding.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: EMG is useful alongside pressure–flow information but is not independently diagnostic.

staging.additional_rules: Functional BOO is the non-anatomical, non-neurogenic category.

follow_up.schedule: Regular follow-up to detect progression or recurrence after treatment.
recommended_tests: Monitor voiding function and clinically relevant complications.
long_term_effects: Persistent obstruction can contribute to worsening voiding or renal function.

conditions.name: Nocturia
conditions.description: The need to pass urine during the main sleep period after falling asleep and before intending to rise. Its causes may be urological, systemic, behavioural or sleep-related.
conditions.epidemiology: More than 2 nightly episodes occur in 4–18% of women aged 20–40 years and 28–62% of women aged > 70 years. Cited systematic reviews associated nocturia with a 1.2-fold increased risk of falls, possibly an approximately 1.3-fold increased risk of fractures, and probably an ~1.3-fold increased risk of death.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Night-time awakenings to void may accompany polyuria, reduced bladder capacity, storage symptoms or sleep disturbance.

subtypes.name: 24-hour polyuria
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Defined as 24-hour urine production > 40 mL/kg.

subtypes.name: nocturnal polyuria
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A disproportionately large share of 24-hour urine is produced during sleep; age-dependent thresholds range from 20% in younger people to 33% at age > 65 years.

subtypes.name: diminished bladder capacity
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Reduced night-time or overall voided volumes suggest an underlying bladder or outlet condition.

subtypes.name: sleep disorders
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Sleep disturbance can be a primary or secondary contributor to night-time voiding.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess sleep, fluid balance, LUTS, cardiovascular, endocrine and renal conditions, medication and urological history.

diagnostic_workup.test: ICIQ Questionnaire-Nocturia, N-QoL or Nocturia Impact Diary
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess nocturia symptoms and changes with treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment or reassessment using an appropriate validated questionnaire.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen for potential causes of nocturia.
Structure initial questions about Sleep, Cardiovascular, Renal, Endocrine and Neurological function.
Measure voiding patterns and calculate indices that help identify polyuria or reduced bladder capacity.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A nocturnal-only diary cannot identify 24-hour polyuria and has not been validated in women.

diagnostic_workup.test: Renal function, thyroid function, HbA1c and calcium blood tests
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate potential systemic contributors.
Identify possible insomnia, restless legs syndrome/periodic limb movements of sleep or parasomnias.

staging.additional_rules: Clinical classification uses diary findings to distinguish 24-hour polyuria, nocturnal polyuria, diminished bladder capacity and sleep disorders.

prognostic_tools.name: nocturia index
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Calculated by dividing nocturnal urine volume by maximum voided volume to help characterise nocturia.

prognostic_tools.name: nocturnal polyuria index
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Calculated by dividing nocturnal urine volume by 24-hour urine volume; interpretation depends on age.

prognostic_tools.name: nocturnal urine production
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Expresses nocturnal urine volume relative to sleep duration.

follow_up.schedule: Individualise according to the underlying cause and treatment.
recommended_tests: Use a validated questionnaire for reassessment during and/or after treatment.
Monitor serum sodium concentration carefully in older patients receiving desmopressin.
long_term_effects: Risk of hyponatraemia with desmopressin increases with age and lower baseline serum sodium concentration.

conditions.name: nocturnal polyuria
conditions.description: A cause of nocturia in which an age-dependent, disproportionately high fraction of daily urine volume is produced during sleep.
conditions.epidemiology: In a study of ~2,000 patients receiving treatment for LUT abnormalities, nocturnal polyuria contributed to nocturia in 89%.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Night-time voiding occurs with elevated urine production during the sleep period.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine nocturnal and 24-hour urine volumes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The nocturnal proportion of 24-hour urine has diagnostic thresholds ranging from 20% in younger people to 33% at age > 65 years.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Quantify the proportion of total daily urine produced overnight.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Nocturnal urine volume is divided by 24-hour urine volume.

recommended_tests: Carefully monitor serum sodium concentration in older patients treated with desmopressin.
long_term_effects: Hyponatraemia risk with desmopressin is greater at older ages and with lower baseline serum sodium concentration.

conditions.name: Pelvic organ prolapse
conditions.description: Descent of pelvic organs involving anterior, posterior or apical vaginal compartments. POP and LUTS frequently coexist, although urinary symptoms can change in either direction after prolapse treatment.
conditions.epidemiology: Prevalence is 3–6% using bothersome symptoms as the definition and 50% using an anatomical definition. Estimated lifetime risk of POP surgery is 12.6%. Parity, vaginal delivery, ageing and obesity are recognised risk factors.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A vaginal bulge may accompany LUTS, BOO, UI, bowel dysfunction or sexual dysfunction. More advanced prolapse can mask SUI, which may become evident after prolapse reduction or treatment.

subtypes.name: anterior
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The bladder-associated vaginal compartment.

subtypes.name: posterior
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The rectum-associated vaginal compartment.

subtypes.name: apical
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The cervix or vaginal-vault compartment.

subtypes.name: occult SUI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Stress leakage becomes demonstrable after POP reduction in a woman who did not report SUI symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Diagnose prolapse and stage descent in each vaginal compartment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: If symptoms do not match the supine POP-Q findings, consider standing measurement or assessment later in the day.

diagnostic_workup.test: Cough stress test with POP reduction
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify occult SUI and inform counselling about additional anti-incontinence surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Continent women being assessed before POP surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: SUI can be demonstrated after reduction in up to 30% of women without reported SUI; no best reduction method has been established.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess occult SUI or selected coexisting LUT dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When additional diagnostic information could affect counselling or management.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The clinical value of detecting occult SUI and the role of urodynamics for POP with LUTS other than SUI remain uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate selected discrepancies or associated problems rather than diagnose routine POP.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Not advised as part of routine POP diagnostic assessment.

definitions.description: No prolapse of the assessed compartment.
The lowest point remains 1 cm above the hymen.
Maximum descent lies between 1 cm above and 1 cm below the hymen.
Descent extends beyond 1 cm below the hymen.

staging.additional_rules: POP-Q uses nine measured points and grades the anterior, posterior and apical compartments separately; the hymenal remnant is central to stage assignment.

recommended_tests: Assess urinary symptoms following treatment and consider postoperative SUI, including new-onset SUI.
long_term_effects: SUI may become apparent after POP surgery.
Combined POP and anti-incontinence surgery has higher adverse-event rates than POP surgery alone.

conditions.name: Urinary fistula
conditions.description: An abnormal communication producing urine leakage. The guideline distinguishes obstetric, iatrogenic, radiation-associated and anatomically distinct urinary fistulae.
conditions.epidemiology: According to the WHO, fistulae affect > 2 million women, predominantly in sub-Saharan African and Asian countries; pooled population-study prevalence is 0.29/1000 pregnancies. In developed settings, pelvic or gynaecological surgery is a major cause of VVF.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Urine leakage is usually painless and most often continuous, although position-dependent leakage can be intermittent.

subtypes.name: obstetric fistula
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Fistula associated with childbirth; the WHO-derived classification distinguishes simple and complex presentations.

subtypes.name: iatrogenic fistula
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Usually follows pelvic surgery or related treatment.

subtypes.name: radiation fistula
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Occurs following radiotherapy and generally has poorer repair outcomes than a non-radiated fistula.

subtypes.name: vesico-vaginal fistula
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A bladder-to-vagina fistula, often presenting with persistent urine leakage.

subtypes.name: uretero-vaginal fistula
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An upper urinary tract fistula connecting a ureter to the vagina, often presenting after hysterectomy.

subtypes.name: urethro-vaginal fistulae
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Communication involving the urethra and vagina; it may follow urethral surgery or treatment.

diagnostic_workup.test: Medical history and focused examination with direct visual inspection
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify leakage and assess for a fistula.

diagnostic_workup.test: Cystoscopy and retrograde bladder filling with coloured fluid and vaginal tampon
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify dye passage and help confirm VVF.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A double-dye test can assist distinction between UVF and VVF.

diagnostic_workup.test: Creatinine measurement in leaked or collected fluid
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish whether the fluid is urine.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Creatinine findings can confirm urinary leakage.

diagnostic_workup.test: Contrast-enhanced CT with late excretory phase
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Locate a urinary fistula and examine ureteric integrity and possible urinoma.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Difficult diagnosis or need for additional anatomical information.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide additional anatomical information about a fistula.
Diagnose and locate a fistula.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly when visual inspection or cystoscopy is negative.

definitions.description: A single fistula < 4 cm, including VVF without closing-mechanism or ureteric involvement, circumferential defect or substantial tissue loss, presenting for a first repair.

Features include fistula > 4 cm, multiple or mixed recto-vaginal or cervical fistulae, closing-mechanism involvement, scarring, circumferential defect, extensive tissue loss, intravaginal ureters, previous failed repair or a radiation fistula.

staging.additional_rules: The adapted WHO system was developed initially for obstetric fistula and may also be relevant to iatrogenic cases. Waaldijk and Goh are also named classifications, but their application to iatrogenic fistula is less relevant.

follow_up.schedule: After repair, maintain bladder drainage until healing is confirmed; the guideline's expert-opinion intervals are ten to fourteen days for simple and/or post-surgical fistulae and fourteen to 21 days for complex and/or post-radiation fistulae.
recommended_tests: After upper urinary tract fistula repair, use functional and anatomical imaging to check for ureteric stricture and declining renal function.
Distinguish fistula closure from postoperative UI when documenting outcomes.
long_term_effects: Persistent or recurrent fistula, UI or LUTS, infection, ureteric obstruction, BOO, sexual dysfunction and other physical or psychological complications can follow repair.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Follow-up reporting should specify when fistula closure and postoperative incontinence were assessed.

conditions.name: vesico-vaginal fistula
conditions.description: A urinary fistula between the bladder and vagina. Cases may follow obstetric injury, pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiotherapy.
conditions.epidemiology: A French epidemiological study attributed two thirds of VVF causes to pelvic surgery. Reported risk of pelvic-organ fistula following hysterectomy ranges from 0.1-4%. Surgical VVF repair series report closure rates of 58-100%.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Typically painless and continuous urine leakage; leakage can occasionally depend on position.

subtypes.name: radiation fistula
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Radiotherapy-associated injury may affect a broad tissue field and is associated with poorer repair outcomes.

diagnostic_workup.test: History and vaginal examination with direct visual inspection
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate urine leakage and inspect for a fistula.

diagnostic_workup.test: Cystoscopy and retrograde bladder filling with coloured fluid and vaginal tampon
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Visualise the fistula or detect dye staining.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A double-dye test may help distinguish VVF from UVF.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm that the leakage is urine.

diagnostic_workup.test: Contrast-enhanced CT with late excretory phase or MRI with T2 weighting
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify difficult diagnoses and assess fistula anatomy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Diagnostic uncertainty or need for further information.

definitions.description: Fistula involving the urethra, subdivided according to whether involvement is circumferential.
Fistula involving another portion of the urinary tract.

staging.additional_rules: Waaldijk incorporates fistula size and site. Goh also considers urethral involvement and the degree of fibrosis. Both originated in obstetric fistula assessment.

follow_up.schedule: Keep the bladder drained until repair has healed; expert-opinion durations are ten to fourteen days for simple and/or post-surgical fistulae and fourteen to 21 days for complex and/or post-radiation fistulae.
recommended_tests: Assess for persistent leakage and postoperative UI.
If postoperative cystography is used before catheter removal, recognise that omission of a voiding phase or a bladder-neck fistula can lead to a missed persistent fistula.
long_term_effects: Possible persistence or recurrence, de novo OAB or SUI, infection, ureteric obstruction, vaginal stenosis and sexual dysfunction.

conditions.name: uretero-vaginal fistula
conditions.description: An upper urinary tract fistula involving a ureter and the vagina, commonly encountered in the early postoperative period after hysterectomy.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Urinary leakage after relevant pelvic surgery may accompany slower-than-expected recovery or dilation of the pelvicalyceal system.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a possible postoperative ureteric injury or urinary leak.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Unexpected fluid leakage or delayed recovery after pelvic surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: High creatinine in drainage fluid supports a urinary source.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish UVF from VVF.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When the source of vaginal urine leakage is uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.test: Contrast-enhanced CT with late excretory phase
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Locate the fistula and evaluate ureteric integrity and possible urinoma.
Detect ureteric stricture or deterioration of renal function.

follow_up.schedule: Follow after repair to detect late ureteric narrowing or worsening renal function; a fixed visit interval is not specified.
recommended_tests: Functional and anatomical imaging.
long_term_effects: Ureteric stricture and renal-function deterioration are potential late concerns.

conditions.name: urethro-vaginal fistulae
conditions.description: Uncommon urethral-to-vaginal fistulae in adults, usually iatrogenic; causes described include SUI or urethral-diverticulum surgery, genital reconstruction, irradiation and pessary use.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Urinary leakage may persist alongside SUI or urethral obstruction after closure.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect and localise a suspected urethro-vaginal fistula.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Clinical examination is often sufficient.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess fistula position and extent.
Clarify difficult diagnoses.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When clinical and endoscopic findings do not establish the anatomy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify anatomical relationships.

follow_up.schedule: Long-term assessment may be needed after repair.
recommended_tests: Assess fistula closure, continence and urethral narrowing.
long_term_effects: SUI, urethral stricture and urethral shortening can complicate repair.

conditions.name: Urethral diverticulum
conditions.description: A sac-like protrusion of the entire urethral wall or its mucosa into the space between peri-urethral tissues and the anterior vaginal wall.
conditions.epidemiology: Estimated prevalence is 1–6%; up to 10% was reported in women with LUTS attending a tertiary referral centre. The true incidence remains uncertain because cases may be asymptomatic or misdiagnosed.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible symptoms include pain, urgency, frequency, recurrent UTI, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, voiding difficulty and UI, but none is diagnostic. A palpable urethral mass may be present, sometimes with expressed purulent material or a stone in the diverticulum.

subtypes.name: Mid-urethral
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Diverticulum situated at the mid-urethra.

subtypes.name: Distal
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Diverticulum situated distally.

subtypes.name: Proximal
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Diverticulum situated proximally; more proximal lesions may pose greater postoperative SUI risk.

subtypes.name: Full length
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Diverticulum extending across the urethral length.

subtypes.name: Single
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Single-cavity configuration.

subtypes.name: Multi-loculated
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Configuration with multiple compartments.

subtypes.name: Saddle shaped
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Saddle-shaped configuration.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a urethral mass, expressed material and associated symptoms.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: No symptom cluster is pathognomonic.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm and characterise the diverticulum, guide repair and assess possible inflammation or tumour.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline identifies MRI as the diagnostic gold standard, while noting that a case series found a 25% discrepancy between MRI and surgical findings.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Locate and count diverticular ostia for surgical planning.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Ostia were seen in 42% of cases in the cited series.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise diverticular configuration.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Antero-posterior and lateral views are needed; false negatives can occur. Reported sensitivity is 73.5%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the number, size, location and contents of a diverticulum.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A meta-analysis reported sensitivity of 82.0% for US of any type; a trans-labial US publication reported 95%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide an alternative means of demonstrating the diverticulum.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When MRI cannot be performed and ostia cannot be identified on cystoscopy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reported sensitivity is 94.7%, but the procedure is technically demanding and can cause pain or UTI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess coexisting voiding dysfunction, obstruction or SUI and distinguish genuine from diverticulum-related apparent leakage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected preoperative cases with concomitant symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess urethral pressure changes at the lesion.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A biphasic pattern or pressure reduction at the diverticulum has been described.

pathology_markers.expected_result: Reported in 8% of cases in a meta-analysis.
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: A reported pathological finding in urethral diverticula.

staging.additional_rules: The limited classification records localisation, configuration, communication and continence status rather than numerical stages.

follow_up.schedule: Follow after surgery for recurrent diverticulum, persistent or new LUTS and UI; no fixed schedule is specified.
recommended_tests: Evaluate recurrent symptoms and new or persistent UI after diverticulectomy.
long_term_effects: Recurrence, de novo SUI, urgency or UUI, urethral stricture and urethro-vaginal fistula are reported after surgery.
For patients managed conservatively, the reported risk of cancer within the diverticulum is 1–6%.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Technically successful diverticulectomy does not necessarily eliminate LUTS or UI.

therapies_index.name: Urinary containment
approved_indications: Temporary symptom control in OAB wet or use when active treatment is unavailable, unsuitable, delayed, or not planned
Management of urinary leakage associated with BOO without correcting the obstruction
therapies_index.administration: Options described include absorbent pads, urinary catheters, external collection devices and intravaginal devices.

therapies_index.name: Incontinence pads
approved_indications: Temporary containment of OAB wet or containment when other treatments are not planned
Containment of leakage while awaiting urinary fistula repair
therapies_index.administration: The guide discusses superabsorbent pads, disposable insert pads and disposable pull-up pants.

therapies_index.name: Bladder training (BT)
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines education with scheduled voiding at progressively longer intervals to improve urgency control and bladder capacity.
approved_indications: First-line treatment of OAB/UUI
First-line treatment of MUI
A possible conservative measure for nocturia
therapies_index.administration: A scheduled voiding programme with gradually increasing intervals; the optimal intensity is unclear.

therapies_index.name: Prompted voiding
therapies_index.mechanism: A carer prompts voiding to prevent or reduce incontinence.
approved_indications: OAB in adults with cognitive impairment
therapies_index.administration: Carer-initiated voiding, mainly in assisted-care settings.

therapies_index.name: Timed voiding
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses predetermined intervals between voids.
approved_indications: A potential strategy to avoid bladder overdistension in women with impaired bladder sensation
therapies_index.administration: Voiding at fixed intervals; evidence of improved continence in cognitively impaired adults is inconsistent.

therapies_index.name: Double voiding
therapies_index.mechanism: Attempts to improve emptying through another void.
approved_indications: Women unable to empty the bladder completely

therapies_index.name: Abdominal straining
therapies_index.mechanism: May assist bladder emptying when accompanied by pelvic floor relaxation.
approved_indications: Discussed as a possible emptying strategy in UAB; efficacy has not been established in an RCT
therapies_index.administration: Voiding by abdominal effort with adequate PFM relaxation.
key_toxicities: Excessive straining may increase POP risk.

therapies_index.name: Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)
therapies_index.mechanism: Training increases PFM strength and endurance; contraction may inhibit urgency and support urethral closure.
approved_indications: First-line treatment of SUI and MUI, including in elderly, antenatal and postnatal women
Conservative treatment of OAB symptoms
Nocturia in women with UI or other storage LUTS
Potential relief of LUTS in women with POP who do not require a pessary or surgery
therapies_index.administration: Supervised, intensive training for at least three months is recommended for SUI or MUI. Programmes should be as intensive as possible.
key_toxicities: Adverse events are described as rare and minor.

therapies_index.name: Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) aimed at pelvic floor muscle relaxation
therapies_index.mechanism: Teaches relaxation of the PFMs and striated urethral sphincter during voiding.
approved_indications: Functional BOO

therapies_index.name: Pelvic floor muscle relaxation training with biofeedback
therapies_index.mechanism: Trains pelvic floor relaxation to facilitate voiding.
approved_indications: Discussed for UAB and dysfunctional voiding; evidence in adult women is limited

therapies_index.name: Biofeedback
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides feedback about PFM contraction during assessment or training.
approved_indications: Described as an adjunct to PFMT; an additional benefit over equally intensive PFMT has not been shown
therapies_index.administration: Described measurement methods include electromyography, manometry, dynamometry, US and MRI.

therapies_index.name: Electrical stimulation (ES)
therapies_index.mechanism: PFM stimulation is used to help identify contractions and is intended to inhibit detrusor contractions in OAB/UUI; these proposed effects lack confirmation from basic mechanistic studies.
approved_indications: Consideration for SUI treatment or for teaching PFM contraction
Investigated for OAB symptoms
therapies_index.administration: Delivery methods vary; ES may be combined with PFMT or biofeedback.
key_toxicities: Pain and discomfort have been reported, and some women cannot tolerate treatment.

therapies_index.name: Posterior tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS)
therapies_index.mechanism: Stimulates the posterior tibial nerve to convey electrical signals to the sacral micturition centre through the S2–S4 nerve roots.
approved_indications: An option for symptomatic improvement of OAB/UUI
therapies_index.administration: Percutaneous and transcutaneous techniques are described; an optimal schedule has not been established.

therapies_index.name: Percutaneous posterior tibial nerve stimulation (P-PTNS)
therapies_index.mechanism: Delivers posterior tibial nerve stimulation toward the sacral micturition centre.
approved_indications: Symptom improvement in OAB/UUI
therapies_index.administration: A fine 34-G needle is placed above the medial aspect of the ankle. Daily and weekly schedules have been described; maintenance treatment has been studied for up to 3 years.

therapies_index.name: Transcutaneous posterior tibial nerve stimulation (T-PTNS)
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides posterior tibial nerve stimulation through electrodes applied to the skin.
approved_indications: Investigated for OAB symptoms and UUI
therapies_index.administration: Surface electrodes do not penetrate the skin; studied courses lasted four to twelve weeks.

therapies_index.name: Acupuncture
approved_indications: Investigated for OAB symptoms; the cited evidence was of low quality

therapies_index.name: Electroacupuncture (EA)
approved_indications: Investigated for SUI and MUI
therapies_index.administration: One MUI trial used 36 sessions over twelve weeks.

therapies_index.name: Lifestyle advice
approved_indications: Women with LUTS before or alongside treatment
Discussed for OAB, nocturia and POP-associated symptoms
therapies_index.administration: Measures discussed include reviewing caffeine and fluid intake, weight, smoking, medication and bowel habits, according to the clinical situation.

therapies_index.name: Caffeine reduction
approved_indications: May improve urgency and frequency in adults with OAB, but not incontinence
Discussed as a conservative measure for nocturia
therapies_index.administration: Reduce caffeine intake.

therapies_index.name: Fluid intake modification
approved_indications: Review of fluid type and quantity in OAB
Reducing intake at particular times is discussed for nocturia
therapies_index.administration: Advice should be informed by bladder-diary measurements of 24-hour intake and urine output. In an OAB trial, reducing fluid intake by 25% improved OAB symptoms but not UI.
key_toxicities: Fluid restriction may worsen constipation or lead to UTI.
monitoring: Assess fluid intake and 24-hour urine output using a bladder diary.

therapies_index.name: Weight loss
approved_indications: Overweight or obese adults with OAB/UI
Overweight or obese women with LUTS/SUI
therapies_index.administration: Encourage weight reduction and maintenance of the reduction.
