recommended_regimens.summary: Offer training directed at pelvic-floor relaxation.

recommended_regimens.name: Uroselective alpha-blockers
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer as an off-label option after discussing potential benefits and adverse events.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A meta-analysis found symptom relief versus placebo in women with LUTS, but no significant difference in Qmax or PVR volume.

alternative_regimens.name: Oral baclofen
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer particularly when EMG activity is increased alongside sustained detrusor contraction during voiding.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Women with BOO, especially the stated functional findings (Weak).

alternative_regimens.name: alfuzosin plus EMS
alternative_regimens.summary: A small non-randomised study suggested greater improvement in one IPSS QoL question than either component alone; this is not a formal recommendation.

not_recommended.name: sildenafil outside a well-regulated clinical trial
not_recommended.reason: Only offer within a trial; current evidence does not show superiority to placebo for symptoms or urodynamic parameters (Strong).

not_recommended.name: thyrotropin-releasing hormone
not_recommended.reason: Do not offer; trials in women with voiding problems of mixed causes found no urodynamic advantage over placebo (Strong).

response_assessment.method: Monitor voiding and obstruction recurrence or progression
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent obstruction can threaten voiding or renal function.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline calls for research into the mechanisms and impact of PFMT on coordinated pelvic-floor relaxation (Strong).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with grade three or four cystocoeles causing BOO who are not eligible for or do not want other treatments
decision_rules: Use physical prolapse reduction when the stated cystocoele and treatment-preference criteria apply.

recommended_regimens.name: Vaginal pessary
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer to improve voiding associated with obstruction from a large cystocoele.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a prospective study of eighteen women, seventeen (94%) voided normally immediately after pessary placement.

response_assessment.method: Assess voiding and residual urine
response_assessment.interpretation: Long-term outcome data for pessary treatment of BOO are unavailable.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with BOO and urinary retention or leakage related to obstruction
decision_rules: Use catheter drainage for retention when needed; distinguish temporary leakage containment from correction of the obstruction.

alternative_regimens.name: Clean intermittent self-catheterisation (CISC)
alternative_regimens.summary: May drain residual urine, including after continence surgery or as an adjunct to treatment of obstruction.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Retention or significant incomplete emptying.

alternative_regimens.name: Urinary containment devices
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer to manage leakage resulting from BOO, not to correct BOO.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Leakage requiring containment (Weak).

not_recommended.name: Intraurethral device
not_recommended.reason: Do not offer for BOO; most users in a cited study needed removal because of discomfort, leakage or technical problems (Strong).

response_assessment.method: Assess residual urine, voiding and complications

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Postoperative transient voiding difficulty often requires only short-term catheterisation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with functional BOO who remain symptomatic
decision_rules: Consider interventions directed at sphincter overactivity or functional retention.

recommended_regimens.name: Intra-sphincteric injection of botulinum toxin
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for functional BOO; small studies report improvement in symptoms and urodynamic measures.

recommended_regimens.name: Sacral neuromodulation
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for functional BOO.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a review of 60 women with urinary retention associated with outlet obstruction, the spontaneous-voiding rate was 72% over a mean follow-up of four years.

response_assessment.timepoint: After treatment and during long-term follow-up
response_assessment.method: Assess spontaneous voiding, need for CISC, PVR volume and adverse events
response_assessment.interpretation: Recurrence or progression of obstruction requires monitoring.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence for both interventions specifically in women with BOO is limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with urethral stenosis or urethral stricture causing BOO
decision_rules: Select an intervention for the anatomical cause and explain the possibility of recurrence or postoperative UI.
For recurrent stricture after failed primary treatment, consider urethroplasty.

recommended_regimens.name: Urethral dilatation
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for urethral stenosis causing BOO, explaining that repeat intervention is likely.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A review pooling 93 women reported a mean success rate of 49% after dilatation to 41 Fr, with mean follow-up of 46 months.

recommended_regimens.name: Internal urethrotomy with postoperative urethral self-dilatation
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for BOO caused by urethral stricture, explaining limited long-term improvement and postoperative UI risk.

alternative_regimens.name: Urethroplasty
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer after recurrence of urethral stricture following unsuccessful primary treatment, with warning about later recurrence.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Recurrent stricture after failed initial treatment (Weak).

not_recommended.name: Urethral dilatation or urethrotomy after mid-urethral synthetic tape insertion
not_recommended.reason: Do not offer to treat BOO in this setting because of the theoretical risk of urethral mesh extrusion (Weak).

response_assessment.method: Monitor for recurrent urethral stricture and voiding difficulty
response_assessment.interpretation: Recurrence may require further treatment.

supportive_care: Explain that after internal urethrotomy, sustained improvement may be limited to PVR volume and QoL (Weak).
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Offer clean intermittent self-dilatation to women with urethral strictures or BOO after UI surgery (Weak).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with BOO secondary to primary bladder neck obstruction
decision_rules: Offer bladder-neck incision when primary bladder-neck obstruction is responsible.
Explain possible postoperative SUI, vesico-vaginal fistula and urethral stricture.

recommended_regimens.name: Bladder neck incision
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for obstruction arising from the primary bladder neck.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The largest cited series reported success in 84.5% of 84 patients after a mean follow-up of 27.4 months (6–78 months).

response_assessment.method: Assess voiding, residual urine, obstruction recurrence and complications

supportive_care: Counsel about the small risks of SUI, vesico-vaginal fistula and urethral stricture (Strong).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with voiding difficulties after anti-UI surgery, including obstruction following sling placement
decision_rules: Offer urethrolysis for voiding difficulty after anti-UI surgery.
Where a sling is implicated, revision techniques described include loosening, division or excision; account for recurrent SUI risk.

recommended_regimens.name: Urethrolysis
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer following anti-UI surgery when voiding difficulties persist.

alternative_regimens.name: Sling revision
alternative_regimens.summary: Reported techniques can restore voiding and lower PVR volume, with a risk of recurrent SUI.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Obstruction or persistent voiding difficulty after sling surgery; no particular revision technique is formally preferred.

not_recommended.name: Urethral dilatation or urethrotomy after mid-urethral synthetic tape insertion
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against these treatments for BOO after synthetic tape because of theoretical urethral mesh-extrusion risk (Weak).

response_assessment.method: Assess voiding, PVR volume, recurrent SUI and obstruction

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: One cited series of 63 women reported overall success of 87%, defined as PVR volume < 150 mL, across sling-revision techniques; no significant success-rate difference between those techniques was demonstrated.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with nocturia and UI or other storage LUTS
decision_rules: Consider the underlying cause and offer lifestyle advice before or alongside other treatment.
Offer PFMT when nocturia accompanies UI or other storage symptoms.

recommended_regimens.name: Lifestyle advice
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer before or concurrently with treatment for LUTS.

recommended_regimens.name: Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer individual or group training for nocturia with UI or other storage LUTS.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited secondary analysis reported a median nocturia reduction of 0.50 episodes per night with biofeedback-assisted PFMT.

response_assessment.method: Assess nocturnal episodes and the underlying cause
response_assessment.interpretation: Follow-up depends on aetiology and treatment.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Conservative measures described include timed reduction of fluids, moderation of caffeine or alcohol, distraction, bladder retraining, medication review and treatment of constipation; their individual effects are generally not quantifiable from the available evidence.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with nocturia and a history suggestive of obstructive sleep apnoea
decision_rules: Refer to a sleep clinic to assess suitability for continuous positive airway pressure.

recommended_regimens.name: Continuous positive airway pressure
recommended_regimens.summary: Arrange assessment for this treatment when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected as a contributor to nocturia.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited SR and meta-analysis involving both sexes reported an average numerical decrease of > 2 nocturia episodes per night.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The Strong recommendation is for referral and assessment of treatment suitability.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with nocturia secondary to nocturnal polyuria
decision_rules: Offer desmopressin after discussing potential benefits and risks, including hyponatraemia.
If OAB also coexists, combination treatment with an anticholinergic may be offered after counselling.

recommended_regimens.name: Desmopressin
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for nocturia due to nocturnal polyuria following risk-and-benefit counselling.

alternative_regimens.name: Anticholinergics plus desmopressin
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer to women whose OAB and nocturia coexist with nocturnal polyuria after discussing risks and benefits.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Concomitant OAB and nocturia due to nocturnal polyuria (Weak).

response_assessment.timepoint: During desmopressin treatment in elderly patients
response_assessment.method: Carefully monitor serum sodium concentration
response_assessment.interpretation: Hyponatraemia risk rises with age and a lower baseline sodium concentration.

supportive_care: Counsel about hyponatraemia.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Avoid prescribing desmopressin when baseline serum sodium concentration is below the normal range (Strong).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with nocturia and UUI or other LUTS
decision_rules: Offer anticholinergic treatment after discussion of expected benefits and risks.

recommended_regimens.name: Anticholinergic treatment
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer when nocturia occurs with UUI or other LUTS.

alternative_regimens.name: Vaginal oestrogen treatment
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer for nocturia after counselling about potential benefits and risks.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An individually considered option (Weak).

response_assessment.method: Assess change in nocturia episodes and clinical importance
response_assessment.interpretation: A statistically significant reduction may still be small clinically.

supportive_care: Explain that adding behavioural therapy to anticholinergic treatment is unlikely to improve efficacy beyond either modality alone (Weak).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with nocturia secondary to polyuria
decision_rules: Consider timed diuretic treatment after discussing potential benefits and risks.

recommended_regimens.name: Timed diuretic treatment
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for nocturia secondary to polyuria after counselling.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The cited trial of afternoon furosemide involved men; the guideline states that no comparable study was conducted in women.

treatment_pathways.condition: Pelvic organ prolapse and lower urinary tract symptoms
treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with POP and LUTS who do not need a vaginal pessary or surgery
decision_rules: Explain the possible LUTS relief from PFMT when a pessary or operation is not needed.

recommended_regimens.name: Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)
recommended_regimens.summary: Inform eligible women of its potential to relieve LUTS.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The evidence summary reports LUTS improvement for up to 6 months in patients without additional pessary or surgical treatment.

not_recommended.name: Preoperative PFMT intended to improve LUTS when pessary therapy or surgery is indicated for POP
not_recommended.reason: Do not offer for this purpose because additional LUTS benefit has not been shown with pessary or surgical treatment (Strong).

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence for POP symptom relief should not be assumed to establish relief of urinary symptoms when a pessary or surgery is also used.

treatment_pathways.condition: Pelvic organ prolapse and lower urinary tract symptoms
treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women requiring surgery for bothersome POP who have symptomatic or occult SUI
decision_rules: Offer simultaneous POP and SUI surgery only after a full discussion comparing combined surgery with POP surgery alone.
Explain the higher adverse-event risk with combined surgery.

recommended_regimens.name: Simultaneous surgery for POP and SUI
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer only after informed comparison of benefits and harms; combined treatment has a higher short-term UI cure rate but carries more adverse events.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited pooled analysis of vaginal POP surgery, surgery-related adverse events occurred in 28% with combined treatment versus 15% with POP surgery alone (RR: 1.8).

alternative_regimens.name: POP surgery alone with later SUI treatment if needed
alternative_regimens.summary: A staged approach can avoid immediate SUI surgery for some women, but SUI may persist after POP repair.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Following individual discussion of the risks and benefits of combined versus POP-only surgery.

response_assessment.method: Assess SUI, voiding symptoms and surgical complications
response_assessment.interpretation: Combined treatment reduces postoperative SUI in some studies but increases complications.

supportive_care: Discuss increased adverse-event risk of combined surgery (Strong).
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The evidence on longer-term benefit of combined POP and SUI surgery versus POP surgery alone conflicts.

treatment_pathways.condition: Pelvic organ prolapse and lower urinary tract symptoms
treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women requiring surgery for bothersome POP without symptomatic or occult SUI
decision_rules: Explain the risk of new SUI after prolapse surgery.
Do not add anti-incontinence surgery during abdominal prolapse surgery in this population.

not_recommended.name: Concomitant anti-incontinence surgery at the time of abdominal prolapse surgery
not_recommended.reason: The guideline explicitly advises against offering it to women without symptomatic or occult SUI (Strong).

response_assessment.method: Assess for de novo SUI
response_assessment.interpretation: New SUI can develop despite preoperative continence.

supportive_care: Inform women about the possibility of de novo SUI (Strong).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with urinary fistula awaiting repair, particularly those with a small recent fistula
decision_rules: Provide urinary catheterisation or diversion initially when appropriate.
Plan repair individually once tissue oedema, inflammation, necrosis or infection has resolved.

alternative_regimens.name: Urinary catheterisation or diversion
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used initially while spontaneous closure is possible or surgery is planned.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Initial management, especially for small fistulae.

response_assessment.method: Assess fistula closure separately from postoperative UI
response_assessment.interpretation: Report the timing of follow-up as well as each outcome (Strong).

supportive_care: Attend to skin care, nutrition, rehabilitation, counselling and support before and after repair as appropriate (Weak).
Pads and barrier cream or local oestrogen may be considered for skin protection while awaiting repair.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The reported spontaneous-closure rate is 13 ± 23%, mainly concerning fistulae < 1 cm; the rate cannot be established with certainty.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women undergoing repair of vesico-vaginal or persistent urogenital fistula
decision_rules: Individualise repair timing after local tissue problems or infection resolve.
Select the approach according to fistula anatomy and the surgical team's competence.
Maintain continuous bladder drainage until healing is confirmed.

recommended_regimens.name: Fistula repair
recommended_regimens.summary: Use a suitably trained surgical team; repair persistent urogenital fistulas abdominally using an available open, laparoscopic or robotic approach.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reported surgical closure rates for vesico-vaginal fistulae range from 58-100%.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Expert opinion suggests postoperative continuous bladder drainage for ten to fourteen days for simple and/or post-surgical fistulae, and fourteen to 21 days for complex and/or post-radiation fistulae.

alternative_regimens.name: Vaginal repair
alternative_regimens.summary: A described approach for accessible vesico-vaginal fistulae; high-quality evidence does not establish a superior route.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When anatomy allows vaginal access.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before stopping postoperative drainage and subsequently
response_assessment.method: Confirm healing; assess fistula recurrence and UI separately
response_assessment.interpretation: Closure does not necessarily mean continence.

supportive_care: Provide continuous bladder drainage until healing is confirmed (Weak).
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence does not establish that early versus delayed repair or one standard repair route gives a higher closure rate.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with radiation-associated fistula requiring repair or diversion
decision_rules: Use an interposition graft when repairing a radiation-associated fistula.
Avoid irradiated tissue if urinary or faecal diversion is needed.

recommended_regimens.name: Interposition graft
recommended_regimens.summary: Use during repair of a radiation-associated fistula.

alternative_regimens.name: Urinary and/or faecal diversion
alternative_regimens.summary: May be required because of extensive radiation-related tissue abnormalities.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected cases in which reconstruction alone is unsuitable.

not_recommended.name: Irradiated tissue for repair when diversion is required
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises avoiding irradiated tissue in this setting (Weak).

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Repair success is lower for irradiated than non-irradiated fistulae.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with upper urinary tract fistula after pelvic surgery
decision_rules: Where expertise and facilities exist, begin with conservative or endoluminal management.
Use operative reconstruction when indicated after these measures fail or when injury requires repair.

recommended_regimens.name: Conservative or endoluminal techniques
recommended_regimens.summary: Use initially for upper urinary tract fistula when local expertise and equipment permit.

alternative_regimens.name: Surgical repair
alternative_regimens.summary: Undertake when required according to sound tissue-repair and anastomotic principles.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Injury needing immediate repair or unsuccessful or unsuitable conservative/endoluminal treatment.

response_assessment.method: Functional and anatomical imaging
response_assessment.interpretation: Monitor for ureteric stricture and worsening renal function.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Do not routinely place ureteric stents solely to prevent injury during routine gynaecological surgery (Strong).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with urethro-vaginal fistula requiring surgical repair
decision_rules: Prefer a vaginal approach when repair is undertaken.

recommended_regimens.name: Vaginal repair
recommended_regimens.summary: Prefer vaginal repair, tailoring reconstruction to the fistula's size, position, cause and tissue loss.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: One cited series reported successful closure at the first vaginal intervention in 90.1% of 71 women, with an additional 7.4% closed at a second vaginal intervention.

response_assessment.method: Assess closure, SUI, urethral stricture and urethral shortening
response_assessment.interpretation: These complications may require ongoing follow-up.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Successful fistula closure may be followed by SUI.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with minimally symptomatic urethral diverticulum who prefer to avoid invasive treatment
decision_rules: Consider conservative management after discussing the small risk of cancer within the diverticulum.

alternative_regimens.name: Conservative management
alternative_regimens.summary: A possible approach when symptoms are minimal and invasive treatment is not preferred.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: After counselling about malignancy risk (Weak).

response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms and coexisting voiding dysfunction or UI

supportive_care: Explain the 1–6% risk of cancer developing within the diverticulum if conservative treatment is chosen (Weak).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with symptomatic urethral diverticulum
decision_rules: Offer surgical removal for symptomatic disease.
Assess diverticular anatomy and coexisting voiding dysfunction or UI before planning surgery.
Counsel that LUTS or UI can begin or persist despite technically successful surgery.

recommended_regimens.name: Urethral diverticulectomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer removal of a symptomatic diverticulum.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reported transvaginal diverticulectomy success, defined as being dry, is 84–98%, with reoperation in 2–13% after primary repair during mean follow-up of twelve to 50 months.

alternative_regimens.name: Marsupialisation
alternative_regimens.summary: A described drainage approach that leaves the diverticular structure in place.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Has been advocated to decompress a diverticulum during pregnancy to permit vaginal delivery; it is not presented as equivalent to definitive removal.

alternative_regimens.name: Endoscopic incision
alternative_regimens.summary: A rarely reported approach that widens the communication with the urethra to permit drainage.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: No formal criteria for preference are provided.

response_assessment.timepoint: After surgery and during longer-term follow-up
response_assessment.method: Assess recurrence, persistent or de novo LUTS, SUI, retention and fistula
response_assessment.interpretation: Successful removal does not preclude persistent or new urinary symptoms.

supportive_care: Counsel about recurrence and de novo SUI.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Carefully question and investigate coexisting voiding dysfunction and UI (Strong).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with symptomatic bothersome SUI accompanying urethral diverticulum who are undergoing diverticulectomy
decision_rules: After counselling, consider treating bothersome SUI at the same operation with a non-synthetic sling.

recommended_regimens.name: Concomitant non-synthetic sling
recommended_regimens.summary: Address bothersome SUI during urethral diverticulectomy after appropriate counselling.

not_recommended.name: Concomitant synthetic MUS
not_recommended.reason: Not recommended at diverticulectomy because synthetic material beside a fresh repair, potentially exposed to infected urine, may increase erosion, extrusion, fistula and foreign-body granuloma risks.

response_assessment.method: Assess SUI and other urinary symptoms
response_assessment.interpretation: SUI may persist, worsen or occur de novo.

supportive_care: Explain the uncertainty about the best timing of surgery for the two coexisting conditions.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Diverticulectomy alone may resolve SUI in some patients, but the evidence does not establish which patients will benefit.

special_populations.considerations: Anticholinergic treatment can improve OAB/UUI, but cognitive effects may accumulate with prolonged exposure. Oxybutynin may impair cognition; short-term studies have not demonstrated cognitive dysfunction with darifenacin, fesoterodine, solifenacin or trospium. Mirabegron has demonstrated efficacy and safety in older women. The applicability of trial subgroup findings to the wider ageing population is uncertain.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use long-term anticholinergic treatment cautiously, particularly when cognitive dysfunction is present or its risk is elevated. Assess anticholinergic burden and co-morbidity before treatment, and assess and monitor mental function when starting an anticholinergic.

special_populations.population: Adults with overactive bladder and cognitive impairment
special_populations.considerations: Carer-initiated prompted voiding has shown a short-term continence benefit in care-dependent older people.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer prompted voiding to adults with OAB who have cognitive impairment.

special_populations.population: Older adults with urinary incontinence and asymptomatic bacteriuria in nursing homes
special_populations.considerations: Eradicating asymptomatic bacteriuria did not change the frequency or severity of UI among nursing home residents.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not routinely treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in older patients for the purpose of improving UI.

special_populations.considerations: Obesity is a risk factor for UI, although its relationship with other OAB symptoms is unclear. SUI surgery can be performed in obese women, but benefit may be less likely and surgical risks may be greater.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Encourage weight loss and maintenance of weight loss in women with OAB/UI or LUTS/SUI. Before SUI surgery, explain the increased risks and potentially lower probability of benefit.

special_populations.population: Older women with stress urinary incontinence
special_populations.considerations: PFMT appears to remain effective in older women; age or frailty alone should not exclude appropriate patients who can participate cognitively. Evidence about surgical outcomes is conflicting, although failure and adverse-event risks appear to increase with age. No surgical procedure has been shown to be more effective or safer than another specifically in older women.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer supervised, intensive PFMT lasting at least three months as first-line treatment. Before surgery, explain the increased risks and the possibility of reduced benefit.

special_populations.considerations: In a Cochrane review, pregnant women undertaking PFMT for combined prevention had a 26% lower risk of UI during pregnancy and the mid-postnatal period. Among women continent before training, the reported risk was 62% lower in late pregnancy and 29% lower three to six months after birth. Evidence does not establish a lasting antenatal PFMT effect beyond six to twelve months postpartum or a reduction in late-pregnancy UI among women already incontinent.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer supervised, intensive PFMT lasting at least three months as first-line treatment when SUI or MUI is present.

special_populations.considerations: Evidence about starting PFMT after delivery differs between populations and studies. Its effect on later UI risk in groups combining continent and incontinent women is uncertain; evidence for persistent UI beyond six to twelve months postpartum is also limited.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer supervised, intensive PFMT lasting at least three months as first-line treatment for SUI or MUI, including in postnatal women.

special_populations.population: Postmenopausal women with genitourinary syndrome of menopause or vulvovaginal atrophy
special_populations.considerations: Vaginal oestrogen may improve symptoms associated with GSM, including a possible OAB component, and has improved SUI over the short term in postmenopausal women. The ideal duration and long-term effects of local treatment remain uncertain.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer vaginal oestrogen to women with LUTS and associated GSM symptoms, and to postmenopausal women with SUI and vulvovaginal atrophy symptoms. If SUI develops or worsens while taking oral conjugated equine oestrogen as HRT, discuss alternative HRT.

special_populations.population: Women with stress-predominant or urgency-predominant mixed urinary incontinence
special_populations.considerations: MUI encompasses differing combinations of stress and urgency symptoms. Women with MUI generally have more severe symptoms and respond less well to treatment than women with SUI or UUI alone. Surgery directed at SUI is less likely to cure UI, and its effect on pre-existing urgency is unpredictable.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Address the most bothersome symptom first. Offer anticholinergic drugs or beta-3 agonists for urgency-predominant MUI. Where licensed, offer duloxetine to selected patients with stress-predominant MUI who have not responded to other conservative treatment and wish to avoid an invasive intervention, after careful counselling about adverse events. Explain that treatment of more than one component may be necessary.

special_populations.population: Women with complicated or recurrent stress urinary incontinence
special_populations.considerations: Complicated SUI includes circumstances such as prior incontinence or extensive pelvic surgery, pelvic irradiation, relevant prolapse, voiding symptoms, neurogenic LUT dysfunction or substantial OAB/UUI. Repeat procedures are generally less effective and carry more complications than primary procedures; evidence does not establish one best operation for recurrent SUI.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer management in centres with appropriate experience. Choose repeat surgery after individual evaluation and consideration of further investigations. Secondary synthetic sling, bulking agents, Burch colposuspension, autologous sling or AUS may be considered. Offer an adjustable mid-urethral sling as primary surgery only within a structured research programme.

special_populations.population: Women with pelvic organ prolapse and symptomatic or occult stress urinary incontinence
special_populations.considerations: Reducing POP can reveal SUI that is not otherwise symptomatic. Combined prolapse and continence surgery lowers short-term postoperative SUI rates compared with prolapse surgery alone, but increases adverse events; evidence about its relative long-term benefit conflicts.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: In continent women, perform a POP reduction test to identify occult SUI and inform counselling. Offer simultaneous POP and SUI surgery only after discussing its potential benefits and risks against POP surgery alone.
conditions: Pelvic organ prolapse and lower urinary tract symptoms

special_populations.population: Women requiring surgery for bothersome pelvic organ prolapse without symptomatic or occult stress urinary incontinence
special_populations.considerations: SUI can develop after prolapse surgery even in women who were continent beforehand.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Explain the risk of de novo SUI. Do not offer concomitant anti-incontinence surgery during abdominal prolapse surgery.
conditions: Pelvic organ prolapse and lower urinary tract symptoms

special_populations.population: Older patients with nocturia receiving desmopressin
special_populations.considerations: The risk of hyponatraemia with desmopressin increases with age and with a lower serum sodium concentration before treatment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Monitor serum sodium carefully in older patients receiving desmopressin; avoid prescribing it when baseline serum sodium is below the normal range.

special_populations.population: Women with nocturia and suspected obstructive sleep apnoea
special_populations.considerations: Sleep disorders can contribute substantially to nocturia. A review and meta-analysis involving both sexes found that continuous positive airway pressure reduced nocturia associated with obstructive sleep apnoea.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer referral to a sleep clinic to assess suitability for continuous positive airway pressure.

special_populations.population: Women with urethral diverticulum during pregnancy
special_populations.considerations: Marsupialisation has been advocated to decompress a diverticulum and permit vaginal delivery. In a small case series, 75% of pregnant women managed expectantly ultimately needed surgery after delivery.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Marsupialisation is described as an option for decompression during pregnancy; the document does not establish it as a general recommendation.

special_populations.considerations: Repair outcomes are poorer for irradiated than non-irradiated fistulae, and surrounding tissue may also be affected. Complex or radiation-associated repairs may require a longer period of postoperative bladder drainage.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use an interposition graft when repairing a radiation-associated fistula and avoid irradiated tissue when diversion is required. Maintain continuous bladder drainage until healing is confirmed; expert opinion suggests fourteen to 21 days for complex and/or post-radiation fistulae.

recommendations.statement: Obtain a comprehensive history of symptoms and co-morbidities and perform a focused physical examination when assessing women with LUTS.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.1.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for history taking and physical examination

recommendations.statement: Include a suitable validated questionnaire in the standardised initial assessment and follow-up of women with LUTS.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.2.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for patient questionnaires

recommendations.statement: Ask women with LUTS to complete a bladder diary during standardised assessment.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for bladder diaries

recommendations.statement: Use a bladder diary covering > 3 days.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for bladder diaries

recommendations.statement: Include urinalysis in the initial assessment of patients with LUTS.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urinalysis

recommendations.statement: Reassess patients with LUTS and a urinary tract infection after treating the infection.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urinalysis

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in elderly patients to improve UI.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.4.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urinalysis

recommendations.statement: Measure post-void residual (PVR) volume at the initial assessment of patients with LUTS.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for post-void residual volume

recommendations.statement: Measure PVR volume using ultrasound.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for post-void residual volume

recommendations.statement: Monitor PVR volume during treatments that could induce or aggravate voiding dysfunction.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for post-void residual volume

recommendations.statement: Report bladder voiding efficiency alongside PVR volume measurements.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.5.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for post-void residual volume

recommendations.statement: Follow International Continence Society standards for good urodynamic practice when testing patients with LUTS.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.6.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urodynamics

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely perform urodynamics when offering treatment for uncomplicated stress urinary incontinence.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.6.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urodynamics

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely perform urodynamics before offering first-line treatment for uncomplicated overactive bladder symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.6.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urodynamics

recommendations.statement: Perform urodynamics when its results could alter the choice of invasive treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.6.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urodynamics

recommendations.statement: Do not grade UI severity using urethral pressure profilometry or leak point pressure.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.6.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urodynamics

recommendations.statement: If conducting a pad test, standardise both its duration and activity protocol.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.7.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for pad testing

recommendations.statement: Use a pad test when UI needs to be quantified, particularly when assessing treatment response.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.7.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for pad testing

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely image the upper or lower urinary tract when assessing LUTS.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.8.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for imaging

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely assess urinary biomarkers or urinary microbiota to diagnose or manage LUT disease in women.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.9.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for urinary biomarkers

recommendations.statement: At the initial evaluation of overactive bladder (OAB), ask patients to keep a bladder diary for at least three days.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.3.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations regarding OAB diagnosis

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely undertake urodynamics before first-line treatment of uncomplicated OAB symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.3.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations regarding OAB diagnosis

recommendations.statement: Ask every patient with overactive bladder (OAB) about current medication use.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.2.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for conservative management of OAB

recommendations.statement: Review newly started medications associated with the onset or worsening of OAB symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.2.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for conservative management of OAB

recommendations.statement: Before choosing urinary containment alone, ensure women with overactive bladder (OAB) and/or their carers know about the available treatment options.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urinary containment

recommendations.statement: Offer incontinence pads and/or containment devices for OAB wet, either temporarily to control symptoms or when no other treatment is planned.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urinary containment

recommendations.statement: Offer prophylactic antibiotics to patients using clean intermittent self-catheterisation or an indwelling catheter who have recurrent urinary tract infection only after discussing the risk of increased antimicrobial resistance.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urinary containment

recommendations.statement: Tell adults with OAB that reducing caffeine may improve urgency and frequency, but not incontinence.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.4.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for lifestyle interventions

recommendations.statement: Review the type and quantity of fluids consumed by patients with OAB.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.4.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for lifestyle interventions

recommendations.statement: Encourage overweight and obese adults with overactive bladder (OAB)/urinary incontinence to lose weight and sustain that loss.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.4.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for lifestyle interventions

recommendations.statement: Provide smoking-cessation strategies to patients with OAB who smoke.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.4.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for lifestyle interventions

recommendations.statement: Offer prompted voiding to cognitively impaired adults with overactive bladder (OAB).
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for behavioural and physical therapies

recommendations.statement: Offer bladder training as first-line treatment to adults with OAB/urge urinary incontinence (UUI).
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for behavioural and physical therapies

recommendations.statement: Make pelvic floor muscle training programmes as intensive as possible.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for behavioural and physical therapies

recommendations.statement: Consider posterior tibial nerve stimulation to improve OAB/UUI symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.1.5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for behavioural and physical therapies

recommendations.statement: Offer anticholinergic drugs to women with overactive bladder (OAB) when conservative treatment fails.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.2.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for anticholinergic drugs

recommendations.statement: Consider extended-release anticholinergic formulations whenever feasible.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.2.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for anticholinergic drugs

recommendations.statement: If anticholinergic treatment is ineffective, consider a higher dose, another anticholinergic formulation, or mirabegron alone or combined with an anticholinergic.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.2.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for anticholinergic drugs

recommendations.statement: Arrange early review of effectiveness and adverse effects in patients receiving anticholinergic medication for OAB.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.2.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for anticholinergic drugs

recommendations.statement: Offer beta-3 agonists instead of anticholinergics to women with OAB whose conservative treatment has failed.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.2.2.2 Summary of evidence and recommendation for Beta-3 agonists

recommendations.statement: Offer mirabegron as an additional treatment when solifenacin 5 mg provides inadequate control.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.2.2.2 Summary of evidence and recommendation for Beta-3 agonists

recommendations.statement: Use long-term anticholinergic treatment cautiously in elderly women, especially those with existing cognitive dysfunction or a risk of developing it.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.2.3.3 Summary of evidence and additional recommendations for use of anticholinergic and beta-3 agonists in elderly patients

recommendations.statement: Assess anticholinergic burden and associated co-morbidities before considering anticholinergic treatment for overactive bladder syndrome in women.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.2.3.3 Summary of evidence and additional recommendations for use of anticholinergic and beta-3 agonists in elderly patients

recommendations.statement: Offer vaginal oestrogen therapy to women who have LUTS alongside symptoms of genitourinary syndrome of menopause.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1.4.2.4.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for oestrogen therapy

recommendations.statement: Offer bladder-wall injections of onabotulinumtoxinA (100 U) for OAB/UUI that remains refractory to conservative or drug treatment.

document_sections.heading: 2. METHODS
document_sections.content: The 2023 guideline update focused its evidence review on systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Recommendation strength reflects evidence quality and certainty, the magnitude and balance of benefits and harms, and patient values and preferences.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Introduction
document_sections.content: For the 2023 Non-neurogenic Female Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms guidelines, Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Libraries were searched for high-level evidence published between 01 September 2021 and 20 February 2022. Investigators identified, retrieved and assessed 345 unique records. The Panel also conducted a new systematic review of OAB syndrome for the 2023 edition. A Strong recommendation generally reflects higher-quality evidence and/or a favourable benefit–harm balance and patient preferences; a Weak recommendation may reflect lower-quality evidence, a less clear balance or uncertain or variable preferences.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Review
document_sections.content: The guidelines underwent extensive peer review before publication in 2021.

document_sections.heading: 2.3 Future goals
document_sections.content: A systematic review of underactive bladder (UAB) in women is planned.

document_sections.heading: 3.1 History and physical examination
document_sections.content: Clinical history is the agreed first assessment step for LUTS despite limited high-level evidence. It should address storage, voiding and post-micturition symptoms; sexual, gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms; and whether UI is SUI, UUI, MUI or overflow incontinence. The latter describes reported UI with a symptomatically overfull bladder and no identified cause. Pain, haematuria, recurrent UTI, previous pelvic surgery or radiotherapy, continuous leakage suggestive of fistula, new enuresis and suspected neurological disease may warrant specialist referral. Neurological, obstetric and gynaecological history, co-morbidity, smoking, surgery and medication use may clarify causes and guide treatment. Although outcome evidence for examination is limited, consensus considers it essential. Assessment includes the abdomen, vagina and/or rectum, oestrogen status, PFM function, POP, cough stress testing for SUI and a focused neuro-urological examination; urethral mobility and PFM contraction strength may also be assessed. In women with prolapse, cough testing agreed well with UDS for detecting SUI.

document_sections.heading: 3.1.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for history taking and physical examination
document_sections.content: The evidence summary assigns LE 4 to the importance of symptom and co-morbidity history plus focused examination. Strong: obtain a complete medical history and perform a focused examination when evaluating women with LUTS.

document_sections.heading: 3.2 Patient questionnaires
document_sections.content: Symptom instruments, PROMs and generic or condition-specific HRQoL measures should be validated in their language of use and, when used to assess outcomes, responsive to change. Studies often combine men and women, limiting applicability to specific female syndromes. ICIQ-FLUTS, QUID, 3IQ and ICIQ-SF may distinguish UI types; OABQ-SF and B-SAQ assess OAB symptoms and bother. OAB-BAT includes symptoms, bother, impacts and treatment satisfaction and was found valid and reliable. A review of 22 studies covering eleven OAB case-finding tools found good sensitivity and specificity; B-SAQ alone screened for warning symptoms such as pain and haematuria and was validated in primary care. Evidence for responsiveness of some questionnaires is inconsistent. A review of 73 studies examined 27 condition-specific and six generic QoL instruments: IQoL had the strongest psychometric support for English-speaking women with UI, whereas evidence for generic instruments was limited. No evidence establishes that questionnaire use improves treatment outcomes. No single instrument meets every assessment need, so clinicians must judge whether to use tools individually or together.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for patient questionnaires
document_sections.content: Condition-specific validated scores aid LUTS screening and classification, and validated scores quantify UI and LUTS severity (LE 3). Condition-specific and general questionnaires measure health status and treatment-related change (LE 3). Questionnaires complement rather than replace consultation and a complete history (LE 4). Strong: include a suitable validated questionnaire in standardised initial and follow-up assessment of female LUTS.

document_sections.heading: 3.3 Bladder diaries
document_sections.content: Bladder diaries provide semi-objective measures of UI, nocturia, voided volume, 24-hour urine production and nocturnal production. Differences between diary records and perceived symptoms can inform counselling. Intake and output records support OAB assessment and recognition of 24-hour or nocturnal polyuria, and diaries can track treatment response. Severe UI may impair accurate recording of 24-hour output. A bladder diary, unlike other historically interchangeable diary terms, records fluid intake, voiding times and volumes, UI, pad use, urgency and UI severity for at least 24 hours. Studies support reproducibility, feasibility, reliability and validity; one reported a therapeutic effect from diary keeping. Observational studies found close correspondence with conventional symptom assessment. The best duration balances precision against adherence; studies commonly use three to seven days.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for bladder diaries
document_sections.content: Diaries lasting three to seven days reliably quantify average voided volume, daytime and night-time frequency, urgency, UI episodes, fluid intake and pad use, and detect changes after treatment (LE 2b for each finding). Strong: request a diary during standardised LUTS assessment. Strong: use a diary lasting > 3 days.

document_sections.heading: 3.4 Urinalysis and urinary tract infection
document_sections.content: Dipstick testing can reveal proteinuria, haematuria or glycosuria and suggest UTI requiring further assessment. Negative nitrite and leukocyte esterase results may exclude bacteriuria specifically in women with LUTS. Include urinalysis in LUTS evaluation and culture urine when necessary. UTI can cause or worsen UI and other LUTS. Eradication of asymptomatic bacteriuria did not change UI frequency or severity among nursing-home residents.

document_sections.heading: 3.4.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urinalysis
document_sections.content: Negative nitrite and leukocyte esterase may exclude bacteriuria in women with LUTS (LE 3). UI and increased LUTS can accompany UTI, which can aggravate existing UI (LE 3 for each finding). Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria does not improve UI in older nursing-home residents (LE 2). Strong: perform urinalysis initially; reassess LUTS after treating a concurrent UTI; do not routinely treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in older patients solely to improve UI.

document_sections.heading: 3.5 Post-void residual volume
document_sections.content: PVR is urine remaining after voiding and indicates emptying efficiency. A substantial residual may worsen symptoms and accompany UTI, UUT dilatation or renal impairment; BOO and DU can contribute. Ultrasound is preferred over catheterisation because of its risk–benefit profile. Evidence from mixed, sometimes neurogenic populations requires caution in non-neurogenic women. No agreed abnormal threshold exists in women: although some authors propose > 100 mL, asymptomatic women may exceed it. The Panel favours BVE, calculated as BVE = voided volume (VV)/(VV+PVR) × 100, as an additional potentially more dependable measure of poor emptying.

document_sections.heading: 3.5.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for post-void residual volume
document_sections.content: Women with LUTS have higher PVR than asymptomatic women (LE 2). Strong: measure PVR initially using ultrasound and monitor it during treatments that might induce or worsen voiding dysfunction. Weak: additionally report BVE when measuring PVR.

document_sections.heading: 3.6 Urodynamics
document_sections.content: Urodynamics may supplement clinical diagnosis, inform treatment choices and support counselling, but usefulness depends on improved care or outcomes. Uroflowmetry assesses Qmax, voided volume, curve shape and PVR; the bladder should be sufficiently full, and patients should indicate whether voiding was representative. A minimum of 150 mL is advised for men, but a corresponding female threshold lacks evidence. Invasive options include multichannel cystometry, pressure–flow testing, ambulatory and video-urodynamics, and urethral function testing. Good testing reproduces symptoms, checks recording quality and interprets findings clinically. Transabdominal near-infrared spectroscopy and US detrusor-wall assessment have not entered routine practice.

document_sections.heading: 3.6.1 Variability
document_sections.content: Within-person variation affects reproducibility, accuracy and prognostic value. ICS standards accept one cystometry and pressure–flow measurement if symptoms recur during testing, although some studies disagree. Evidence conflicts for reproducibility of MUCP; VLPP lacks standardisation and has minimal reproducibility evidence. Reproducibility studies of ambulatory monitoring in non-neurological patients have not been published.

document_sections.heading: 3.6.2 Diagnostic accuracy
document_sections.content: Symptoms and cystometry can disagree, and asymptomatic women may have urodynamic abnormalities. Urethral pressure profilometry and urethral retro-resistance pressure perform poorly for diagnosing SUI; VLPP did not reliably indicate UI severity in a surgical SUI cohort. Urethral pressure reflectometry might be more accurate, but its role is uncertain. Ambulatory studies may detect more unexpected physiological variation than conventional cystometry without established clinical relevance. Pressure–flow testing can distinguish BOO, DU and their coexistence and may identify dysfunctional voiding. Female BOO lacks an accepted diagnostic cutoff. Measures of contraction strength have limited validation and omit contraction speed and persistence. Video-urodynamics may locate anatomical or functional obstruction and identify diverticula or marked reflux.

document_sections.heading: 3.6.3 Predictive value
document_sections.content: A Cochrane review of eight RCTs found more drug prescribing after urodynamics in women with UI, without more surgery or evidence of altered outcomes. A meta-analysis of four RCTs found no difference in surgical cure or complications between urodynamics and office assessment for self-reported SUI or stress-predominant MUI. A retrospective multicentre study classified only 36% as uncomplicated; findings differed from the prior diagnosis in 1,276 of 2,053 patients (62.2%), identified voiding dysfunction in 394 (19.2%), and prompted cancellation or alteration of planned surgery in 304 of 1,582 patients (19.2%) with available information. Urethral function tests have inconsistent links to surgical success. Preoperative DO in stress-predominant MUI was associated with postoperative UUI but did not predict overall failure after MUS or colposuspension. DO did not predict response to antimuscarinics, onabotulinumtoxinA or SNS for OAB. Evidence does not establish whether preoperative urodynamics predicts augmentation cystoplasty results, although most clinicians regard testing as essential beforehand. Pressure–flow measures poorly predict postoperative voiding dysfunction in selected SUI populations. If clinical findings and urodynamics disagree, reassess both before invasive therapy. The Panel considers urodynamics potentially helpful for choosing management and discussing expectations, while recognising inconsistent predictive evidence.

document_sections.heading: 3.6.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urodynamics
document_sections.content: The evidence summary describes comprehensive LUT assessment (LE 4), variability and potential disagreement with history or other tests (LE 3), no treatment-outcome effect of a DO diagnosis in OAB (LE 1a), no surgical benefit from routine preoperative testing in uncomplicated demonstrable SUI (LE 1b), inconsistent prognostic performance of urethral tests (LE 3), and uncertain links between preoperative DO, MUS failure and persistent urgency (LE 3). Strong: follow ICS good-practice standards; avoid routine urodynamics for uncomplicated SUI treatment or first-line uncomplicated OAB treatment; do not grade UI severity using urethral pressure profilometry or leak point pressure. Weak: perform urodynamics if findings could alter invasive treatment.

document_sections.heading: 3.7 Pad testing
document_sections.content: Timed or exercise-based absorbent-pad tests quantify leakage and can document treatment response. A review of eighteen studies found a 1-hour test more accurate but less reproducible than longer tests. With standardised exercise, a 1-hour threshold of 1.4 g had good specificity but lower sensitivity for SUI and MUI; a 24-hour threshold of 4.4 g was more reproducible but difficult to standardise across activity levels. A negative short provocation test should be repeated with stronger provocation. Prognostic and severity-quantification value remains uncertain, although pad tests respond to successful treatment. A study of 25 women suggested standardising bladder volume at 50% of cystometric capacity; no test format has proven superior.

document_sections.heading: 3.7.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for pad testing
document_sections.content: Pad testing can identify UI and treatment-related changes, while standardising bladder volume and provocation improves reproducibility (LE 2). For home testing, twenty-four hours balances accuracy and adherence (LE 1a). Pad tests are useful in research and optional clinically (LE 4). Strong: standardise test duration and activity. Weak: use pad testing when leakage must be quantified, particularly to assess response.

document_sections.heading: 3.8 Imaging
document_sections.content: US and MRI have largely displaced X-ray for pelvic-floor evaluation; US may offer less costly and more accessible 3D and 4D images. UUT imaging is unnecessary unless high-pressure bladder, severe POP, chronic retention or abnormal renal tests are suspected or present. Urography or CT may be appropriate when an UUT anomaly or uretero-vaginal fistula is suspected as the source of UI.

document_sections.heading: 3.8.1 Ultrasound
document_sections.content: LUT US can aid differential diagnosis in female LUTS and haematuria. Abdominal, transvaginal, transrectal, perineal and transurethral approaches permit assessment of the bladder neck, urethra and their movement during straining, coughing or PFM contraction. Measures explored for SUI include bladder-neck descent or mobility, urethro-vesical angle and urethral rotation. US can assess PFM function, and 3D transperineal US can examine levator ani integrity. It may also show anatomical changes accompanying persistent post-treatment symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 3.8.2 Detrusor wall thickness
document_sections.content: The proposed relationship between OAB, DO and greater DWT/BWT remains unconfirmed; measuring wall thickness has not been shown to improve OAB care, and no standard measurement bladder volume is accepted. In a retrospective study of 227 women with voiding difficulty, 74 (32.6%) met the study's voiding-dysfunction criteria. After accounting for DO, DWT did not relate to urodynamic indicators of BOO.

document_sections.heading: 3.8.3 Magnetic resonance imaging
document_sections.content: MRI offers a broad pelvic-floor assessment, including POP, defecation and support structures, but interpretation varies substantially between observers. Evidence of clinical value for LUTS/UI is limited, and MRI has not been shown conclusively more useful than vaginal examination for POP. Imaging studies suggest MUS may reduce mid-urethral but not bladder-neck mobility; a greater pubic-symphysis-to-sling distance after MUS correlated with a lower SUI cure probability.

document_sections.heading: 3.8.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for imaging
document_sections.content: Evidence does not consistently support routine urinary-tract imaging for LUTS assessment or treatment, or BWT/DWT measurement for OAB management (LE 3 for each). Strong: do not routinely image the UUT or LUT during LUTS assessment.

document_sections.heading: 3.9 Urinary biomarkers and microbiome
document_sections.content: NGF, BDNF, prostaglandin E2, ATP and P2X have been studied for OAB; BNP, urinary 6-sulfaoxymelatonin, CRP, melatonin and vasopressin for nocturia; and urinary IL 12-70, uNGF, NTx and microbiota for SUI. Biomarker studies have methodological shortcomings and conflicting results. A review reported differing proportions of Lactobacillus, Gardnerella and Atopobium vaginae among women with different UI types and controls. Microbiota also differed with anticholinergic treatment response, but its clinical role remains undefined.

document_sections.heading: 3.9.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for urinary biomarkers
document_sections.content: Evidence is insufficient to establish diagnostic accuracy or validity of urinary biomarkers for female LUT disease (LE 3). Microbiota differences have been associated with LUT dysfunction types and treatment responses (LE 3). Strong: do not routinely use urinary biomarkers or microbiota estimates for diagnosis or management.

document_sections.heading: 4.1 Overactive bladder
document_sections.content: OAB is diagnosed from symptoms, not from urodynamic DO. Management spans conservative, pharmacological and invasive options selected according to response, risks and patient circumstances.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.1 Epidemiology, aetiology, pathophysiology
document_sections.content: ICS defines OAB by urgency, generally with frequency and nocturia, with or without UUI, when UTI or another clear pathology is absent. It is chronic and may substantially impair QoL. DO is its characteristic urodynamic finding but is not required for diagnosis. The EPIC survey across five countries found OAB symptoms in 11.8% overall, 10.8% of men and 12.8% of women. Proposed neural and bladder-receptor mechanisms have not established a definitive cause.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.2 Classification
document_sections.content: Wet and dry OAB distinguish whether UI accompanies the syndrome.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.3 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Assess OAB symptoms using the general female LUTS evaluation pathway.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.3.1 Bladder diaries
document_sections.content: Diaries quantify frequency, urgency and UI and can track change and treatment response. Observational studies found close agreement with conventional symptom assessment. Three to seven days is commonly used, balancing accuracy with adherence.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.3.2 Urodynamics
document_sections.content: Urodynamics establishes DO, but absence of DO does not exclude symptom-defined OAB. A Cochrane review of seven RCTs found testing increased drug prescribing or avoidance of surgery without evidence of improved clinical outcomes. An RCT sub-analysis found that DO did not predict response to fesoterodine versus placebo.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.3.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations regarding OAB diagnosis
document_sections.content: Diaries of three to seven days may quantify OAB symptoms and treatment change (LE 3); DO on urodynamics does not affect OAB treatment outcomes (LE 1a). Strong: obtain at least a three-day initial diary and avoid routine urodynamics before first-line treatment of uncomplicated OAB.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.3.4 Urinary biomarkers
document_sections.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis found higher uNGF, BDNF-to-creatinine and uNGF-to-creatinine ratios in women with OAB than in healthy controls, but no difference in PGE2/ Cr or ATP/Cr ratios. Data are inadequate to assess other potential OAB biomarkers.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1 Conservative management
document_sections.content: Non-surgical approaches are conventionally used first because they generally present less harm. Non-pharmacological conservative therapies retain this advantage, but cognitive and other adverse effects of OAB drugs, particularly anticholinergics, require full patient counselling.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.1 Addressing associated medical co-morbidities
document_sections.content: Especially in older patients, LUTS coexist with cardiac or renal failure, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, neurological disease, cognitive impairment, sleep disorders including sleep apnoea, depression and metabolic syndrome. Review changes in co-morbidity or its treatment when temporally linked to worsening LUTS. In one study of middle-aged women with type 1 diabetes mellitus, 10% had UUI; early intensive versus conventional insulin treatment was not associated with different UUI occurrence, and later UI prevalence also did not differ.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.2 Adjustment of other medication
document_sections.content: Drug-associated LUTS reports largely come from uncontrolled cases and post-marketing monitoring, so causation often cannot be established. A scoping review found no study testing whether adjustment of specific medicines changes existing OAB symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.2.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for conservative management of OAB
document_sections.content: Evidence that improving co-morbidity improves OAB is lacking (LE 3), and evidence that changing co-morbidity medication modifies existing OAB is sparse (LE 3). Strong: document all current medicines in OAB and review new medicines linked to onset or worsening.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.3 Urinary containment
document_sections.content: Containment can address OAB wet when active treatment fails, is delayed or is unavailable, or when patients prefer it. Options include pads, catheters, external collectors and intravaginal devices. A review of five RCTs favoured superabsorbent over standard pads; skin outcomes for disposable versus washable pads were inconsistent. Crossover trials favoured disposable insert pads for light female UI and disposable pull-up pants for moderate/severe female UI. A Cochrane review found no long-term indwelling catheter material or type superior. Nonrandomised studies found similar UTI and UUT outcomes for suprapubic versus urethral drainage, with fewer urethral complications after suprapubic drainage. Evidence for anticholinergics against catheter discomfort is conflicting. In a retrospective study of 40 women, mostly neurogenic, intravesical botulinum toxin was associated with less catheter pain and bypass leakage and a significant 83% reduction in leakage. Evidence for catheter washout benefit is inconsistent. Reviews found antibiotic prophylaxis reduced symptomatic UTI during CISC or indwelling catheter use, but potential harms were incompletely assessed and resistance is a concern.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urinary containment
document_sections.content: Pads contain leakage (LE 1b). Antibiotic prophylaxis may lower UTI incidence with indwelling catheters or CISC but increases antimicrobial-resistance risk (LE 1a). Strong: explain active options before choosing containment alone; offer pads and/or devices for temporary or longer-term OAB-wet management; restrict prophylactic antibiotics in catheter users to those with recurrent UTI after discussing resistance.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.4 Lifestyle interventions
document_sections.content: Obesity, smoking, physical activity, bowel habits and fluid intake may be associated with UI; altering them may improve OAB symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.4.1 Caffeine intake
document_sections.content: A scoping review of fourteen intervention and twelve observational studies suggested caffeine reduction may lessen urgency, but certainty was low and study populations differed substantially.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.4.2 Fluid intake
document_sections.content: Base fluid advice on 24-hour diary measurements of intake and output. Intake should prevent thirst; investigate unusually low or high 24-hour output. Female RCT findings are inconsistent and adherence difficult to assess. One RCT found a 25% intake reduction improved OAB symptoms but not UI. Another found personalised advice added to anticholinergics did not improve continence versus generic advice. Warn that restriction may aggravate constipation or cause UTI.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.4.3 Weight loss
document_sections.content: Epidemiological studies associate overweight or obesity with LUTS and increasing BMI with both UUI and SUI prevalence. Because evidence concerns mainly obesity and SUI, a definite relationship between obesity and OAB prevalence cannot be inferred.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.4.4 Smoking cessation
document_sections.content: Smoking cessation is a general health measure, with only a weak association with improvement in urgency, frequency and UI. A health-technology review judged its LUTS effect uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.4.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for lifestyle interventions
document_sections.content: Reducing caffeine may improve frequency and urgency (LE 2); a 25% fluid reduction may improve OAB but not UI (LE 1b); personalised fluid advice adds no demonstrated benefit to OAB pharmacotherapy (LE 2). Obesity is a female UI risk factor, with unclear links to other OAB symptoms (LE 1b); evidence for OAB improvement after smoking cessation is weak (LE 3). Strong: explain that less caffeine may improve urgency and frequency but not incontinence; encourage weight loss and its maintenance in overweight or obese adults with OAB/UI; provide smoking-cessation strategies to smokers with OAB. Weak: review fluid type and quantity.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.5 Behavioural and physical therapies
document_sections.content: Behavioural and physical approaches are often delivered with lifestyle counselling and patient education.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.5.1 Prompted voiding and timed voiding
document_sections.content: With prompted voiding, carers initiate toileting to reduce UI, mainly in assisted care. A review of nine RCTs, predominantly involving women, suggested short-term benefit over standard care. Timed voiding uses predetermined intervals whether or not cognition is impaired; a Cochrane review of four RCTs found inconsistent continence improvement in cognitively impaired adults.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.5.2 Bladder training
document_sections.content: BT combines education and scheduled voiding with progressively longer intervals to address frequent urination, urgency, capacity, UI and confidence. Its optimal format or intensity is unknown. A Cochrane review of seven RCTs found inconsistent comparative cure results for anticholinergics versus BT, although significantly more patients improved with anticholinergics. Adding anticholinergics to BT improved subjective but not objective outcomes. Cognitive behavioural approaches include distraction, relaxation and mindfulness; one review found their content poorly specified and their independent contribution insufficiently studied. Another review of 12 studies found high-level evidence for improved UUI symptom severity versus placebo and moderate-level evidence for QoL, psychological symptoms and satisfaction, although objective results were inconsistent.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.5.3 Pelvic floor muscle training
document_sections.content: PFM contraction can inhibit urgency, detrusor contraction and leakage. Regular intensive training strengthens contraction and endurance and changes pelvic-floor morphology, but mechanistic evidence linking morphology change to OAB improvement is lacking. A review of eleven RCTs found significant reductions in frequency and UUI in five trials; six found no significant difference, with substantial variation in protocols and outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.5.4 Electrical stimulation
document_sections.content: ES delivery varies and may be combined with PFMT or biofeedback. It is used to help patients identify PFMs or potentially inhibit detrusor contractions, without mechanistic confirmation. A review of 63 trials involving 4,224 adults found moderate-quality evidence favouring ES over sham, no therapy, PFMT and drugs for OAB symptoms. Its benefit versus sham for UUI and comparative adverse-event rates remained unclear. A review of nine studies found no pooled differences between intravaginal ES and T-PTNS for frequency, nocturia or QoL, or between T-PTNS and PTNS for urgency, frequency or QoL.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.5.4.1 Posterior tibial nerve stimulation
document_sections.content: PTNS stimulates the sacral micturition centre through S2–S4 roots. P-PTNS uses a 34-G needle near the medial ankle; transcutaneous delivery uses surface electrodes. Daily and weekly schedules have been described, without an established optimum. A review of five RCTs involving 408 women found PTNS reduced UUI episodes significantly more than antimuscarinics but did not significantly differ for overall symptom scores, frequency or urgency. A review of three studies found no statistically significant improvement from adding antimuscarinics to PTNS for mean symptom score, frequency, nocturia or UUI episodes.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.5.4.2 Percutaneous posterior tibial nerve stimulation
document_sections.content: The reviewed evidence included a systematic review, two twelve-week sham-controlled RCTs, a PTNS-versus-tolterodine RCT and a three-year maintenance extension. Female OAB studies consistently reported significant, sustained improvement from baseline, with improvement similar to tolterodine.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.5.4.3 Transcutaneous posterior tibial nerve stimulation
document_sections.content: A review of thirteen trials examined T-PTNS over four to twelve weeks in mixed adult populations, sometimes including neurogenic OAB. Pooled sham-controlled data from two RCTs showed a mean ICIQ-UI-SF reduction of −3.79 points. In an RCT of older women, T-PTNS added to PFMT and BT increased the likelihood of improvement. Another small RCT found both P-PTNS and T-PTNS more effective than BT alone; efficacy was similar, while T-PTNS required less preparation, caused less discomfort and yielded greater satisfaction.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.5.5 Acupuncture
document_sections.content: A review and meta-analysis of ten low-quality RCTs involving 794 patients, including 590 women, suggested acupuncture might reduce OAB symptoms versus sham. Comparisons included electro-acupuncture against sham and electro-acupuncture plus tolterodine against tolterodine alone.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.1.5.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for behavioural and physical therapies
document_sections.content: Prompted voiding improves short-term continence in older care-dependent people (LE 1b). BT benefits female UUI but appears less effective than pharmacotherapy (LE 1b). PFMT may improve OAB frequency (LE 1b). ES may improve OAB, although delivery is poorly standardised (LE 1a). PTNS lowers UUI episodes more than antimuscarinics without a difference for other OAB symptoms (LE 1a); P-PTNS maintenance benefit has been shown for up to 3 years (LE 2a). T-PTNS appears effective versus sham and not inferior to P-PTNS for urgency, frequency and QoL (LE 1a for each). Strong: offer prompted voiding to cognitively impaired adults with OAB; offer BT first-line for OAB/UUI; make PFMT as intensive as possible; consider PTNS for OAB/UUI symptom relief.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.1 Anticholinergic drugs
document_sections.content: Anticholinergic or antimuscarinic drugs are a principal pharmacological OAB treatment; agents differ pharmacologically and pharmacokinetically. The Panel review of twelve studies involving 11,179 women found significantly greater improvement than placebo in OABQ scores, daily frequency, urgency, UUI and functional bladder capacity, alongside significantly more dry mouth, cognitive impairment, UTI and constipation. IR products allow flexible dosing, including off-label on-demand use, but generally cause more adverse effects than ER products. Oxybutynin also has transdermal and gel formulations. A network meta-analysis of 128 RCTs in both sexes found reasonable cure or improvement with every assessed anticholinergic except imidafenacin, with small efficacy differences. A female-only review found the agents examined superior to placebo for UUI cure, but absolute benefit was small. The table presents agent-specific UI cure and adverse-event discontinuation estimates. Separate trial data reported continence in 29–33% with darifenacin versus 17–18% with placebo.
