Transdermal oxybutynin improved leakage episodes and daily micturitions without reporting UI cure; oxybutynin gel improved UUI and cure versus placebo.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.1.1 Comparison of different anticholinergic agents
document_sections.content: A network meta-analysis and systematic review found no clearly superior anticholinergic for cure, improvement or QoL. Another analysis of 53 RCTs found solifenacin 5 mg/day better than tolterodine 4 mg/day for UUI episodes but less effective than solifenacin 10 mg/day for micturition episodes; dry-mouth risk was lower with solifenacin 5 mg/day, without significant blurred-vision or constipation differences. An analysis of 128 RCTs found more dry mouth with every anticholinergic than placebo, with the smallest difference for transdermal oxybutynin. ER formulations generally cause less dry mouth than IR. Comparative dry-mouth patterns differ by formulation and dose: oxybutynin IR exceeds tolterodine IR and trospium IR but is below darifenacin 15 mg daily; oxybutynin ER exceeds tolterodine ER overall, though moderate or severe cases are similar; transdermal oxybutynin causes less than oxybutynin IR and tolterodine ER but more withdrawal from skin reactions; solifenacin 10 mg daily exceeds tolterodine ER; fesoterodine 8 mg daily exceeds tolterodine 4 mg daily. Discontinuation may remain similar despite dry-mouth differences. Nearly all primary studies were industry-sponsored, often used unequal dose-titration arrangements, lasted twelve weeks and prioritised symptom change over UUI cure; most were low or moderate quality, limiting real-world applicability.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.1.2 Anticholinergic drugs versus conservative treatment
document_sections.content: More than 100 RCTs and high-quality reviews address relative outcomes of anticholinergics and conservative care, mainly for UUI. A U.S. assessment judged most trials low or moderate quality.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.1.2.1 Anticholinergic drugs in combination with other conservative treatment versus anticholinergic drugs alone
document_sections.content: Female OAB trials found no added continence benefit from BT plus solifenacin versus solifenacin alone; a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence that PFMT adds benefit to medication for female UI. In contrast, the Panel review of thirteen RCTs found antimuscarinics combined with various adjunctive treatments improved urgency, UUI, frequency, nocturia and mean symptom scores more than antimuscarinic monotherapy, without significant differences in dry mouth, constipation or voiding dysfunction.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.1.3 Anticholinergic drugs: adherence and persistence
document_sections.content: Most drug studies lasted twelve weeks, with trial adherence likely exceeding routine practice. Oxybutynin discontinuation at twelve months was 68–95%; two fesoterodine 8 mg extensions reported two-year adherence of 49–84%. A longitudinal database reported discontinuation of 74.8% at one year and 87% at three years. Reported reasons for poor adherence included inadequate efficacy (41.3%), adverse events (22.4%) and cost (18.7%). IR formulation, younger age, unrealistic expectations and ethnicity were also associated with lower persistence; female patients had better adherence or persistence.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for anticholinergic drugs
document_sections.content: Compared with placebo, anticholinergics improve OAB symptoms and voided volumes but cause more adverse events (LE 1a). Once-daily ER has fewer adverse events than IR (LE 1b); transdermal oxybutynin reduces dry mouth relative to oral drugs but increases withdrawal from skin reactions (LE 1b). Higher doses increase efficacy and adverse effects (LE 1a). No agent is clearly superior for OAB/UUI cure or improvement (LE 1a). Combination treatment may outperform antimuscarinics alone (LE 1a). Adherence is low, declines with time, and most patients stop within the first three months (LE 2a). Strong: offer anticholinergics after conservative-treatment failure, favour ER where possible, and review efficacy and harms early. If ineffective, consider a higher dose, another anticholinergic formulation or mirabegron alone or combined with an anticholinergic.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.2 Beta-3 Agonists
document_sections.content: Stimulation of beta-3 receptors in detrusor smooth muscle is thought to relax the detrusor. Mirabegron was the first available beta-3 agonist; vibegron is marketed in some countries. Reviews of industry-sponsored phase II and III studies found mirabegron 25, 50 and 100 mg reduced UI, urgency and micturition frequency significantly more than placebo, without a difference in common adverse-event rates. Dry rates were generally 35–40% for placebo and 43–50% for mirabegron; consistent significant differences concerned UI improvement rather than cure. Previous anticholinergic use did not materially change improvement. Mirabegron-group events included hypertension (7.3%), nasopharyngitis (3.4%) and UTI (3%), with overall frequency similar to placebo. A pooled review of three RCTs involving 2,120 patients found vibegron 75 mg or 100 mg improved urgency, UUI and average voided volume versus placebo with a favourable safety profile. Another review found efficacy similar to imidafenacin and tolterodine, with less dry mouth.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.2.1 Beta-3 agonists versus anticholinergics
document_sections.content: A review including seven RCTs, three nonrandomised comparisons and eleven observational studies found no short-term symptom difference between mirabegron and anticholinergics up to twelve weeks, but favoured mirabegron at one year. A pooled analysis of four studies involving 371 women found beta-3 agonists significantly better for nocturia, without significant differences in other symptoms or voided volume. Antimuscarinics caused more dry mouth, but constipation rates did not significantly differ. Post hoc trials linked symptom improvement to HRQoL improvement. No QTc prolongation or increased intraocular pressure was observed up to 100 mg, although uncontrolled hypertension and arrhythmia were exclusion criteria. At twelve months, adherence was 5.5% with tolterodine and 3.6% with mirabegron, with significantly more dry mouth after tolterodine; Canadian database data suggested better mirabegron adherence than anticholinergic adherence. An RCT found that adding mirabegron 50 mg after inadequate response to solifenacin 5 mg yielded more clinically meaningful UI improvement than increasing solifenacin alone.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.2.2 Summary of evidence and recommendation for Beta-3 agonists
document_sections.content: Mirabegron and vibegron improve OAB/UUI versus placebo, with comparable adverse-event rates (LE 1a). Beta-3 agonists have efficacy comparable to antimuscarinics and less dry mouth (LE 1a). Adding mirabegron may benefit patients inadequately treated with solifenacin 5 mg more than escalating solifenacin (LE 1b). Strong: offer a beta-3 agonist as an alternative to anticholinergics after conservative-treatment failure. Weak: add mirabegron for inadequate response to solifenacin 5 mg.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.3 Anticholinergics and beta-3 agonists: elderly patients and cognition
document_sections.content: An older review found cognitive effects inconclusive; two more recent longitudinal cohorts associated anticholinergic use with worsening cognition, altered central metabolism and brain atrophy. Most trials lasted four to twelve weeks, limiting conclusions about long-term effects in specific cohorts. Oxybutynin IR may impair cognition, and a prospective study associated prolonged anticholinergic exposure, with mean follow-up of 7.3 years, with cumulative decline. A study of 376 nursing-home residents aged 65 or older receiving oxybutynin and tolterodine found reduced daily functioning after a median 141 days despite cholinesterase inhibitors. Short-term solifenacin studies generally found no cognitive impairment, although adverse events were more frequent above 80 years; solifenacin 5–10 mg improved symptoms and QoL above 75 years after failed tolterodine. Tolterodine trials reported broadly comparable age-group efficacy and safety, but follow-up was short. Elderly darifenacin RCTs found efficacy without detected memory change; cognition was affected more often with oxybutynin ER than darifenacin in another study. Trospium appeared not to cross the blood–brain barrier in healthy individuals and small studies did not show cognitive impairment over six months or twelve weeks, but comparative age-group data are unavailable. Fesoterodine pooled analyses supported 8 mg, not 4 mg, above 75 years; adherence was lower in that age group. A later trial found no twelve-week cognitive difference in vulnerable older people. Pooled mirabegron trials supported efficacy and safety in elderly patients.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.3.1 Applicability of evidence to the general elderly population
document_sections.content: Whether subgroup results from large RCTs apply to the general ageing population is uncertain. Assess and monitor mental function when starting anticholinergics in older patients; no preferred cognition test has achieved consensus.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.3.2 Anticholinergic burden
document_sections.content: When prescribing an additional drug with anticholinergic effects, consider cumulative cognitive exposure. Two reviews of mostly retrospective cohorts associated long-term use with cognitive dysfunction. Longitudinal studies over two to four years found greater cognitive decline with anticholinergic exposure; whether drug-related dysfunction directly increases later dementia risk is unclear.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.3.3 Summary of evidence and additional recommendations for use of anticholinergic and beta-3 agonists in elderly patients
document_sections.content: Anticholinergics and mirabegron are effective in older women with OAB, and mirabegron has shown safety (LE 1b). Cognitive effects of anticholinergic drugs accumulate with exposure in older women (LE 2); oxybutynin may worsen cognition (LE 2). Short-term studies have not demonstrated cognitive dysfunction with darifenacin, fesoterodine, solifenacin or trospium (LE 1b). Strong: use long-term anticholinergics cautiously in older women, especially those with cognitive risk or impairment. Weak: assess anticholinergic burden and co-morbidity before anticholinergic therapy.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.4 Oestrogens
document_sections.content: Oestrogen has been studied orally, transdermally and vaginally for UI. Vaginal therapy principally addresses postmenopausal atrophy; evidence largely concerns SUI and may not apply to predominantly OAB/UUI. Consider GSM when LUTS accompany menopausal vulvovaginal and LUT changes. A review found vaginal oestrogens superior to placebo for objective and subjective GSM measures, while only some trials found benefits for UI, recurrent UTI, urgency or frequency. Doses and formulations did not differ significantly. Compared with vaginal lubricants and moisturisers, objective atrophy measures improved, but subjective outcomes did not. Available evidence does not associate vaginal oestradiol or oestriol with the thromboembolism, endometrial hypertrophy and breast-cancer risks observed with systemic administration.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.4.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for oestrogen therapy
document_sections.content: Vaginal oestrogen may improve GSM symptoms, potentially including OAB (LE 1a). Weak: offer vaginal oestrogen when LUTS coexist with GSM symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.2.5 Placebo and nocebo
document_sections.content: Placebo produces statistically significant OAB symptom improvements, some potentially clinically meaningful. A review of 57 studies involving 12,901 patients reported standardised mean differences of -0.45 for daily micturition episodes, -0.33 for daily nocturia, -0.46 for UUI, -0.50 for daily urgency, -0.51 for daily incontinence and 0.25 for voided volume per micturition. A review of 57 RCTs involving populations with up to 80% females reported nocebo dry mouth averaging 4.9% and constipation 2.6%. Its authors advised clinicians to consider favourable and adverse treatment expectations. The appreciable placebo response supports placebo controls in OAB RCTs.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.1 Bladder wall injection of botulinum toxin A
document_sections.content: OnabotulinumtoxinA (onabotA; BOTOX®) 100 U is licensed in Europe for persistent or refractory OAB with UUI in adults. Other onabotA doses and abobotulinumtoxin A or incobotulinumtoxin A formulations are not licensed for this indication; doses cannot be transferred between brands. Repeat treatment usually retains efficacy, although discontinuation may be common. Important harms are UTI and increased PVR potentially requiring CISC. A review of ten studies involving 2,055 patients found intravesical onabotA improved symptom scores and reduced urgency, UUI, frequency and nocturia versus placebo, without a statistically significant difference in average voided volume or maximum cystometric capacity. Voiding dysfunction and UTI increased significantly at both 100 unit and 200 unit doses. A separate Cochrane review found no significant PVR difference versus placebo. I-QOL improved > 2.5 times from baseline in the onabotA group. Cohorts showed benefit in frail older patients, potentially with lower success and more PVR > 150 mL. Median retreatment-request time across two RCTs was 24 weeks; follow-up over 3.5 years found a median effect duration of 7.5 months. Two RCTs involving 545 patients found more UUI cures than with antimuscarinics, but no significant difference in mean UUI-episode reduction and more voiding dysfunction and UTI. Urodynamic DO did not appear to alter injection outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.1.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for bladder wall injection of onabotulinumtoxinA
document_sections.content: A single onabotA 100 U injection session improves or cures OAB/UUI and improves QoL versus placebo (LE 1a). Reduced efficacy after repeat injection has not been demonstrated, although discontinuation is high (LE 2a). Voiding dysfunction, increased PVR and UTI are risks (LE 1a); post-injection bacteriuria risk is high, with uncertain clinical importance (LE 1b). Compared with antimuscarinics, onabotulinumtoxinA cures UUI more often, yields similar average episode reductions and causes more voiding dysfunction (LE 1a). Strong: offer bladder-wall onabotulinumtoxinA 100 U after conservative or drug treatment fails; first explain limited response duration, UTI risk and possible prolonged CISC.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.2 Sacral nerve stimulation
document_sections.content: SNS places electrodes by sacral roots and stimulates them through an implanted battery; its mechanism is not fully understood. Test stimulation precedes permanent implantation in most centres and is the only reliable success predictor identified. Randomised studies cannot fully blind treatment allocation because participants must respond during a test phase. ROSETTA randomised 386 women with refractory UUI to SNS (n = 194) or onabotA (n = 192): at two years, mean symptom scores and daily UUI reductions did not differ significantly; satisfaction favoured onabotA, whereas recurrent UTIs were 24% versus 10%, respectively. SNS removal and revision rates were 9% and 3% at two years. INSITE assigned 70 patients (94% women) to SNS and 77 (92% women) to antimuscarinics; SNS achieved significantly more successes at six months, defining success as > 50% improvement in daily UUI or frequency. Adverse events occurred in 30% and 27%, respectively, without serious events; implant-site infection and lead migration each occurred in 3.4% of SNS cases. A Cochrane review identified three RCTs mainly comparing immediate with delayed implantation; one found > 90% UUI improvement in 50% versus 1.6% at six months, with unclear QoL benefit. A review with > 6 months follow-up reported dry rates of 43–56%, adverse events in 50% and revision in 33–41%. Success did not differ by presence of urodynamic DO in an RCT subgroup.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.2.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for sacral nerve stimulation
document_sections.content: SNS outperforms continuation of unsuccessful conservative OAB/UUI treatment, though sham controls were absent (LE 1b). It is as effective as onabotA 200 U at 24 months (LE 1b). Among implanted patients, > 50% maintain at least 50% UUI improvement, and 15% may remain cured at four years (LE 3). Strong: offer SNS for OAB/UUI refractory to anticholinergic therapy.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.3 Laser treatment
document_sections.content: A review of short-term vaginal-laser studies found minimal OAB improvement. It included no RCTs, judged study quality weak and lacked long-term safety information.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for laser treatment
document_sections.content: Short-term vaginal-laser studies show minimal OAB symptom benefit and few reported complications, without established long-term efficacy or safety (LE 3). Strong: do not offer vaginal laser for OAB outside a well-regulated clinical research trial.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.4.1 Augmentation cystoplasty
document_sections.content: Augmentation cystoplasty inserts a detubularised bowel segment into a surgically opened bladder. Most evidence comes from neuropathic dysfunction; one study found no outcome difference between sagittal and coronal opening, and open and robotic approaches had similar success, with longer robotic operating time. No RCT directly compares augmentation with other OAB/UUI treatments. A mixed idiopathic/neurogenic series including 51 women reported, at mean follow-up of 74.5 months, 53% continent and satisfied, 25% with occasional leakage and 18% with disabling UUI; outcomes were 58% for idiopathic DO versus 90% for neurogenic UUI. Malignancy was absent from that series but documented elsewhere, with fewer than 60 cases reported worldwide, almost all beyond ten years after surgery. A review spanning five to seventeen years and > 267 cases, including 61 non-neurogenic UUI cases, reported short-term bowel obstruction (2%), infection (1.5%), thromboembolism (1%), bleeding (0.75%) and fistula (0.4%). Longer-term findings included CISC (38%), asymptomatic bacteriuria (70%), changed bowel symptoms (25%), UTI (20%), metabolic disorders (16%), stones (13%), renal deterioration (2%) and bladder perforation (0.75%).

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.4 Cystoplasty/urinary diversion
document_sections.content: This section considers major reconstructive approaches for refractory OAB/UUI, including augmentation cystoplasty, detrusor myectomy and urinary diversion, and their substantial potential complications.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.4.1 Augmentation cystoplasty
document_sections.content: Whether mucolytic agents reduce mucus accumulation is uncertain. The only RCT comparing them found no significant benefit from N-acetylcysteine, aspirin or ranitidine. In a small study (n = 40), subcutaneous octreotide given immediately before surgery and for fifteen days afterward significantly reduced mucus production, irrigation needed to clear blockages and mean hospital stay. Patients should be informed of all potential complications and supported by stoma/continence nurses before and after surgery. Depending on relative costs, augmentation cystoplasty can be cost-effective within 5 years compared with onabotA if complications are infrequent and onabotA has an effect lasting < 5 months.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.4.2 Detrusor myectomy (bladder auto-augmentation)
document_sections.content: This operation incises or removes part of the detrusor to form a mucosal bulge or pseudo-diverticulum, aiming to increase capacity and lower storage pressure. It was initially proposed as an alternative to bladder augmentation in children. Two adult case series involving idiopathic and neurogenic dysfunction found poor long-term outcomes because the pseudo-diverticulum became fibrotic. The technique is now rarely used, if at all.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.4.3 Urinary Diversion
document_sections.content: Urinary diversion remains an option for intractable UI after multiple pelvic interventions, radiotherapy or pelvic disease causing irreversible sphincter incompetence or fistula. Options comprise ileal conduit diversion, orthotopic neobladder and heterotopic neobladder with a Mitrofanoff continent catheterisable conduit. Evidence cannot establish which gives the greatest QoL improvement. A small comparison found no difference in relative risks of UUT infection or uretero-intestinal stenosis between ileal and colonic conduits, but these techniques have not been studied specifically for intractable OAB/UUI. Selection requires detailed preoperative counselling, access to stoma/continence nurses and consideration of patient circumstances and preferences.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4.3.4.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for cystoplasty/urinary diversion
document_sections.content: The evidence table describes limited effectiveness data specifically for idiopathic OAB or UUI, substantial short- and long-term complication risks, frequent CISC after augmentation and no direct evidence comparing augmentation with diversion; its LE entries are 3. Strong: arrange specialist-nurse or equivalent counselling and lifelong support around major OAB surgery. Weak: offer augmentation only after every other option has failed and complications have been explained. Strong: explain the high likelihood of CISC, confirm the patient's ability and willingness to perform it, and explain lifelong surveillance. Weak: do not offer detrusor myectomy for UUI. Weak: reserve diversion for patients who have failed less-invasive OAB/UUI treatment, accept a stoma and understand the possible small malignancy risk.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.5 Follow-up
document_sections.content: Follow-up for women with OAB depends on the intervention and local service capacity, making a uniform schedule difficult. The recommendations draw on best practice and clinical-trial standards.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.5.1 Recommendations for follow-up of patients with overactive bladder
document_sections.content: The table gives Strong recommendations for early review after starting anticholinergic or beta-3 agonist therapy, repeat onabotulinumtoxinA injections when previously effective as needed subject to the manufacturer's minimum interval, and lifelong monitoring of SNS implants for lead movement, malfunction and battery depletion. It gives a Weak recommendation for cystoscopic surveillance after augmentation cystoplasty because of the small malignancy risk.

document_sections.heading: 4.2 Stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: This section addresses the epidemiology, assessment, treatment and follow-up of stress urinary incontinence.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.1 Epidemiology, aetiology, pathophysiology
document_sections.content: SUI means involuntary urinary loss during effort or physical exertion and has substantial social and economic consequences. The estimated number of US women with UI rises from 18.3 million in 2010 to 28.4 million in 2050. SUI prevalence appears highest at ages 45–59 years. Evidence about ethnicity is inconsistent, although several studies find more SUI among white women than African American or Asian American women. Positive associations include parity, obesity, previous hysterectomy or pelvic surgery, diabetes mellitus, pulmonary disease and physical activity level. A meta-analysis of six studies involving 3,678 cases found three times the SUI risk with metabolic syndrome. Two frequently overlapping mechanisms are inadequate bladder-neck and urethral support causing hypermobility, and intrinsic sphincter weakness associated with trauma, radiotherapy, surgery, neurological disease or ageing. Under the vaginal hammock hypothesis, pelvic support normally helps compress and close the urethra; support damage can instead allow downward urethral movement and bladder-neck funnelling during raised abdominal pressure. Nearly all treatments address both mechanisms, but most tend to work better when some urethral hypermobility is present than with isolated sphincter weakness.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.2 Classification
document_sections.content: The Panel distinguishes uncomplicated from complicated SUI. Uncomplicated SUI excludes previous SUI surgery, extensive pelvic surgery or irradiation, neurogenic LUT dysfunction, bothersome genitourinary prolapse, voiding symptoms and LUT-affecting medical conditions; significant additional storage symptoms, particularly OAB, prompt consideration of MUI. Complicated SUI encompasses previous incontinence or extensive pelvic surgery, irradiation, anterior or apical POP, voiding symptoms, neurogenic dysfunction, significant OAB/UUI or congenital abnormalities such as bladder exstrophy. Neurogenic LUT dysfunction is addressed in separate EAU guidance, while POP-associated LUTS are considered elsewhere in this guideline.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3.1 History and physical examination
document_sections.content: History is the agreed first assessment step for UI and helps identify probable SUI, complexity and the need for prompt specialist referral. Although trials offer little evidence that examination improves outcomes, consensus regards it as essential. Examination includes abdominal, vaginal, perineal, POP, PFM-strength and neuro-urological assessment, with an attempt to demonstrate leakage. A standing cough test is more sensitive than a supine test. The ICS standardised female cough test specifies a supine/lithotomy position, 200–400 mL in the bladder and one to four coughs.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3.1.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for history and physical examination
document_sections.content: The evidence table rates the greater sensitivity of a standing versus supine cough stress test LE 1b. Strong: obtain a full history and comprehensive examination, including a standardised cough stress test, for every woman presenting with SUI.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3.2 Patient questionnaires
document_sections.content: Much questionnaire and PROM validation research did not study homogeneous groups of adult women with SUI, limiting applicability. Instruments differ in use for prevalence or outcome assessment, and evidence of responsiveness is inconsistent. No evidence establishes that QoL or condition-specific questionnaires alter treatment results; no single instrument meets every assessment requirement.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3.2.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for patient questionnaires
document_sections.content: The table assigns LE 3 to validated scores assisting UI screening and classification, assessing SUI severity and bother, and condition-specific or general questionnaires measuring health status and treatment-related change. Strong: include an appropriate validated questionnaire in standardised SUI assessment.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3.3 Post-void residual volume
document_sections.content: PVR assessment matters in SUI, particularly with voiding symptoms or POP. The frequency of clinically significant PVR is uncertain because no standard abnormality definition exists; most PVR studies excluded SUI, so extrapolation to non-neurogenic SUI needs caution. A cohort of > 900 women with SUI found good agreement between ultrasound estimates and catheter measurements.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for post-void residual volume
document_sections.content: The table rates as LE 3 both the observation that most women with SUI lack substantial PVR and the ultrasound–catheterisation correlation. Strong: measure PVR particularly with voiding symptoms or complicated SUI; prefer ultrasound to catheterisation; and monitor PVR before interventions, including SUI surgery, that might cause or aggravate voiding dysfunction.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3.4 Urodynamics
document_sections.content: The role of urodynamics for SUI remains disputed. Clinical and cystometric diagnoses can disagree; urethral pressure profilometry and VLPP have poor diagnostic accuracy, MUCP relates only weakly to severity, its reproducibility is disputed, recording methods are not meaningfully interchangeable, and VLPP lacks standardisation and reliable severity assessment. Treatment-outcome prediction is unclear. A Cochrane review of seven RCTs found more avoidance of surgery after urodynamics but no evidence of changed clinical outcomes in trial populations. In an RCT (n = 630), urodynamics altered diagnosis in 56% but not SUI severity or secondary outcomes at twelve months after surgery. Another study found no inferior results when preoperative urodynamics were omitted. Among patients with discordant assessments (n = 109), immediate surgery was not inferior to tailored treatment. In an RCT of 145 women, preoperative VLPP strata (< or > 60 cm H2O) did not relate to outcomes after either synthetic MUS route. Another study instead found that VLPP or MUCP in the lowest quartile predicted synthetic MUS failure at twelve months. The Panel considers routine testing unnecessary for clinically demonstrable uncomplicated SUI, while its role in complicated SUI remains debated. By consensus, carefully consider testing when storage symptoms coexist, the UI type is unclear, voiding dysfunction is suspected, POP is present or SUI surgery was performed previously.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3.4.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urodynamics
document_sections.content: The table rates lack of surgical benefit from preoperative urodynamics in uncomplicated demonstrable SUI LE 1b; inconsistent associations of urethral function tests with surgical outcome and of preoperative DO with MUS failure LE 3. Weak: perform preoperative urodynamics in SUI with storage symptoms, uncertain UI type, suspected voiding dysfunction, POP or previous SUI surgery, and when results might alter invasive treatment selection. Strong: do not use urethral pressure profilometry or leak point pressure to grade UI severity.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3.5 Pad testing
document_sections.content: The guideline directs readers to Section 3.7 and Section 3.7.1 for pad-test diagnostic accuracy, predictive value, evidence and recommendations concerning quantification of SUI.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3.6 Imaging
document_sections.content: Imaging has a limited SUI assessment role: no particular urethro-vesical movement pattern identifies SUI, and greater postpartum mobility does not appear to predict new SUI. Studies suggest MUS reduces mid-urethral rather than bladder-neck mobility, while a larger symphysis-to-sling gap correlates with less chance of cure. In a study of 72 women after synthetic suburethral MUS, trans-labial US suggested that tape position relative to the urethra influences outcome. The broader assessment and follow-up role of US remains uncertain. Imaging can show pelvic-floor structural findings, but no imaging test has predicted SUI treatment outcome and evidence linking levator findings to treatment benefit is limited.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3.6.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for imaging
document_sections.content: The table notes that imaging measures bladder-neck and urethral mobility reliably but has no demonstrated clinical benefit for UI (LE 2b). Strong: omit routine UUT or LUT imaging from SUI assessment.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.1 Obesity and weight loss
document_sections.content: Overweight and obesity are epidemiological risks for LUTS and SUI; UUI and SUI prevalence increase with BMI, and excess weight is common among patients undergoing incontinence surgery. Young elite athletes and women exercising for fitness also have high UI/SUI prevalence. Three SRs and five further RCTs found improvement in UI after weight loss, including surgical weight reduction. In a prospective series of 160 women, bariatric-surgery-associated weight loss significantly improved pelvic-floor disorders including UI. Other prospective single-centre studies found substantially less UI at eleven months and three years after bariatric surgery.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.1.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for obesity and weight loss
document_sections.content: The table identifies obesity as a LUTS/UI risk (LE 3), benefit from non-surgical weight loss (LE 1a) and benefit from surgical weight loss (LE 1b). Strong: encourage overweight or obese women with LUTS/SUI to lose weight and maintain the reduction.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.2 Urinary containment
document_sections.content: The evidence and recommendations for SUI containment draw on the OAB-wet containment literature discussed in Section 4.1.4.1.3 and Section 4.1.4.1.3.1.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.3 Pelvic floor muscle training
document_sections.content: PFMT aims to improve pelvic-floor function and structure and thereby urethral stability. One PFM contraction narrows the levator hiatus, raises urethral closure pressure and lifts the bladder and rectum. An RCT of intensive training over six months versus no treatment found increased strength, endurance and muscle volume alongside structural changes. PFMT can be used for prevention during pregnancy or recovery after birth, but more often treats existing SUI. Clinician observation, palpation or apparatus-based biofeedback may accompany it; electrical stimulation and vaginal cones are also used on a proposed similar mechanistic basis.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.3.1 Efficacy of pelvic floor muscle training
document_sections.content: A Cochrane review found women with SUI receiving PFMT eight times more likely to report cure than controls, with improvements in leakage, QoL, satisfaction and sexual outcomes and an average reduction of one leakage episode per day. Short pad tests favoured PFMT despite heterogeneity; adverse events were uncommon and minor. A review suggested possible additional benefit from biofeedback, but attention and training frequency favoured that arm. An RCT controlling both factors, with 61.3% MUI, found no additional benefit. Group training was cost-effective, and an RCT with matched dosage and attention found it non-inferior to individual treatment; reviewed programmes first assessed and instructed participants individually. Reviews found vaginal cones better than no treatment but could not establish their relative effectiveness against structured PFMT; discomfort, retention difficulties and low adherence occur. Reviews and guidelines cited LE 1a support for PFMT in SUI/MUI, with greater effects from intensive supervision and lesser effects when MUI or UUI is included. NICE recommends three months of supervised first-line PFMT, noting effectiveness comparable to surgery for around half of women with SUI. In an RCT of 460 women with moderate-to-severe SUI comparing PFMT with synthetic MUS, 49% of the physiotherapy arm and 11.2% of the surgery arm crossed over; subjective improvement at twelve months was 64.4% and 90.8%, respectively.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.3.2 Efficacy of electrical stimulation
document_sections.content: There is no consensus on ES for SUI. A Cochrane review judged it probably better than no active treatment for subjective cure with moderate-quality evidence; comparisons with sham, PFMT and other treatments were less certain or supported by low- or very-low-quality evidence. One assessor-blinded RCT found PFMT superior to cones or ES. ES may cause pain or discomfort and is not tolerated by everyone. In an RCT of 132 women initially scoring 0–1 on the modified Oxford grading scale, achievement of score 2 after eight weeks occurred in 63.6% with palpation, 69.7% with palpation plus pelvic tilt, 33.3% with intravaginal ES and 18.2% with verbal instruction. Palpation outperformed ES, including on ICIQ-UI-SF, although one third of the ES group learned contraction. In another RCT of 64 women initially scoring 0-1, contraction was acquired by 36% with ES versus 12% without treatment, with a mean ICIQ-UI-SF advantage of 2 points.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.3.3 Long-term efficacy of pelvic floor muscle training
document_sections.content: A SR followed 1,141 women in nineteen studies for one to fifteen years after SUI PFMT. Heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis; only two studies intervened during follow-up. Loss to follow-up was 0%–39%, long-term adherence 10%–70%, responder-based long-term success 41%–85%, and later surgery 4.9%–58%. Five studies found sustained initial SUI/MUI success. The reviewers considered maintenance of short-term gains possible without ongoing training incentives, while emphasising substantial methodological and treatment heterogeneity.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.3.4 Efficacy of pelvic floor muscle training in childbearing women
document_sections.content: Pregnancy and postpartum studies do not report SUI separately from other UI. A Cochrane review associated antenatal PFMT in women with or without UI with a 26% lower UI risk during pregnancy and the mid-postnatal period. Among initially continent pregnant women, late-pregnancy UI was 62% less likely and UI three to six months after birth had 29% lower risk. Evidence beyond six to twelve months postpartum is insufficient. For women already incontinent antenatally, there is no evidence of reduction in late-pregnancy or postnatal UI versus usual care; certainty ranges from very low to low. Postpartum trials are fewer and include no primary-prevention study. In mixed continent/incontinent postpartum groups, late-postnatal benefit is uncertain (three trials, 826 women; moderate-quality evidence). For persistent postpartum UI, there is no evidence of a difference at more than six to twelve months (three trials; 696 women; low-quality evidence). Another RCT reported persistent UI in 57% with intervention versus 82% of controls and bladder-related problems in 27% versus 60%. Better-quality postpartum RCTs are needed.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.3.5 Efficacy of Pelvic floor muscle training in elderly women
document_sections.content: Few RCTs focus on women > 65 years, and interventions are often combined. PFMT appears similarly effective in older and general populations. A SR covering 23 trials, nine of moderate-to-high quality, found that PFMT with physical exercise reduced UI and improved QoL; prompted voiding and toileting assistance with functional exercise also reduced UI, whereas night-time prompting and waking routines did not. ICI consensus states that age or frailty alone should not exclude patients cognitively able to participate, despite limited frail-elderly evidence. More rigorous studies are needed in frail and healthy women > 80 years of age.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.3.6 Composite treatments for PFMT
document_sections.content: A Cochrane review could not establish added benefit from PFMT alongside other active SUI/MUI therapies; comparisons mostly involved small single trials, and absence of adverse-event reporting limited safety assessment. In a single-blind RCT, peri-operative supervised PFMT added to synthetic MUS improved symptom-defined SUI cure (OR > 3) versus a standard-care handout, but did not improve pad-test continence or postoperative filling and voiding symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.3.7 Summary of evidence and recommendations for pelvic floor muscle training
document_sections.content: The table covers PFMT effectiveness and low adverse-event rates (LE 1a), greater benefit with intensive supervision (LE 1a), no additional biofeedback benefit (LE 1b), potential long-term maintenance (LE 2a), antenatal and postpartum outcomes (LE 1a or 1b), superior MUS results for moderate-to-severe SUI (LE 1b), conflicting evidence about adding ES (LE 2a), and possible ES benefit and assistance with learning contraction (LE 1b). Strong: offer all women with SUI or MUI, including older and antenatal/postnatal women, intensive supervised PFMT for at least three months as first-line treatment; make programmes as intensive as possible; and weigh its efficacy and low adverse-event risk against expected surgical benefit and complications. Weak: consider ES for SUI treatment or for teaching PFM contraction.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.4 Electromagnetic stimulation
document_sections.content: In a double-blind RCT involving 70 women with SUI, EMS produced no outcome advantage over sham.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.1.5 Electroacupuncture
document_sections.content: A SR of 15 RCTs reported that EA improved ICIQ-SF scores and reduced 1-hour leakage compared with sham EA, physical exercise or medication in women with SUI.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.2.1 Oestrogen
document_sections.content: Conjugated equine oestrogens, oestradiol, tibolone and raloxifene are used as HRT. SUI studies have examined oral, transdermal and vaginal oestrogen. Vaginal oestradiol and oestriol do not appear to carry the increased thromboembolism, endometrial hypertrophy and breast-cancer risks associated with systemic treatment; local treatment principally targets postmenopausal vaginal atrophy. A Cochrane SR including seventeen SUI-focused studies found short-term SUI improvement with vaginal oestrogen. Small low-quality comparisons found local oestrogen less likely than PFMT to improve UI, without differences against the other comparators. A ring-versus-pessary trial found similar UI outcomes but greater preference for the ring. One trial reported no significant adverse effects after two years of vaginal oestradiol. Preparations include conjugated equine oestrogen, oestriol and oestradiol delivered through pessaries, rings or creams; optimal duration and long-term outcomes are unknown. A review found vaginal-ring improvement versus placebo and subjective preference over pessaries. An RCT found benefit from adding intravaginal oestriol to ES and PFMT. Large systemic conjugated-equine-oestrogen trials found more new or worsening UI than placebo and no SUI benefit. A single raloxifene RCT found no associated onset or worsening, while two small oral oestriol or oestradiol RCTs suggested improvement but provided unclear evidence.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.2.1.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for oestrogens
document_sections.content: The table records short-term vaginal-oestrogen benefit in postmenopausal SUI (LE 1a), lack of benefit as a surgical adjunct (LE 2b), and lack of improvement and possible worsening with systemic conjugated equine oestrogens (LE 1a). Strong: offer vaginal oestrogen to postmenopausal women with SUI and vulvovaginal atrophy; discuss alternative HRT if SUI develops or worsens during oral conjugated equine oestrogen use.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.2.2 Duloxetine
document_sections.content: Duloxetine inhibits presynaptic reuptake of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT) and noradrenaline (NE), increasing pudendal motor-neuron stimulation and urethral striated-sphincter tone and contraction. Three SRs found greater UI improvement than placebo in female SUI/MUI without a clear difference between conditions; one study found 10% cured, and another found no improvement in its primary UI QoL endpoint. In a comparison using duloxetine, 80 mg daily, leakage fell relative to PFMT or no treatment; combining duloxetine and PFMT improved global outcomes and QoL versus no treatment, while PFMT alone did not differ significantly from no treatment in that trial. Two open-label studies with > 1 year follow-up had substantial withdrawals owing to limited efficacy and adverse events including nausea and vomiting in > 40% of patients, dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, insomnia, somnolence and fatigue. A SR found efficacy alongside greater adverse-event risk, including mental-health problems and suicidal ideation. A meta-analysis of four RCTs in 1,910 women with SUI reported no suicidality, violence or akathisia events but suggested adverse-event withdrawal around one in seven and possible harm exceeding benefit. A separate analysis of twelve placebo-controlled trials involving almost 3,000 patients with major depressive disorders found no significant difference in suicide-related events.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.2.2.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for duloxetine
document_sections.content: The table rates improvement with a low probability of cure LE 1a and potentially substantial gastrointestinal and central nervous system adverse effects with frequent withdrawal LE 1a. Strong: offer duloxetine where licensed to selected patients whose SUI has not responded to other conservative measures and who wish to avoid invasive care, with careful adverse-event counselling. Strong: titrate the dose when starting and stopping.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.2.3 Adrenergic agonists
document_sections.content: A Cochrane SR of 22 RCTs involving 673 women assessed seven adrenergic drugs: phenylpropanolamine in eleven trials, midodrine in two, norepinephrine in three, clenbuterol in another three, terbutaline in one, eskornade in one and Ro 115-1240 in one. Evidence for SUI improvement was weak; adverse effects occurred but were usually minor. Comparisons with other medicines or PFMT need more evidence.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.1 General considerations
document_sections.content: Long-term concerns about polypropylene synthetic MUS have led some countries, including the UK, to pause use. A parliamentary review published in July 2020 recognised benefit for many women but potentially catastrophic complications for others and an unknown true complication count. Reported concerns include pain, recurrent infection, impaired mobility, new or recurrent UI, frequency or prolapse, bleeding, bowel and sexual problems, mesh erosion, autoimmune issues and psychological harm. Clinicians should comply with national or local mesh rules and explain deficiencies in long-term complication evidence. The Panel agrees with recommendations that surgical teams need procedure-specific training and adequate volume, alternative treatment capability, complication-management expertise and long-term follow-up arrangements. It recommends complete registries of operations, patient characteristics and complications. The Panel assessed effectiveness, safety and cost-effectiveness using ESTER and earlier SRs, considering continence, PROMs, complications and general, UI-specific, sexual and bowel QoL. Some studied products are unavailable, limiting transferability of findings. The Panel strongly recommends restricting new devices to structured research and registry monitoring until adequate efficacy and safety evidence exists.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.1.1 Shared decision making
document_sections.content: Shared decision-making is particularly important for SUI surgery because options differ in effectiveness and harm. The Panel calls for patient participation, individualised factual benefit–risk information, disclosure of clinician and institutional expertise, confirmation of understanding, documentation of preferences, time for deliberation and confirmation, and help implementing the final decision.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.1.2 Recommendations for surgical treatment
document_sections.content: All table recommendations are Strong: after conservative options have been explored or failed, offer an appropriate choice of surgical procedures and discuss each one's advantages and disadvantages; limit new SUI devices to structured research with registry or well-regulated-trial outcome monitoring; and use shared decision-making.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2 Surgery for women with uncomplicated stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: The principal procedures assessed for uncomplicated SUI are open or laparoscopic colposuspension, autologous traditional slings, bulking agents and synthetic MUS.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.1 Open- and laparoscopic colposuspension surgery
document_sections.content: Open Burch colposuspension was formerly the benchmark surgical approach for SUI and consequently served as a comparator for newer, less-invasive procedures, including laparoscopic colposuspension.

document_sections.heading: Open colposuspension
document_sections.content: A Cochrane review included 55 trials and 5,417 women, predominantly using open Burch colposuspension as comparator. Complete continence in the first year was 85–90%; recurrent-UI failure was 17% up to five years and 21% at > 5 years. Estimated reoperation was 6% within five years and 10.8% within nine years; repeat surgery specifically for UI was 2%. At five years, enterocoele/vault/cervical prolapse occurred in 42% after Burch versus 23% after TVT, and rectocele in 49% versus 32%; cystocoele rates were 37% versus 41%. The review concluded that open colposuspension treats SUI effectively and that around 70% can expect dryness at five years.

document_sections.heading: Laparoscopic colposuspension
document_sections.content: A Cochrane review of twelve trials found similar subjective cure with laparoscopic and open Burch approaches, with limited evidence of poorer objective outcomes after laparoscopy. The ESTER network meta-analysis of nine trials found better twelve-month effectiveness for open surgery, based on low-quality evidence; SUCRA was 76.7% for open and 48.9% for laparoscopic colposuspension. Laparoscopy involved shorter surgery and hospital stay and might be slightly more cost-effective at 24 months. Single-port laparoscopic Burch is another possible approach, although confirming data are limited.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: ESTER reported voiding difficulty after laparoscopic colposuspension versus retropubic MUS at 7.5% vs. 5.1%. Open colposuspension versus retropubic MUS showed 7.8% vs. 7.5%; OR: 0.87. New urgency/UUI comparisons for open colposuspension and retropubic MUS, 11% vs. 8%, OR: 1.49, favoured neither procedure and had wide confidence intervals. Bladder or urethral perforation was higher with laparoscopic than open colposuspension: 3.7% vs. 0.7%; OR: 4.65.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.1.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for open and laparoscopic colposuspension surgery
document_sections.content: The evidence table reports high subjective cure with both approaches, higher objective cure with open surgery, more long-term POP after colposuspension than MUS, shorter admission and potentially better cost-effectiveness with laparoscopy, more perforation and voiding dysfunction with laparoscopy, and comparable new urgency across SUI operations; all are LE 1a. Strong: offer open or laparoscopic colposuspension to women seeking SUI surgery after a thorough comparison of benefits and risks with other procedures.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.2 Autologous sling
document_sections.content: Rectus-sheath or fascia-lata autologous slings have the strongest evidence among historically used sling materials. ESTER assessed three trials against open colposuspension, six against retropubic MUS and one against transobturator MUS; overall evidence was very low quality. One-year cure estimates favoured fascial slings without statistical significance: OR: 1.24 against open colposuspension, OR: 1.06 against retropubic MUS and OR: 1.44 against transobturator MUS. SUCRA for autologous-fascial-sling cure was 89.4%. A Cochrane subanalysis favoured autologous slings over colposuspension at one to five years. In an RCT, five-year complete continence fell to 24.1% after Burch and 30.8% after fascial sling; satisfaction remained 73% and 83%, respectively, and tracked continence.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Adverse-event rates were similar after Burch and sling, 10% and 9%, but postoperative obstruction occurred only with sling. Voiding difficulty was more common with autologous sling than retropubic MUS (15.4% vs. 10.2%; OR: 1.46). Traditional sling had less bladder or urethral perforation than open colposuspension (0.6% vs. 3.0%; OR:0.20).

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.2.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for autologous sling
document_sections.content: The evidence table associates autologous slings with high SUI cure and higher cure than colposuspension, similar overall adverse-event rates to open colposuspension but more voiding dysfunction and postoperative UTI and less POP and perforation; all LE 1a. Strong: offer an autologous sling to women requesting SUI surgery after discussing its comparative benefits and risks.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.3 Urethral bulking agents
document_sections.content: Injecting material within or around the urethra aims to create cushions, increase outlet resistance and improve continence. A Cochrane SR of 2,004 patients across fourteen trials of multiple agents judged the evidence insufficient to direct practice. A SR of 56 studies supported Bulkamid® and Macroplastique®, reporting short-term efficacy of 30%–90% and 40%–85%, respectively, and long-term efficacy of 42%–70% and 21%–80%; it found no Bulkamid® erosion or migration but did not directly compare agents. A SR of 23 Macroplastique© studies involving 958 patients reported 75% improvement and 43% dryness at < 6 months, and 64% improvement and 36% cure at > 18 months. Among 514 older women, 73% had reduced pad weight at one year irrespective of agent. Population and material heterogeneity and limited follow-up constrain conclusions. Most studies suggested short-term improvement; one RCT found no difference between saline and autologous-fat injection. In 30 women, mid-urethral versus bladder-neck injection showed a weak, non-significant satisfaction advantage without better continence. Retention followed periurethral injection in 30% (six out of 20) versus 5% (one out of 20) after transurethral injection in one small trial. Another small RCT found similar collagen efficacy at mid-urethra and bladder neck. One post-radiotherapy Bulkamid® study reported ~25% short-term cure. Injection is generally safe, with UTI the most frequent adverse event, but autologous fat and hyaluronic acid should not be used because of fatal-embolism and local-abscess risks, respectively. A study associated surgeon volume > 75 career injections with better cure and fewer postoperative hospital contacts, and department volume > 15 procedures yearly with fewer 30-day hospital contacts.

document_sections.heading: Comparison with other surgical procedures
document_sections.content: Two RCTs comparing injections with conventional SUI operations reported better effectiveness but more complications with open surgery. In a primary-SUI non-inferiority trial, TVT yielded better satisfaction and cure than Bulkamid®; cough testing was negative in 95.0% versus 66.4%. A SR quantitatively synthesising six studies and 710 patients found lower subjective improvement with bulking than other surgery (relative risk [RR] = 0.70; 95% CI: 0.53-0.92), but lacked a common objective effectiveness endpoint.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for urethral bulking agents
document_sections.content: The table describes possible short-term SUI improvement and cure (LE 1b), lower cure than MUS, Burch or autologous sling and possible repeat injections (LE 1b), higher adverse-event risk with autologous fat or hyaluronic acid (LE 1a), fewer adverse events than open surgery (LE 2a), no demonstrated best agent (LE 1b), and possible greater retention after peri-urethral than transurethral injection (LE 2b). Strong: offer agents after thorough comparison with surgical alternatives; they may suit women seeking lower procedural risk who understand lower effectiveness, probable repeat treatment and unestablished long-term safety and durability. Strong: do not offer autologous fat or hyaluronic acid as bulking agents.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.4 Laser treatment
document_sections.content: A SR of sixteen studies involving 899 SUI patients reported ICIQ-SF changes at one, two and six months of -5.49, -4.97 and -5.48; 1-hour pad-weight changes at one, three and twelve months were -5.59, -4.96 and -5.82. PISQ-12 increased by 5.39 (95% CI: 1.20-9.58). Type and severity of UI contributed to heterogeneity. Six studies reported adverse effects, generally affecting few patients and resolving without intervention or within days; that SR viewed vaginal laser treatment favourably. Another SR of 31 studies and 1,530 women suggested benefit for prolapse and UI but stressed low-quality evidence, no preferred laser type and absent long-term cost-effectiveness data. A SR of 27 studies, including 23/27 case series (LE:4), found at most modest mild-SUI improvement lasting thirteen to sixteen months with Er:YAG; Fractional CO2 had limited supportive studies and no long-term data. Adverse-event reporting was unsystematic. A sham-controlled study found better ICIQ-UI-SF after Er:YAG, but subjective dryness was 21% versus 4% with sham. Variation in settings and protocols, brief follow-up and inadequate objective and adverse-event reporting mean lasers cannot currently be recommended for SUI.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.4.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for laser treatment
document_sections.content: The table catalogues important methodological and reporting shortcomings in vaginal-laser SUI studies (LE 1b). Strong: do not offer vaginal laser treatment for SUI outside a well-regulated clinical research trial.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.5 Mid-urethral slings
document_sections.content: Early studies specified non-autologous synthetic sling mesh as monofilament, nonabsorbable, typically polypropylene, 1–2 cm wide, macroporous and coloured to assist removal. MUS are the most frequently performed SUI operation for women in Europe.

document_sections.heading: Transobturator route versus retropubic route
document_sections.content: A 2017 Cochrane meta-analysis covering January 1947 to June 2014 found, across 55 studies, broadly comparable short-term subjective cure: retropubic 71–97% and transobturator 62–98%, without a short-term objective-cure difference. ESTER's network analysis of 36 moderately rated trials favoured retropubic MUS at twelve months (OR: 0.74; SUCRA 89.1% vs. 64.1%) without a significant cure difference; symptom-improvement analysis of 40 trials similarly favoured retropubic MUS without significance (RR: 0.76). An equivalence RCT confirmed objective-cure equivalence at twelve but not 24 months; at 24 months rates were 77.3% retropubic and 72.3% transobturator. Success declined over time, and equivalence was not confirmed at 24 and 60 months. At five years, objective success was 51.3% versus 43.4%, a 7.9% retropubic advantage that did not satisfy equivalence criteria; satisfaction remained 79% versus 85%. One study found de novo OAB in 14% ten years after TVT-O. A prospective TOT study identified prior failed continence surgery as the only SUI-recurrence predictor. Retropubic TVT cohort outcomes at ten years were 89.9% objective cure, 76.1% subjective cure and 82.6% high satisfaction. A transobturator cohort reported 78.9% objective and 62.6% subjective cure at 145 months without significant deterioration. Another TVT cohort reported cured or improved proportions of 95.3%, 97.6%, 97.0% and 87.2% at five, seven, eleven and seventeen years. ESTER ranked retropubic MUS, transobturator MUS and traditional sling highest on efficacy, without incorporating complications; short- to medium-term adverse-event data were sparse. Economic findings conflict: a review of 26 evaluations considered MUS among the most cost-effective over ten years; one five-year analysis favoured transobturator over TVT on cost; ESTER estimated retropubic MUS least costly and most effective over a lifetime, with high uncertainty.

document_sections.heading: Insertion using a skin-to-vagina direction versus a vagina-to-skin direction
document_sections.content: A Cochrane review found no short- or medium-term subjective-cure difference between inside-out and outside-in directions. Inside-out TOT may produce more voiding dysfunction but fewer vaginal perforations (RR: 0.25); whether that translates to less erosion remains unclear. Another RCT meta-analysis found similar efficacy and fewer perforations with inside-out insertion (2.6% vs. 11.8%, OR: 0.21). A prospective non-RCT found objective five-year success of 82.6 vs. 82.5%. An E-TOT secondary analysis found nine-year patient-reported success of 63.2% inside-out versus 65.5% outside-in (OR: 1.11), without a difference.

document_sections.heading: Complications of synthetic mid-urethral slings
document_sections.content: ESTER noted incomplete adverse-event data, particularly beyond direct MUS comparisons. Retropubic MUS had more bladder perforation than transobturator MUS (5% vs. 0.2%); 36 studies favoured transobturator MUS for new voiding dysfunction (OR: 0.51). Pain definitions varied substantially. Groin pain was more common with transobturator MUS (6.3% vs. 1.3%; OR: 3.80); the reported suprapubic-pain comparison was 1.2% vs. 4.0%; OR: 0.37 and favoured transobturator MUS. Visceral injury was lower in transobturator groups (0.5% vs. 2.4% OR: 0.36), as were mean operating time, blood loss and hospital stay. Vaginal erosion rates were low and similar; tape exposure/extrusion was 2.1% vs. 2.4%; OR: 1.10. Most contributing studies followed patients < 12 months and few > 2 years. Repeat UI surgery was more common after transobturator MUS (RR = 8.79), on limited low-quality data. A Scottish population study of > 16,000 women found similar mesh and non-mesh complication rates; a UK study of > 92,000 found 9.8% complications using broader criteria and longer follow-up, with poor detail on complication type. These findings require fully informed consent. Available publications do not suggest substantially greater MUS morbidity than other SUI operations overall, although the Panel acknowledges possible under-reporting and limited-quality adverse-event data. ESTER's seven reintervention studies had wide CIs, including twelve-month OR 1.37. At one to five years, repeat continence surgery was 18.3% after transobturator versus 0.5% after retropubic MUS, based on only two studies; longer follow-up showed a similar uncertain trend. Retropubic bottom-to-top insertion was 10% more effective for subjective cure than top-to-bottom and involved less voiding dysfunction, perforation and vaginal erosion.

document_sections.heading: Single-incision mid-urethral slings
document_sections.content: Single-incision devices differ substantially, so class-wide conclusions can mislead; withdrawn devices such as TVT Secur®, Minitape and MiniArc® remain represented in meta-analyses. These procedures may be quicker and cause less early thigh pain, without demonstrated chronic-pain differences. Direct comparisons among devices are insufficient. ESTER's low-quality evidence favoured retropubic and transobturator MUS over single-incision sling at twelve months (TVT, OR: 0.50; TOT, OR: 0.68); single-incision cure SUCRA was 39.8%. Not all devices have comparative RCT evidence. A multicentre non-inferiority RCT of Ajust® and Altis® versus conventional MUS followed patients for 36 months. At that time, patient-reported success was 177 of 246 (72.0%) with single-incision and 157 of 235 (66.8%) with MUS. Investigators concluded non-inferiority at fifteen months and similarly maintained success proportions at 36 months.

document_sections.heading: Complications of single-incision slings
document_sections.content: Mesh erosion/extrusion was similar between single-incision and transobturator MUS (4.8% vs. 3.7%; OR: 1.23). Postoperative pain was higher after retropubic MUS than single-incision surgery (19.2% vs. 6.8%; OR: 0.21). In a non-inferiority RCT at 36 months, groin or thigh pain was 14.1% versus 14.9%, mesh exposure 3.3% versus 1.9%, and additional SUI surgery 2.5% versus 1.1%. Another RCT comparing Ajust® (n = 100) with standard TOT (n = 56) found significantly less immediate pain with single-incision sling, non-significantly more new dyspareunia (38.5% vs. 25%), and twelve-month objective cure of 90% vs. 88%. ESTER reported unspecified pain comparisons at twelve months of 1.0% vs. 5.2%; OR: 0.24, and at 24 months of 1.4% vs. 10.4%; OR: 0.16, favouring single-incision over transobturator MUS. Repeat surgery was 5.1% vs. 2.9%; OR: 1.57 and, at > 3 years, 10.3% vs. 7.6%; OR: 1.42, respectively.

document_sections.heading: Sexual function after synthetic mid-urethral sling surgery
document_sections.content: A SR found contradictory sexual-function outcomes after synthetic MUS, although more studies reported improvement or stability as coital incontinence, anxiety and avoidance diminished. Dyspareunia was the commonest reason for deterioration and its frequency is difficult to establish because of incomplete reporting. A meta-analysis suggested more improvement after single-incision than standard MUS but found conflicting evidence. A recent RCT found broadly similar QoL and sexual outcomes except dyspareunia: among 290 questionnaire respondents, 11.7% reported it after single-incision versus 4.8% after conventional MUS.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.5.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for mid-urethral slings
document_sections.content: The evidence table covers retropubic cure versus colposuspension (LE 1a); similar one-year outcomes between retropubic and transobturator MUS (LE 1a) but better longer-term retropubic cure (LE 1b); durability beyond 10 years (LE 2b); route-specific perforation, voiding dysfunction and groin pain (LE 1a); insertion-direction results up to nine years (LE 2a or 1b); non-inferiority of Ajust® and Altis® at fifteen and 36 months, shorter operation, less blood loss and immediate pain, but more mesh exposure, repeat surgery and dyspareunia at 3 years (LE 1b). Evidence on other single-incision adverse outcomes is absent (LE 1b); sexual-function findings conflict (LE 1a). Much single-incision evidence concerns a discontinued device. Strong: offer MUS after discussing comparative benefits and risks; explain superior long-term outcomes with retropubic versus transobturator insertion, complications and alternatives; explain that Ajust® and Altis® appear similarly effective in the short term but that long-term single-incision effectiveness is uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.6 Other treatments for uncomplicated stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Vesair® is a gas-filled bladder balloon intended to dampen intravesical pressure changes rather than increase outlet resistance. Two sham-controlled RCTs reported significantly less UI and pad weight but no significant QoL difference, alongside frequent adverse events and device removal or withdrawal. Dysuria, urgency, visible haematuria and UTI were most common. Mechanical devices support the bladder neck or urethra or occlude the lumen; an eight-RCT Cochrane review and another SR found insufficient or inconclusive evidence versus no treatment, between devices or against other approaches. Better trials are needed. Reviews support investigation of ACT® and AUS compression devices, which are largely reserved for recurrent or complicated SUI but have also been used in uncomplicated cases.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.2.6.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for other treatments for uncomplicated stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: The table describes possible improvement or cure with artificial sphincter and possible ACT® improvement, alongside frequent complications, malfunction and explantation; each statement is LE 3. Strong: restrict mechanical devices for mild-to-moderate SUI after conservative-treatment failure to well-conducted research trials. Strong: explain substantial malfunction, complication and explantation risks with AUS or ACT®, despite possible cure.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.3 Surgery for women with complicated stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: This section addresses complicated SUI as previously defined; associated prolapse is addressed separately. Principal options include colposuspension or synthetic/autologous sling after failed primary surgery, ACT® or AUS compression devices, and adjustable slings.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.3.1 Colposuspension or mid-urethral sling (synthetic or autologous) following failed primary stress urinary incontinence surgery
document_sections.content: UI after SUI surgery can reflect persistent or recurrent SUI, new UUI or both, requiring careful evaluation including urodynamics. Most surgical evidence concerns primary procedures; secondary-treatment groups are too small or incompletely reported to establish a preferred recurrent-SUI operation. ESTER found more repeat surgery after transobturator than retropubic MUS. An update of two trials reported five-year retreatment-free survival of 87% after Burch, 96% after autologous fascial sling, 97% after transobturator MUS and 99% after retropubic MUS; retreatments comprised autologous fascial sling (19), bulking agent (18) and synthetic sling (1). The authors suggested MUS may not be preferred in recurrent SUI. Across these cohorts, 6% underwent retreatment within five years, mostly injections or fascial sling, and not all women with recurrent SUI chose surgery. A Cochrane review identified 58 records but none eligible for quantitative recurrent-SUI analysis, leaving no basis to endorse or reject a particular strategy after failed MUS. A twelve-study SR reported subjective cure of 78.5% after repeat MUS following any operation at mean 29 months, and 73.3% after failed MUS at sixteen months; its authors favoured retropubic over transobturator tape. A conflicting SR of ten RCTs and 350 women at mean 18.1 months found no significant cure/improvement differences between MUS routes or between Burch and retropubic MUS. Older evidence suggested poorer repeat-Burch outcomes than autologous fascial sling; one non-randomised series after more than two previous operations reported cure of 0% with Burch and 38% with fascial sling.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.3.1.1 Summary of evidence for surgery in those with recurrent stress urinary incontinence following failed primary surgery
document_sections.content: The evidence table records apparently higher single-incision failure and higher repeat-surgery incidence after primary transobturator than retropubic MUS (LE 1a), apparently higher five-year Burch failure than sling procedures (LE 2b), inconsistent evidence favouring retropubic MUS for recurrent SUI (LE 1a), lower effectiveness of most second-line procedures (LE 2a), similar short-term Burch and TVT cure in recurrence (LE 1b), and apparently better recurrent-SUI results with autologous sling than Burch (LE 2b).

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.3.2 Adjustable slings
document_sections.content: Adjustable slings are used mainly for complicated SUI but may be considered for uncomplicated SUI. No outcome RCTs exist; cohort studies vary in selection and definitions and generally have small samples or short follow-up. A prospective Remeex study of 230 women found, at mean 89 months, 165 cured (71.7% ITT; 80.5% PP), 40 still incontinent (17.4% ITT; 19.5% PP), and 88 needing readjustment. Tension was increased in 82 for recurrent SUI and decreased in six for obstruction. Differences in device designs prevent reliable class-wide conclusions.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.3.2.1 Summary of evidence for adjustable slings
document_sections.content: The table describes only low-level evidence of possible adjustable-MUS benefit (LE 3) and no evidence of superiority over standard MUS (LE 4).

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.3.3 External compression devices
document_sections.content:
ACT® and AUS are intracorporeal urethral compression devices usually used after previous failed surgery, particularly for marked intrinsic sphincter failure, although primary use is possible. ACT® positions two adjustable balloons beside the bladder neck. A SR of eight studies published between 2007 and 2013, with one to six years of follow-up, reported perceived cure in 15–44%, satisfaction in 66–78.4% and explantation in 19–31%, together with significantly fewer daily pads and improved QoL. Its authors considered ACT® a possible less-invasive option, especially after failed standard surgery. AUS series comprised 45–215 women followed from one month to 25 years, with heterogeneous selection. Subjective cure was 59–88%, revision for mechanical failure < 42% at ten years and explantation 5.9–15%. Among 215 women followed for mean six years, older age, previous Burch and pelvic irradiation predicted failure.

Early reports of laparoscopically implanted AUS include too few patients and insufficient follow-up to support conclusions.

A review of seventeen non-comparative case series found that 69.1–100% of women had undergone previous anti-incontinence surgery before AUS implantation. Complete continence ranged from 61–100%; explantation from 0–45%; erosion from 0–22%; and mechanical failure from 0–44%. The review concluded that AUS can produce excellent functional outcomes for SUI due to intrinsic urethral sphincter deficiency, although morbidity is high.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.3.3.1 Summary of evidence for external compression devices
document_sections.content: The evidence summary, graded LE 3 throughout, indicates that an artificial sphincter can improve or cure SUI caused by sphincter insufficiency, and that AUS and ACT® may improve complicated SUI. Complications, mechanical failure and explantation are frequent with both devices. AUS explantation is more frequent in older women and after Burch colposuspension or pelvic radiotherapy.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.3.4 Recommendations for complicated stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Strong: Restrict management of complicated SUI to centres with suitable experience. Strong: Select surgery for recurrent SUI after careful individual assessment, considering investigations such as cystoscopy and multichannel urodynamics when appropriate. Weak: Explain that a procedure used second-line generally has lower efficacy and more complications than when used first-line. Strong: Use an adjustable mid-urethral sling as primary SUI surgery only within a structured research programme. Weak: Consider a secondary synthetic sling, bulking agents, Burch colposuspension, an autologous sling or AUS for complicated SUI. Strong: Explain to women offered AUS or ACT® that cure is possible but complications, mechanical failure and explantation remain substantial risks even in expert centres.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.4 Surgery for stress urinary incontinence in special patient groups
document_sections.content: This section examines SUI surgery in women with obesity and in older women.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.4.1 Stress urinary incontinence surgery in obese women
document_sections.content: Evidence on surgical outcomes in obese women is not consistent. A secondary RCT analysis, stratified at BMI < 30 and > 30, found objective dryness of 85.6% vs. 67.8% at one year and 87.4% vs. 65.9% at five years; subjective cure was 85.8% vs. 70.7% at one year and 76.7% vs. 53.6% at five years. Among patients initially dry after surgery, 6.7% at one year and 16.3% at five years subsequently had a positive pad test. Conversely, a MiniArc® study found objective cure at two years of 86% in non-obese and 81% in obese women, with similar questionnaire improvement. Altis® objective cure at two years was likewise similar: 88% and 87%, respectively.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.4.2 Stress urinary incontinence surgery in elderly women
document_sections.content: Age may affect SUI surgical results, but findings conflict. In an RCT of 537 women, increasing age above 50 years independently predicted failure; another RCT of 162 women linked age to recurrence at one year. A trial-cohort analysis of 655 women at two years found more positive stress tests and SUI retreatment, and less reported improvement in stress symptoms and UUI, among older women; time to normal postoperative voiding did not differ. An RCT comparing immediate TVT with no or delayed surgery in older women found benefits in QoL and satisfaction but more complications with surgery. A review found MUS successful in patients aged > 65 years, with persistent SUI reported by 5.2–17.6%; it found no age-group difference in de novo UUI, persistent UUI or persistent SUI.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4.3.4.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for stress urinary incontinence surgery in special patient groups
document_sections.content: The evidence summary states that surgery can be performed safely in obese women, although benefit may be lower (LE 1). Failure and adverse-event risks appear to increase with age (LE 2b); no procedure has demonstrated superior efficacy or safety specifically in older women (LE 4). Weak: Inform women with obesity or older women with SUI about increased surgical risks and a lower likelihood of benefit.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.5 Follow-up
document_sections.content: SUI follow-up depends on treatment. Conservative or physical treatment needs enough time for its effect to become apparent; drug treatment warrants early review. Most surgical procedures require short-term review of efficacy and early complications. The Panel supports long-term registry assessment and notes the shortage of high-quality long-term surgical complication data.

document_sections.heading: 4.3 Mixed urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: MUI encompasses balanced stress and urgency symptoms, predominance of either component, and USUI or USI with DO or with clinical urgency but without DO. This breadth complicates comparisons of treatment and outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.1 Epidemiology, aetiology and pathophysiology
document_sections.content: Population prevalence and subtype-specific risks remain uncertain because studies differ in definitions, questionnaires, populations, response rates and outcomes. Most studies place MUI second to SUI, with prevalence of 7.5–25%; approximately one-third of women with UI may have MUI. In a secondary trial analysis of 655 women, patient-reported questionnaires classified 50−90% as MUI, whereas objective urodynamic criteria classified only 8%. MUI generally combines factors involved in SUI and UUI. Oestrogen deficiency and histological or microstructural abnormalities may contribute. One proposed mechanism links sphincter and bladder-neck incompetence during stress to a urethro-detrusor reflex; another study found that urine passing across urethral mucosa increased micturition-reflex excitability. A single mechanism is unlikely to explain all presentations.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.2 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Assessment starts with a detailed urinary history and follows the general LUTS diagnostic pathway. Categorising MUI by its predominant stress or urgency component is conventional.
