Presentations vary: detrusor contractions may be stress-provoked, spontaneous or absent despite urgency-associated leakage. Some women experience urgency without UUI because the sphincter prevents leakage. The contribution of urodynamics is uncertain, although objective assessment of SUI and DO may assist counselling about initial treatment.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.2.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnosis of mixed urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Evidence does not show that urodynamics changes MUI treatment outcomes (LE 3). Strong: Obtain a thorough history and examination. Weak: Identify stress-predominant or urgency-predominant MUI when possible. Strong: Include bladder diaries and urodynamics in multimodal assessment to inform management.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3 Disease management
document_sections.content: The guideline considers conservative, pharmacological and surgical management of MUI.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3.1 Conservative management
document_sections.content: Women with MUI generally have more severe symptoms and respond less well than women with SUI or UUI alone. Clinicians are encouraged to start with conservative treatment directed at the most troublesome component and reserve surgery for last.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3.1.1 Pelvic floor muscle training
document_sections.content: An RCT of 71 women found no difference between PFMT with or without an audiotape; mean daily leakage episodes fell from 3.9 overall to 3.2 among participants with MUI. Six months after exercise, approximately one third of all participants still reported good or excellent improvement and wanted no further therapy. An RCT of 34 women with SUI or MUI found that eight weeks of PFMT improved PFM strength and QoL and reduced UI episodes versus no treatment; another RCT supported these findings. In a trial of 467 women with moderate-to-severe MUI, EA delivered in 36 sessions over twelve weeks with 24 weeks of follow-up was non-inferior to PFMT–solifenacin 5 mg/day over 36 weeks for reducing 72-hour leakage episodes; the between-group difference was –1.34%. In a comparison of behavioural therapy plus PFMT and MUS against MUS alone, twelve-month data were available for 416 (86.7%) participants. UDI scores fell from 178.0 to 30.7 with combined treatment and from 176.8 to 34.5 with sling alone; the estimated between-group difference did not reach the minimal clinically important threshold. Adherence was not reported. A Cochrane review of 31 RCTs included only one MUI study and one UUI study, neither reporting subgroup cure, improvement or episode counts. Evidence did not establish additional benefit from biofeedback in a predominantly MUI population.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3.1.2 Bladder training
document_sections.content: The ICI 2017 considered PFMT and BT effective first-line conservative options for UUI or MUI. An RCT allocated 108 women—SUI n = 50, UUI n = 16 and MUI n = 42—to six weeks of BT plus PFMT or BT alone. More participants reported cure and symptom improvement with combined therapy overall and in the SUI and MUI subgroups.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3.1.3 Electrical stimulation
document_sections.content: A Cochrane review included SUI and stress-predominant MUI; twenty-five percent of trials had high risk of bias, including baseline imbalance or industry funding. Low-quality evidence favoured ES over no active treatment or sham for subjective SUI cure or improvement.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3.2 Summary of evidence and recommendations for conservative management in mixed urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: PFMT appears less effective in MUI than SUI alone (LE 2), but improves UI and QoL compared with no treatment (LE 1a). Combining BT with PFMT may help (LE 1b). Weak: Address the most bothersome MUI symptom first. Strong: Offer BT first-line to adults with MUI. Strong: Offer every woman with MUI, including older and postnatal women, supervised intensive PFMT for at least three months as first-line treatment.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3.3 Pharmacological management
document_sections.content: Many RCTs enroll MUI with predominantly stress or urgency symptoms, but few separately report MUI outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3.3.1 Anticholinergics
document_sections.content: In an RCT of 854 women with MUI, tolterodine ER improved UUI but not SUI, suggesting that concomitant SUI did not diminish its UUI effect. Another study of n = 1,380 found comparable reductions in urgency and UUI with tolterodine irrespective of associated SUI. Similar findings were reported for solifenacin.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3.3.2 Duloxetine
document_sections.content: An RCT of 588 women stratified MUI into stress-predominant, urgency-predominant and balanced groups. Duloxetine improved incontinence and QoL in all groups, with better findings in stress-predominant MUI. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 61.3% and discontinuation in 15.7%; adverse events were more frequent with concomitant antidepressants. Secondary analysis of another RCT (n = 553) found equal efficacy in SUI and MUI but reported no adverse-event data.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3.3.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for pharmacological management of mixed urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Limited evidence supports anticholinergics for the UUI component of MUI (LE 2). Duloxetine improves SUI and MUI symptoms but has high adverse-event rates (LE 1b). Weak: Treat the most troublesome symptom first. Strong: Offer anticholinergics or beta-3 agonists for urgency-predominant MUI. Weak: Where licensed, offer duloxetine to selected patients with stress-predominant MUI who have not responded to other conservative treatment and wish to avoid invasive treatment, after careful adverse-event counselling.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3.4 Surgical management
document_sections.content: MUI surgical choices encompass the anti-incontinence operations described for SUI, but RCTs rarely provide separate MUI results. Post hoc analyses associated preoperative urgency, particularly greater urgency severity, with poorer results after autologous fascial sling, Burch colposuspension or MUS; an earlier study instead reported similar outcomes irrespective of urgency. An RCT of 93 patients with MUI found better continence and QoL with TVT plus botulinum toxin A (Botox®) than with either alone. A secondary TVT analysis found no difference between inside-out and outside-in transobturator approaches at nine years: patient-reported success was 63.2% and 65.5%, respectively. Single-incision sling trial results can be generalised to predominant SUI without other severe LUT dysfunction, but do not adequately guide surgical choice in MUI, severe POP or previous SUI surgery. Research should define MUI precisely and compare treatments in well-defined MUI populations.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3.4.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for surgery in patients with mixed urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: SUI surgery cures UI less often in women with MUI than in women with SUI alone (LE 2); its effect on existing urgency is unpredictable (LE 1b). Weak: Treat the most bothersome MUI symptom first. Strong: Warn that MUI surgery is less likely to succeed than surgery for SUI alone. Weak: Explain that a single intervention may not resolve UI and that other components may also need treatment.

document_sections.heading: 4.4 Underactive bladder
document_sections.content: ICS defines UAB by slow stream, hesitancy and straining, with possible incomplete-emptying sensation and storage symptoms; diagnosis is clinical, and presentation and causes vary. DU instead denotes a urodynamic contraction of insufficient strength and/or duration causing delayed or incomplete emptying. An acontractile detrusor has no measurable contraction. ICS-defined female voiding dysfunction combines symptoms and investigation findings of abnormally slow and/or incomplete urination, preferably confirmed repeatedly; pressure–flow testing may be needed to identify its cause.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.1 Epidemiology, aetiology, pathophysiology
document_sections.content: This section describes the variable frequency, causes and mechanisms of female UAB and DU.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.1.1 Epidemiology
document_sections.content: Inconsistent DU definitions and overlap with other symptoms complicate characterisation of UAB. Reported prevalence in women is 12-45%, increasing with age and in institutionalised older women; ambulatory DU estimates are around 12–19%. In a population internet survey of 15,861 women aged > 40 years, weak flow affected 20.1%, incomplete emptying 27.4% and terminal dribbling 38.3%. Filling-phase DO and voiding-phase DU can coexist; one study found this in over 30% of older women.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.1.2 Aetiology
document_sections.content: DU appears multifactorial. Idiopathic cases may partly reflect age-related loss of contractility, although young women can also be affected. Secondary causes include neurological disorders or pelvic nerve injury; myogenic contributors such as prolonged overdistension, diabetes mellitus and BOO; and iatrogenic causes such as pelvic surgery.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.1.3 Pathophysiology
document_sections.content: UAB may involve failed integration or processing in central circuits, impaired detrusor activation through efferent pathways, premature termination of the voiding reflex through afferent pathways, or loss of intrinsic muscle contractility. A cause may act at several sites: diabetes mellitus mainly affects afferent pathways and detrusor muscle, while neurological disease may affect central, efferent and afferent pathways. Figure 1 relates sites of dysfunction, major aetiological factors and proposed mechanisms.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.2 Classification
document_sections.content: No established UAB classification exists. Presumed cause or mechanism can be used descriptively, but longitudinal and high-level evidence is insufficient for a clinically or prognostically useful classification.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.3 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Clinical symptoms and urodynamic assessment contribute to evaluation, although symptoms alone cannot reliably identify DU.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.3.1 Symptoms associated with detrusor underactivity
document_sections.content: A retrospective study of 1,788 patients, including 1,281 women, defined female DU using PdetQmax < 20 cm H2O, Qmax < 15 mL/s, BVE < 90% and no video-urodynamic obstruction. Compared with women with normal pressure and flow, affected women significantly more often had weak or interrupted flow, hesitancy, incomplete-emptying sensation, palpable bladder and reduced or absent sensation. A small qualitative study reported both storage and voiding symptoms in over half of patients, with storage symptoms generally more bothersome. No defining symptom or symptom cluster can currently identify DU. ICIQ-UAB was developed as a research PROM.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.3.2 Urodynamic studies
document_sections.content: Uroflowmetry, PVR and BVE may help identify possible DU but overlap with BOO; invasive pressure–flow studies alone reliably distinguish them, and both may coexist. Women may void through pelvic-floor relaxation without detectable detrusor contraction or raised abdominal pressure. There is no agreed diagnostic cut-off. In a retrospective study of 1,015 women, DU prevalence was 14.9% with Qmax < 12 mL/s or PVR > 150 mL; 9.6% with PdetQmax < 30 cm H2O plus Qmax < 10 mL/s; and 6.4% with PdetQmax < 20 cm H2O, Qmax < 15 mL/s and BVE < 90%. Watt’s factor, PIP, BCI and Projected isovolumetric pressure 1 estimate aspects of contraction strength; PIP and BCI were developed mainly in men, whereas Projected isovolumetric pressure 1 was developed in women. Among voluntary, mechanical and continuous-occlusion stop tests, a study found the continuous-occlusion test most reliable and most sensitive to drug-induced changes, with similar mechanical-test results. These measurements describe a particular void rather than potential optimal performance, do not measure contraction duration and do not establish that low measured strength prevents adequate emptying. Table 4 compares the commonly used female detrusor-contraction parameters, their basis, study populations and reported values.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4 Disease management
document_sections.content: Multiple UAB mechanisms make prevention and treatment difficult to define. Early recognition after major surgery or labour might limit harm from prolonged overdistension; nerve-sparing radical pelvic surgery favours earlier bladder-function recovery. Female DU treatment may ensure drainage, increase contraction, lower outlet resistance or combine approaches. Goals include symptom and QoL improvement, complication reduction and recognition of situations in which intervention is inappropriate.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.1 Conservative management
document_sections.content: Conservative approaches include altered voiding behaviour, pelvic-floor relaxation, catheter-based drainage and intravesical stimulation.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.1.1 Behavioural interventions
document_sections.content: Scheduled voiding is used to avoid overdistension when bladder sensation is impaired. Abdominal straining with pelvic-floor relaxation and double or triple voiding may improve emptying, but no RCT has established efficacy. Excessive abdominal straining may be associated with POP; a small retrospective study in neurogenic acontractile detrusor suggested more rectal prolapse with Valsalva voiding than with CISC.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.1.2 Pelvic floor muscle relaxation training with biofeedback
document_sections.content: There are no RCTs of this intervention in adult women with UAB. Individual studies observed PFM relaxation after contraction and faster relaxation after training. Paediatric evidence, including an RCT, found that adding biofeedback-assisted relaxation to a combined programme increased voiding episodes, reduced PVR and voiding time, and significantly increased maximum flow relative to the combined programme alone.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.1.3 Clean intermittent self-catheterisation
document_sections.content: CISC is the most frequently used therapy for high PVR or retention and reduces complications associated with incomplete emptying. Comparative effects of clean versus sterile IC, coated versus uncoated catheters and other regimens are not established. Hydrophilic catheters might reduce UTI, but supporting data come from neurogenic populations. Average use is four to six times daily, commonly with 12–16 Fr catheters; five daily aseptic catheterisations reduced UTI in one report. Frequency must fit individual needs and abilities while avoiding recurrent overfilling. Candidates require detailed instruction on technique, frequency, equipment and harms. A Cochrane review found no superior catheter or regimen; a narrative review suggested single-use catheters might reduce trauma and UTI in certain populations.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.1.4 Indwelling catheter
document_sections.content: An indwelling catheter may be an option after other treatments fail when a woman cannot perform CISC. Potential complications are UTI, stones and urethral injury. Suprapubic rather than urethral placement may lessen urethral pain and trauma.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.1.5 Intravesical electrical stimulation
document_sections.content: IVES stimulates A-delta mechanoreceptor afferents and requires intact afferent pathways and healthy detrusor muscle. In a retrospective study of sixteen patients, eleven female, two-thirds of those with weak detrusor after prolonged overdistension regained balanced voiding.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.2 Pharmacological management
document_sections.content: Drug approaches discussed for UAB include parasympathomimetics, alpha-adrenergic blockers and intravesical prostaglandins.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.2.1 Parasympathomimetics
document_sections.content: Proposed drug approaches stimulate detrusor muscarinic receptors with carbachol or bethanechol, or inhibit acetylcholinesterase with distigmine, pyridostigmine or neostigmine. A review of ten RCTs found significant improvement in three, none in six and significant worsening in one; it established no meaningful drug-specific or outcome-specific differences. Its authors concluded that the studies do not support parasympathomimetics for UAB, particularly given frequent or serious gastrointestinal symptoms, blurred vision, bronchospasm and bradycardia.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.2.2 Alpha-adrenergic blockers
document_sections.content: Lowering outlet resistance through sympathetic blockade has been investigated to improve emptying. A prospective tamsulosin study reported good uroflowmetry responses in 39.4% of women with BOO and 32.7% with DU. A longitudinal study of fourteen women with DU reported clinical and urodynamic improvement with tamsulosin. A single-blind RCT found the best results with combined alpha-blocker and cholinergic treatment rather than either alone.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.2.3 Prostaglandins
document_sections.content: Prostaglandins E2 and F2 promote smooth-muscle contraction and have been administered intravesically for postoperative retention. A Cochrane review associated treatment with successful voiding, but success was 32% with a wide 95% CI; included RCTs were underpowered, methodologically limited and yielded very low-certainty evidence. Treatment is rarely used and needs further study.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.3 Surgical management
document_sections.content: The interventions discussed are SNS, urethral-sphincter onabotulinumtoxinA, bladder-neck incision and detrusor myoplasty.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.3.1 Sacral nerve stimulation
document_sections.content: SNS is often used for non-obstructive retention; proposed mechanisms include sensory-afferent and central modulation and inhibition of the guarding reflex, but its mechanism is not established. An RCT allocated 37 patients to implantation and 31 to standard medical therapy and reported lower mean PVR and higher mean voided volume with implantation. A meta-analysis of seven studies found mean PVR reduction of 236 mL and mean voided-volume increase of 299 mL. Trial-phase response ranged from 33-90% (mean 54.2%) and permanent-implant success from 55-100% (mean 73.9%). Selection is important; one study suggested lower response with anatomical BOO, suspected intrinsic loss of detrusor contractility or neurogenic dysfunction.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.3.2 Onabotulinumtoxin A
document_sections.content: Injections of onabotulinumtoxinA into the external striated urethral sphincter may reduce outlet resistance and guarding reflex activity in DU. Retrospective cases report better symptoms, spontaneous voiding and urodynamic measures. Relief usually lasts three months; reported de novo SUI incidence is low.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.3.3 Transurethral incision of the bladder neck
document_sections.content: A retrospective refractory-DU series found satisfactory spontaneous voiding with efficiency > 50% in 40/82 (48.8%) women. Five (6.1%) developed SUI and two (2.4%) a vesico-vaginal fistula.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.3.4 Myoplasty
document_sections.content: One retrospective multicentre study of latissimus dorsi detrusor myoplasty for an acontractile bladder reported complete spontaneous voiding recovery in 71%, with mean PVR of 25 mL. Independent replication has not been published.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.4 Summary of therapeutic evidence on detrusor underactivity
document_sections.content: Evidence for most DU interventions is weak. Despite limited supporting evidence, CISC remains the standard means of reducing adverse consequences of high PVR and incomplete emptying.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.4.4.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for underactive bladder
document_sections.content: The evidence table covers behavioural emptying, PFM relaxation, drainage, stimulation, medicines and surgery, with LE 3 for most interventions; parasympathomimetics are graded 1b, alpha-blockers 2b, intravesical prostaglandins 1a with very low certainty, and SNS 1b. Weak: Encourage double voiding when complete emptying is not possible and warn women with UAB who strain about POP risk. Strong: Use CISC as standard treatment when patients cannot empty the bladder and thoroughly teach its technique and risks. Weak: Use indwelling urethral or suprapubic drainage only if other drainage approaches fail or are unsuitable; do not routinely recommend IVES. Strong: Do not routinely recommend parasympathomimetics. Weak: Offer alpha-blockers before more-invasive interventions; restrict postoperative-retention intravesical prostaglandins to well-regulated clinical trials; and consider external-sphincter onabotulinumtoxinA before more-invasive treatment after explaining the low-quality evidence. Strong: Offer SNS for UAB refractory to conservative treatment. Weak: Do not routinely offer detrusor myoplasty for DU.

document_sections.heading: 4.4.5 Follow-up
document_sections.content: The long-term natural history of female DU is poorly understood, with no described longitudinal cohorts. Follow-up intervals depend on patient features, treatment and urinary-complication frequency.

document_sections.heading: 4.5 Bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: ICS defines BOO by raised detrusor pressure together with reduced urinary flow during voiding; precise diagnosis requires pressure–flow urodynamics. Female voiding dysfunction may arise from BOO, DU or non-obstructive causes, so it is not synonymous with BOO. Dysfunctional voiding is a distinct condition involving intermittent or fluctuating flow caused by involuntary intermittent peri-urethral striated-muscle contraction in neurologically normal individuals.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2 Epidemiology, aetiology, pathophysiology
document_sections.content: Female BOO varies in reported frequency and may have anatomical or functional causes.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.1 Epidemiology
document_sections.content: Estimated female BOO prevalence ranges from 2.7-29%; a large LUTS urodynamic series diagnosed ~20%. Variation reflects diagnostic definitions, populations and study methods. Estimated BOO-related LUTS prevalence is 18.7–18.9% in women versus 24.3–24.7% in men. Voiding LUTS correlate with age, parity, prolapse and previous continence surgery. In a referred series of 1,142 women, storage symptoms could predominate: 69% reported excess daytime frequency.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.2 Pathophysiology
document_sections.content: Anatomical BOO entails physical blockage, including external compression, fibrosis, stricture, urethral injury or prolapse-related kinking; peri-urethral fibrosis after mesh tape or sling surgery may contribute. In one retrospective series of 192 women, 64% had mechanical obstruction. Functional BOO involves non-anatomical, non-neurogenic failure of bladder-neck, sphincter or PFM relaxation, or increased tone or contraction during voiding. Proposed causes include sympathetic hyperactivity or bladder-neck smooth-muscle hypertrophy in primary bladder-neck obstruction and learned behaviour in dysfunctional voiding, although exact causes often remain unclear.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2.3 Aetiology
document_sections.content: Associated anatomical conditions include POP, prior incontinence surgery, urethral stricture or stenosis, diverticulum, caruncle, malignancy and paraurethral masses. Functional associations include primary bladder-neck obstruction, dysfunctional voiding and Fowler’s syndrome. The bladder neck fails to open adequately without anatomical blockage in primary bladder-neck obstruction, estimated in 4.6–16% of women presenting with voiding symptoms. Dysfunctional voiding involves intermittent involuntary peri-urethral or levator contraction in neurologically normal women; faulty learned toileting behaviour is proposed, and some evidence links it to sexual abuse history. Fowler’s syndrome involves a hypertrophied external sphincter that fails to relax and may inhibit detrusor contraction; it occurs most often, though not exclusively, in young women with retention. Alpha-adrenergic agonists such as pseudoephedrine may cause functional obstruction or retention through bladder-neck contraction. Neurological causes are outside this guideline’s scope.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.3 Classification
document_sections.content: Female BOO is categorised as anatomical or functional.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.3.1 Anatomic bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: Anatomical BOO is a physical impediment to urine outflow unrelated to urethral or pelvic-muscle tone.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.3.2 Functional bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: Functional BOO is non-anatomical and non-neurogenic, arising from absent relaxation or raised tone of the bladder neck, urethral sphincter or PFMs. Neurological causes are addressed elsewhere. Table 5 lists principal functional and anatomical causes.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.3.3 Recommendation for classification of bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: Strong: Use standardised anatomical-versus-functional classification for female BOO and fully characterise research populations accordingly.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.4 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Although formal pressure–flow studies underpin female BOO diagnosis, clinical assessment and non-invasive tests may raise suspicion.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.4.1 Clinical history
document_sections.content: Symptoms can involve storage as well as voiding. Presentation may be delayed until recurrent UTI, chronic retention or acute or chronic kidney disease occurs. Small retrospective studies provide inconclusive evidence on diagnostic symptom utility. In a study of > 5,000 symptomatic women, including 163 with BOO, 54% of those with BOO had additional urodynamic diagnoses, supporting the need for urodynamic evaluation.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.4.2 Clinical examination
document_sections.content: No study establishes diagnostic utility of examination in suspected female BOO, but it is widely considered important for inspecting the urethra and vagina for mechanical causes and assessing pelvic-floor causes of functional obstruction.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.4.3 Uroflowmetry and post-void residual volume
document_sections.content: Low Qmax and incomplete emptying can reflect poor detrusor contraction or increased outlet resistance. In a retrospective study of 157 women, anatomical obstruction had significantly lower Qmax than functional obstruction, with substantial overlap. An analysis of > 1,900 symptomatic patients, > 800 with urodynamic BOO, reported functional BOO > 6 times as often as anatomical BOO, contrary to most other epidemiological studies. Flow rate alone was insufficient; PVR > 200 mL differentiated bladder-neck dysfunction from other BOO causes with ROC AUC 0.69. Another retrospective study of 101 women presenting mainly with SUI found correlation between abnormal flowmetry and urodynamic obstruction of phi = 0.718.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.4.4 Ultrasound
document_sections.content: US primarily identifies possible complications, including bladder-wall changes and upper-tract dilatation or hydronephrosis. A 2021 review of 16 non-randomised studies found moderate pooled sensitivity and high specificity for DWT; 6 studies of UEBW found high sensitivity and specificity. In a study of 27 patients with cystoscopically confirmed bladder-neck obstruction, ARFI was more accurate than SWE, and combining them performed better than either alone.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.4.5 Magnetic resonance imaging
document_sections.content: MRI can assess peri-urethral fibrosis in pathological urethral stricture, but the clinical and prognostic meaning of that finding is unestablished.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.4.6 Electromyography
document_sections.content: EMG has chiefly been investigated in Fowler’s syndrome. Abnormal urethral activity may accompany sphincter non-relaxation, raised urethral pressure, impaired bladder sensation and reduced detrusor strength. Complex repetitive discharges and decelerating bursts occur in high-tone sphincters but also in asymptomatic volunteers. A review of 65 studies found few assessing PFM EMG diagnosis; combining EMG with pressure–flow findings may help distinguish anatomical from functional obstruction. A retrospective study of 157 women associated low PFM EMG activity with anatomical obstruction. Other neurophysiological tests can assess somatic S2–4 integrity, but their role in non-neurogenic BOO remains uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.4.7 Cystourethroscopy
document_sections.content: Cystourethroscopy can show the nature, position and calibre of mechanical obstruction and is considered essential because pelvic malignancy can cause anatomical BOO. Urethral calibration may assist in stricture-associated BOO; reported calibre thresholds range from 14-20 Fr.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.4.8 Urodynamics and video-urodynamics
document_sections.content: Pressure–flow testing is central to BOO diagnosis, typically demonstrating low flow with high detrusor pressure, but no female threshold has been clinically validated as a standard. The Blaivas-Groutz nomogram may overestimate obstruction; adding fluoroscopy provides a video-urodynamic criterion, though clinical and predictive validation remains limited. In a retrospective series of 1,914 patients, including 810 with BOO, ROC analyses identified PdetQmax > 30 cm H2O for distinguishing BOO from bladder dysfunction or normal findings (AUC = 0.78); Abrams-Griffiths number > 30 for anatomical versus functional BOO (AUC = 0.66); and PdetQmax > 30 cm H2O for dysfunctional voiding versus poor external-sphincter relaxation (AUC = 0.93). The Solomon–Greenwell female index is BOOIf = PdetQmax-2.2Qmax. Its stated interpretation is BOOIf < 0: < 10% obstruction probability; 5 < BOOIf < 18: equivocal with > 50% likelihood; and BOOIf > 18: 90% likelihood. In 21 consecutive treated women, asymptomatic postoperative patients had significantly improved Qmax, PdetQmax and BOOIf. A proposed pressure-curve-area measure from 103 women has not been independently validated. VCUG, alone or with pressure–flow studies, may localise obstruction through bladder-neck appearance, proximal urethral dilatation or other radiographic features. Functional BOO may prevent a patient from producing flow during testing because failure of PFM relaxation can reinforce the guarding reflex.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.4.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for diagnosis of bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: The evidence summary finds history and examination alone insufficient (LE 3), flow studies insufficient (LE 3), US diagnostically inaccurate (LE 2b), and EMG alone insufficient although potentially useful with pressure–flow testing (LE 3). Cystourethroscopy may characterise mechanical blockage (LE 4); urodynamics, often with fluoroscopy, is the standard evaluation (LE 3). Strong: Take a full history and perform a thorough examination when BOO is suspected. Strong: Do not diagnose female BOO from flow studies alone. Strong: Perform cysto-urethroscopy for suspected anatomical BOO and urodynamics for suspected BOO.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5 Disease management
document_sections.content: Treatment aims to reduce outlet resistance, increase flow and emptying, and relieve voiding and storage LUTS. The underlying cause generally determines the choice.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5.1 Conservative management
document_sections.content: Conservative approaches address voiding behaviour, pelvic-floor relaxation, prolapse-related obstruction and urinary drainage or containment.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5.1.1 Behavioural modification
document_sections.content: Individualised education, symptom monitoring, lifestyle changes, constipation avoidance and altered voiding technique aim to coordinate detrusor and sphincter activity. Components have not been assessed separately; guidance is largely consensus-based, and any effect cannot be quantified.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5.1.2 Pelvic floor muscle training +/- biofeedback
document_sections.content: Physiotherapy seeks to teach relaxation of PFMs and the striated urethral sphincter during voiding. PFM contraction has been associated with significantly reduced resting vaginal pressure and surface EMG activity in women with pelvic-floor dysfunction. Supporting dysfunctional-voiding training evidence largely comes from children.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5.1.3 Electrical stimulation
document_sections.content: Electrically controlled PFM contraction and relaxation might facilitate relaxation during voiding, but no critical evaluation in female BOO has been published.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5.1.4 Use of vaginal pessary
document_sections.content: A pessary may correct POP-related obstruction and improve emptying. In a prospective study of eighteen women with grade three or four cystocoeles and urodynamic BOO defined by PdetQmax > 25 cm H2O and Qmax < 15 mL/s, seventeen (94%) voided normally immediately after pessary placement. Other outcomes and long-term BOO data were unavailable.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5.1.5 Urinary containment
document_sections.content: Containment may temporarily provide social continence for BOO-associated retention and overflow UI; published female-BOO-specific outcome and adverse-event studies are absent.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5.1.6 Urinary catheterisation
document_sections.content: CISC or indwelling drainage can bypass obstruction, either as treatment or alongside urethral dilatation, urethrotomy or bladder-neck incision. Temporary postoperative voiding difficulty usually needs short-term catheterisation; chronic retention may require longer-term CISC or indwelling drainage. In a small post-urethrotomy RCT, CISC twice daily for one week, daily for four weeks and weekly for seven weeks yielded twelve-week freedom from stricture recurrence of 78.5% versus 55.4% without catheterisation. In 20 patients with dysfunction after TVT, a CISC programme produced 59% cure, defined by consistent PVR < 100 mL; half voided normally within twelve weeks.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5.1.7 Intraurethral inserts
document_sections.content: A valved, pump-assisted silicone urethral insert permits externally controlled emptying and is ordinarily replaced monthly. In a study of 92 women with varied causes of voiding dysfunction, 60% had it removed within seven days because of discomfort, leakage or technical problems, and a further 20% discontinued later. Continuing users were satisfied and had PVR < 100 mL. Six insertions migrated into the bladder and four symptomatic UTIs occurred. Extended long-term results are unavailable.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5.1.8 Extracorporeal magnetic stimulation
document_sections.content: Repeated magnetic stimulation induces PFM contraction and relaxation and is proposed to help voluntary pelvic-floor relaxation during voiding. A small non-randomised prospective study (n = 60) compared alfuzosin, EMS and their combination in functional BOO. Qmax increased significantly and IPSS decreased significantly in every group; the combined group had significantly greater improvement in the IPSS QoL question.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.5.1.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for conservative treatment of bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: The evidence table covers possible benefit from relaxation training with biofeedback (LE 3), the absence of published ES-effect evidence (LE NA), pessary benefit for large cystocoeles (LE 3), less recurrent stricture with regular CISC after urethrotomy (LE 1b), a 59% CISC-programme cure rate after TVT (LE 3), frequent intraurethral-insert removal despite lower PVR (LE 3), and possible additive benefit of alfuzosin with EMS (LE 2a). Weak: Offer relaxation-focused PFMT for functional BOO. Strong: Prioritise research into how PFMT affects coordinated relaxation during voiding. Weak: Offer a pessary for grade three or four cystocoeles with BOO when other options are unsuitable or unwanted; offer containment for leakage, not to correct BOO; and offer clean intermittent self-dilatation for urethral stricture or post-UI-surgery BOO. Strong: Do not offer an intraurethral device for BOO.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.6 Pharmacological management
document_sections.content: Drug interventions considered for female BOO include alpha-blockers, muscle relaxants, oestrogens, sildenafil and TRH.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.6.1 Alpha-adrenergic blockers
document_sections.content: Alpha-blockers are proposed to relax bladder-neck smooth muscle and reduce outlet resistance. A meta-analysis of fourteen RCTs in women with LUTS found symptom improvement versus placebo, without significant differences in Qmax, PVR or adverse events; non-comparative studies reported additional improvements relative to baseline. In the sole placebo-controlled BOO subgroup RCT in the Panel review, eight weeks of alfuzosin (n = 58) versus placebo (n = 59) showed no significant difference in IPSS, sub-scores, Qmax, PVR or diary results. It did not use EMG or voiding cysto-urethrography to distinguish functional subtypes. In a small comparison of 37 women meeting IPSS > 8, Qmax < 12 mL/s and PVR > 50 mL, tamsulosin yielded complete satisfaction in 16/20 versus 9/20 with prazosin after three months. Both groups improved from baseline; no further statistical between-group comparison was performed. A larger AUA symptom-score reduction was observed with tamsulosin, and adverse events numbered thirteen versus one case with prazosin and tamsulosin, respectively.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.6.2 Striated muscle relaxants
document_sections.content: Baclofen acts as a GABA agonist on sacral interneurons involved in striated-sphincter relaxation. A placebo-controlled crossover RCT gave 60 women with BOO and increased voiding EMG activity oral baclofen 10 mg three times/day for four weeks. Compared with placebo, void counts were lower and Qmax and PdetQmax improved significantly. PVR, maximum cystometric capacity, MUCP and overall adverse-event rates did not differ significantly; common events were somnolence, dizziness and nausea. Patient-reported symptom and QoL outcomes were not assessed.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.6.3 Oestrogens
document_sections.content: Oestrogen deprivation might reduce urethral-wall compliance in atrophic urethritis and contribute to obstruction; benefit from oestrogen treatment remains theoretical because no female-BOO-specific studies have been published.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.6.4 Sildenafil
document_sections.content: Sildenafil inhibits phosphodiesterase five and is proposed to promote urethral relaxation through increased nitric oxide. In a placebo-controlled crossover RCT of twenty women with retention or obstructive voiding, high MUCP and US-estimated sphincter volume > 1.6 cm, symptom and urodynamic measures improved relative to baseline on sildenafil but not significantly versus placebo.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.6.5 Thyrotropin-releasing hormone
document_sections.content: Intravenous TRH has been proposed to induce urethral relaxation, although the mechanism is unclear. An RCT of sixteen women with voiding difficulty assigned eight, including three with BOO, to 200 μg intravenous TRH and eight, including three with BOO, to saline. Between-group changes in functional profile length and MUCP did not differ, despite improvement from baseline with TRH; BOO-specific results were not reported.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.6.6 Summary of evidence and recommendations for pharmacological management
document_sections.content: Evidence summaries state that alpha-blockers may improve symptoms but not urodynamic outcomes versus placebo (LE 1a); tamsulosin may improve symptom scores more than prazosin (LE 1b); baclofen improves Qmax and PdetQmax but has poorly reported symptomatic effects (LE 1b); sildenafil has not shown superiority to placebo (LE 1b); and mixed-aetiology studies found no urodynamic benefit of intravenous TRH over placebo (LE 1b). Weak: After discussing potential benefits and harms, offer uroselective alpha-blockers off-label for functional BOO. Weak: Offer oral baclofen for BOO, particularly with raised voiding EMG activity and sustained detrusor contraction. Strong: Restrict sildenafil to well-regulated clinical trials and do not offer TRH for BOO.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.7 Surgical management
document_sections.content: Surgical management addresses functional sphincter obstruction, prolapse, urethral or bladder-neck narrowing, and obstruction following anti-incontinence surgery.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.7.1 Intra-sphincteric botulinum toxin injection
document_sections.content: Botulinum toxin reduces urethral-sphincter tone by inhibiting presynaptic acetylcholine release; reduced urethral noradrenaline release is also proposed. Female-BOO evidence consists mainly of small, often mixed-population case series without a dedicated comparative trial. A mixed-sex RCT (n = 73) reported lower IPSS and greater voided volume after 100 U onabotulinumtoxinA than saline among 31 participants with dysfunctional voiding, but supplied no female subgroup analysis. Two small female case series using 100 U found improved symptoms and PVR; one also reported higher Qmax and improved UPP. One reported average symptom-free duration of 16.8 weeks. UTI and temporary CISC occurred; SUI was not reported.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.7.2 Sacral nerve stimulation
document_sections.content: SNS is proposed to reduce urethral tone through modulation of inhibitory afferent activity. No comparative female-BOO neuromodulation trial was identified; most reports mix indications or do not confirm the retention mechanism. Among 60 women with obstruction-associated retention selected by UPP > 100 cm H2O, sphincter volume > 1.8 mL and characteristic EMG findings, 72% voided spontaneously over mean follow-up of four years. Those still requiring CISC up to twice daily needed it less often than before surgery. There were 99 adverse events and 63 revisions. Postoperative CISC-assisted voiding occurred in 27% after two-stage versus 17% after one-stage implantation; more serious adverse events were associated with the one-stage procedure.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.7.3 Pelvic organ prolapse surgery
document_sections.content: Repair of POP can relieve urethral kinking or compression; reviews report improved voiding in most patients with POP-related BOO after cystocoele repair. In 277 women with at least grade two symptomatic POP, voiding symptoms and PVR fell significantly one year after surgery. A retrospective study of 50 women undergoing laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy found significantly higher Qmax and lower PdetQmax and PVR among those aged > 65 years; OAB scores improved, but postoperative ICIQ-SF did not change significantly.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.7.4 Urethral dilatation
document_sections.content: Progressively larger dilators disrupt fibrotic narrowing; dilatation is considered the primary procedure for suspected female urethral stricture. Described target sizes include 30–40 Fr, 43 Fr, 30 Fr and 35 Fr, without an established standard technique. A review pooling 93 women found mean success of 49% after dilatation to 41 Fr over mean 46 months; mean time to failure was 12 months. Success was 58% without prior treatment versus 27.2% after previous dilatation. In an RCT of 50 women with OAB and urodynamic BOO unrelated to stricture, persistent urgency at six weeks and six months was more frequent after cystoscopy alone than after cystoscopy with distension and dilatation. Neither group had significant urodynamic improvement at six weeks, QoL comparisons were affected by baseline imbalance, and six patients (12%) developed SUI. In a prospective study of 86 women with primary stricture, scheduled dilatation to 24 Fr every two months improved Qmax and PVR more than on-demand dilatation. New or worsened SUI, frequency and urgency are concerns; SUI risk is lower than with urethrotomy or reconstruction.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.7.5 Urethrotomy
document_sections.content: Endoscopic incision opens obstructive urethral scar tissue. In ten women with strictures, Otis urethrotomy to 40 Fr followed by six weekly dilatations significantly improved IPSS, QoL, voided volume, Qmax and PVR at six months. At mean 82 months, only PVR and QoL improvements persisted.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.7.6 Bladder neck incision/resection
document_sections.content: Transurethral incision opens hypertrophied bladder-neck muscle in primary obstruction. Unilateral, bilateral and four-incision positions have been described using knives or laser, sometimes with additional resection; techniques have not been directly compared. A review of non-comparative studies reported 76–100% success. In seventeen women, incision and V-Y-reconstruction gave similar symptomatic and PVR improvement, but V-Y plasty required longer operation and catheter times and had poorer uroradiological improvement and more transfusions and adverse events. Prospective series generally found improved symptoms and urodynamics. In the largest series of 84 women, success was 84.5% after mean 27.4 months (6–78 months); VVF occurred in 3.6%, SUI in 4.7% and urethral stricture in 3.6%. In that series, VVF and SUI occurred after five- and seven-o’clock incisions but not after two- and ten-o’clock incisions. Reported postoperative SUI across studies ranges from 3–33%; recurrence and reoperation are also possible.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.7.7 Urethroplasty/urethral reconstruction
document_sections.content: Extensive female stricture may be reconstructed with vaginal or labial flaps, vaginal or buccal grafts, or other described tissues. Dorsal, ventral and circumferential approaches differ in proposed support, vascularity, mobilisation and potential sphincter, clitoral or fistula risks. Reviews report success of 57–100%. Pooled vaginal or labial flap success was 91% at mean 32 months; vaginal or labial graft success was 80% at mean 22 months. Oral mucosal grafts averaged 94% success at mean fifteen months. A dorsal buccal-graft review reported 62–100% success, pooled at 86%; another study found 23.1% recurrence at mean 32 months.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.7.8 Urethrolysis
document_sections.content: Urethrolysis after SUI surgery may restore urethral mobility by removing peri-urethral sutures or scar and fibrosis. Case series report improved voiding, symptoms, QoL, residual volumes and urodynamics. One reported de novo SUI in 39%; another linked greater delay before urethrolysis to persistent postoperative bladder symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.7.9 Removal/excision/section/loosening of mid-urethral sling
document_sections.content: For BOO after MUS, reported operations include tape loosening, division, partial excision or removal. Small retrospective series generally report improved emptying and symptoms, lower PVR and durable benefit, although SUI can recur. In 63 women with persistent PVR > 100 mL after tape surgery, revision approaches achieved 87% overall success, defined as PVR < 150 mL; success did not significantly differ by technique. Further surgery for recurrent SUI was more frequent after partial excision without an additional anti-SUI procedure (23% vs. 2.2 and 0). Another study associated release > 180 days after initial surgery with less recurrent SUI than earlier release (15% vs. 46%).

document_sections.heading: 4.5.7.10 Summary of evidence and recommendations for surgical management of bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content:
The evidence summary covers improvement after sphincter botulinum toxin (LE 2), SNS in idiopathic retention (LE 3), more serious complications with one-stage neuromodulation (LE 3), benefit from POP repair (LE 3), improvement but inconsistent urodynamic benefit after urethral dilatation (LE 1b), better results with scheduled than on-demand dilatation (LE 3), poorly sustained dilatation benefit (LE 3), benefit from urethrotomy plus dilatation (LE 3), bladder-neck incision benefit and its potential complications (LE 3), urethroplasty outcomes including recurrence (LE 3; comparison with dilatation LE 2), and benefits and recurrent-SUI risk after urethrolysis or sling revision (LE 3). Weak: Offer intra-sphincteric botulinum toxin or sacral neuromodulation for functional BOO. Weak: Advise that prolapse-associated voiding symptoms may improve after prolapse surgery. Weak: Offer dilatation for stenosis-related BOO while explaining likely repeat treatment; offer internal urethrotomy plus postoperative self-dilatation for stricture-related BOO while explaining limited long-term benefit and UI risk. Weak: Do not offer urethral dilatation or urethrotomy for BOO after synthetic mid-urethral tape because of the theoretical risk of urethral mesh extrusion.

Weak: Do not offer urethral dilatation or urethrotomy for BOO after mid-urethral synthetic tape insertion because of the theoretical risk of urethral mesh extrusion. Weak: Explain that, in the long term, internal urethrotomy has shown improvement only in post-void residual volume and quality of life. Weak: Offer bladder neck incision for BOO caused by primary bladder neck obstruction. Strong: Counsel patients undergoing bladder neck incision about the small postoperative risks of SUI, vesico-vaginal fistula and urethral stricture. Weak: Offer urethroplasty after unsuccessful primary treatment of recurrent urethral stricture causing BOO, and warn about possible stricture recurrence during long-term follow-up. Weak: Offer urethrolysis for voiding difficulties after anti-UI surgery.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.8 Follow-up
document_sections.content: Women with BOO require regular monitoring because persistent or progressive obstruction can further impair voiding or renal function. After treatment, assess for recurrent BOO; specifically monitor for recurrent stricture after urethral dilation, urethrotomy or urethroplasty.

document_sections.heading: 4.6 Nocturia
document_sections.content: The ICS definition from 2002 concerns waking at night one or more times to void; its 2019 quantification counts voids during the main sleep period, from falling asleep until intending to get up. The EAU Guidelines Panel on Urinary Incontinence reviewed nocturia in women, searching evidence through 2017 and updating it with a scoping search in 2020.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.1 Epidemiology, aetiology, pathophysiology
document_sections.content: More than 2 nightly episodes occur in 4–18% of women aged 20–40 years and 28–62% of women aged > 70 years. In a study of 1,000 community-dwelling older adults, nocturia in women correlated with greater age, African American race, UI history, leg oedema and hypertension. A report involving > 5,000 adults aged 30–79 years found nocturia in around 28% and additional associations with cardiac disease, type 2 diabetes and diuretic use. A GRADE-assessed review found that the higher nocturia incidence associated with hypertension was more pronounced, at 1.2 to 1.3-fold, among Black and Asian women, independently of age or BMI; certainty was moderate. Another review, also with moderate certainty, associated nocturia with a 1.2-fold higher fall risk and possibly an approximately 1.3-fold higher fracture risk. A further review concluded that an ~1.3-fold higher mortality risk was probable. Causes may be urological—OAB, BOO, DU or dysfunctional voiding—or non-urological, including 24-hour polyuria, congestive heart failure, sleep apnoea, restless leg syndrome, peripheral vascular disease, sleep disorders, night-time eating, dependent oedema and excessive fluid intake. Proposed mechanisms comprise 24-hour polyuria, nocturnal polyuria, reduced bladder capacity and primary or secondary sleep disorders; examples include diabetes mellitus, primary polydipsia, diabetes insipidus, behavioural factors, peripheral oedema, obstructive sleep apnoea, glycosuria, hormonal or cardiac abnormalities, OAB syndrome/DO, PFM dysfunction, BOO, pharmaceuticals, LUT stones or tumours, and neurological bladder dysfunction. In postmenopausal women, reduced endogenous oestrogen is thought to aggravate all principal underlying mechanisms.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.2 Classification
document_sections.content: Classification uses diary-derived nocturnal urine volume, which includes the first morning void but excludes the last pre-sleep void; the largest single volume passed in 24 hours; nocturia index, calculated as nocturnal volume divided by maximum voided volume; nocturnal polyuria index, calculated as nocturnal volume divided by 24-hour urine volume; and nocturnal urine production, calculated as nocturnal volume divided by hours asleep. These measurements help distinguish 24-hour polyuria, nocturnal polyuria, diminished bladder capacity and sleep disorders.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.3 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Assessment should cover sleep, fluid balance, other LUTS, cardiovascular and endocrine conditions, kidney disease, medications and urological history, alongside examination. The ICI Questionnaire-Nocturia, Nocturia Quality of Life Questionnaire (N-QoL) and Nocturia Impact Diary have demonstrated useful measurement properties, although some originated in male populations. TANGO aims to screen for causes; the PLANET study proposed SCREeN history questions covering Sleep, Cardiovascular, Renal, Endocrine and Neurological function. A bladder diary is an essential initial investigation and determines subsequent testing. Reduced nocturnal or day-and-night voided volumes suggest low nocturnal or overall bladder capacity and possible OAB syndrome, BOO or DU. The definition of 24-hour polyuria is urine production > 40 mL/kg over 24 hours. Age-dependent nocturnal polyuria thresholds extend from 20% in younger people to 33% at age > 65 years of 24-hour output produced during sleep. Possible associations include disrupted circadian rhythm, cardiovascular disease and sleep apnoea. In a study involving ~2,000 patients receiving treatment for LUT abnormalities, nocturnal polyuria contributed to nocturia in 89%. A nocturnal-only diary studied in men cannot diagnose 24-hour polyuria and remains unvalidated in women. A 2022 review and NGT consensus drawing on fourteen observational mixed-population studies recommended initial blood tests for renal and thyroid function, HbA1c and calcium. Another 2022 review and NGT consensus drawing on thirteen mixed studies—nine cohort, three cross-sectional and one case-control—recommended screening questions for insomnia, restless legs syndrome/periodic limb movements of sleep and parasomnias to support primary-care conservative treatment.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for diagnosis of nocturia
document_sections.content: The evidence table presents levels 4, 3 and 2 for history and sleep screening, questionnaire responsiveness, diary-based identification of causes, the male-only evidence for nocturnal-only diaries, and consideration of renal, thyroid, HbA1c and calcium tests. Strong: Obtain a full history, including sleep-disorder screening, from women with nocturia. Weak: Use a validated questionnaire for assessment and reassessment during and/or after treatment. Strong: Assess nocturia in women using a three-day bladder diary.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.4 Disease management
document_sections.content: When interpreting nocturia-treatment trials, distinguish clinically meaningful effects from statistically significant but small reductions in nightly episodes.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.4.1 Conservative management
document_sections.content: Potential self-management measures include timing fluid reduction, moderating caffeine or alcohol, distraction, bladder retraining, PFMT, medication review and constipation treatment; most have not been separately critically evaluated or had their effects quantified. Studies of conservative care are heterogeneous: a review found three studies favourable to PFMT and another that did not confirm benefit. In a secondary analysis involving 131 patients, PFM-contraction training including four biofeedback-assisted sessions reduced nocturia by a median 0.50 episodes per night and significantly outperformed anticholinergic treatment or placebo; evidence certainty was moderate. An RCT in 50 women allocated 1:1 found fewer nocturia complaints with BT plus PFMT than without treatment. In an underpowered RCT of 24 women comparing PFMT with Interferential Therapy plus, between-group differences were not significant, although within-group changes were; certainty for these two trials was low. In an RCT involving n = 647 women, a two-hour class and a 20 minutes video showed no significant between-group nocturia difference at 3 months or 12 months. At 24 months, the 2 hour class group was less likely to have fewer episodes than the 20 minutes video group (OR = 0.5; 95 % CI: 0.3−0.7; p = 0.005); the authors considered the evidence insufficient to favour either strategy. In an open-label RCT including 30/78 women, checklist-based CBT achieved a mean rate of 64.4%; IPSS Q7 night-frequency scores did not significantly differ at four weeks, but FVC-recorded episodes were 1.9 ± 0.9 with CBT and 2.4 ± 1.3 in controls (p = 0.039). A secondary analysis involving 210 women with UUI found no significant difference in nocturia or nocturnal incontinence between tolterodine ER 4 mg alone and the drug plus PFMT; episode differences were small and certainty low. Another RCT found similar effects of individual and group PFMT: at one year, > 30% of those initially experiencing > 2 nightly episodes no longer met that threshold. In an RCT of 39 women, functional magnetic stimulation reduced nocturia, voiding frequency and pad use relative to no treatment. A review of five mixed-sex RCTs found continuous positive airway pressure effective for nocturia associated with obstructive sleep apnoea, with an average reduction of > 2 episodes per night.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.4.1.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for conservative management of nocturia
document_sections.content: The evidence table assigns 1b to comparable nocturia reductions with individual and group PFMT and to generally favourable PFMT findings in women with additional urinary symptoms; it assigns 1a to continuous positive airway pressure for nocturia secondary to obstructive sleep apnoea. Strong: Give lifestyle advice to women with LUTS before or alongside treatment. Strong: Offer individual or group PFMT for nocturia when women also have UI or other storage LUTS. Strong: Refer women with nocturia and a history suggestive of obstructive sleep apnoea for sleep-clinic assessment of suitability for continuous positive airway pressure.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.4.2 Pharmacological management
document_sections.content: The following subsections assess desmopressin, anticholinergics, oestrogens and timed diuretic treatment for nocturia, distinguishing evidence in women from evidence in mixed or male populations.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.4.2.1 Desmopressin
document_sections.content: Desmopressin is a synthetic vasopressin analogue chiefly used when nocturnal polyuria causes nocturia. A review found three women-only trials. A crossover trial in 25 women reported significantly lower nocturnal urine output after six weeks with 20 g desmopressin versus placebo. A double-blind RCT involving 141 women found significant decreases in nocturnal frequency and diuresis at three weeks with bedtime oral doses of 0.1, 0.2 or 0.4 mg; excluding nonresponders during titration increased the likelihood of a favourable result. Another double-blind RCT assigned 58 women for four weeks to placebo (twelve), 10 μg (twelve), 25 μg (eleven), 50 μg (eleven) or 100 μg (twelve). It reported a dose–response pattern, greater apparent sensitivity in women than men, significant nocturnal-volume effects at higher doses and a tendency for the nocturnal polyuria index to favour treatment, especially higher doses. Certainty for these trials was low. In a multicentre RCT of 97 patients with OAB and nocturnal polyuria, post hoc comparison of three-month daily desmopressin 25 μg/tolterodine 4 mg (n = 49) against tolterodine 4 mg/placebo (n = 57) favoured combination treatment for nocturnal void volume and time to first nocturnal void; certainty was moderate. Pooled results from three RCTs found that most patients did not develop clinically significant hyponatraemia, but risk rose with age and lower baseline serum sodium. The authors advised careful sodium monitoring in older patients and avoidance when baseline sodium is below the normal range.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.4.2.2 Anticholinergics
document_sections.content: A review identified three RCTs involving oxybutynin 2.5 mg/day or tolterodine 4 mg/day. A secondary analysis of 131 women assessed at eight weeks found fewer nocturia episodes with immediate-release oxybutynin 2.5 mg once daily, permitting self-titration up to 5 mg three times daily, than with placebo. Adding behavioural therapy also significantly reduced episodes relative to placebo and oxybutynin alone. An RCT of 305 women assessed at eight weeks found baseline improvements in nocturia and nocturnal incontinence with tolterodine tartrate 4 mg, whether given alone or with behavioural training, but no between-group difference; certainty was moderate. An RCT of 97 women with OAB and nocturnal polyuria found fewer mean nocturnal voids from baseline after three months in both the daily desmopressin 25 μg/tolterodine 4 mg group (n = 49) and tolterodine 4 mg/placebo group (n = 57); certainty was moderate. A comparative study of 407 women with OAB and nocturia followed for four weeks found baseline improvements with tolterodine alone and with tolterodine plus estazolam; the combination gave significantly greater improvements in nocturia, urgency and UUI episodes in 24 hours and volume per void, although certainty was very low. In a small multicentre RCT comparing oxybutynin patch with mirabegron, both improved N-QoL at four weeks; mirabegron showed a statistical difference at eight weeks and was the only treatment to significantly decrease nocturnal frequency and water intake and prolong uninterrupted sleep at eight weeks.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.4.2.3 Oestrogens
document_sections.content: A review found one nocturia-specific oestrogen RCT: among 251 women followed for six months, an oestradiol-releasing vaginal ring and an oestriol pessary did not differ in the number reporting nocturia. Both groups improved significantly from baseline, with > 50% responding in each arm; outcome certainty was low.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.4.2.4 Diuretic treatment
document_sections.content: In a placebo-controlled study confined to older men, afternoon furosemide 40 mg taken six hours before bedtime reduced night-time frequency by 0.5 episodes and percentage night-time voided volume by 18% among the 43 completers. No corresponding study was conducted in women.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.4.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for pharmacological management of nocturia
document_sections.content: The evidence table reports levels 1b, 1a and 3 for desmopressin efficacy and age-related hyponatraemia risk; anticholinergic effects; combinations with PFMT or desmopressin; possible vaginal-oestrogen benefit in around 50% of women; the male-only furosemide evidence; and the importance of clinical, rather than solely statistical, significance. Strong: Offer desmopressin for nocturia secondary to nocturnal polyuria after counselling about benefits and risks, including hyponatraemia. Strong: Carefully monitor serum sodium in older recipients and avoid desmopressin if baseline sodium is below normal. Strong: Offer anticholinergics for nocturia with UUI or other LUTS after discussing benefits and risks. Weak: Explain that behavioural therapy combined with anticholinergics is unlikely to outperform either alone. Weak: Consider the offered combination of anticholinergics and desmopressin for women with OAB and nocturia secondary to nocturnal polyuria after counselling. Weak: Offer vaginal oestrogen after discussing benefits and risks. Weak: Offer timed diuretic treatment for nocturia secondary to polyuria after comparable counselling.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.4.4 Surgical management
document_sections.content: Surgery is generally reserved for an underlying LUT disorder that can be corrected; its effects on nocturia are considered in the relevant condition-specific sections.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.5 Follow-up
document_sections.content: The cause of nocturia and the treatment used determine follow-up.

document_sections.heading: 4.7 Pelvic organ prolapse and lower urinary tract symptoms
document_sections.content: This section addresses the relationship between POP and LUTS, including how prolapse assessment and treatment may affect urinary symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.1 Epidemiology, aetiology, pathophysiology
document_sections.content: POP prevalence is 3–6% using bothersome symptoms and 50% using anatomy alone; estimated lifetime surgical risk is 12.6%. Common recognised risks include parity, vaginal delivery, ageing and obesity. Although causation remains incompletely understood, birth-related levator ani injury is considered central. An intact complex closes the genital hiatus and reduces physical-activity stress on endopelvic supporting structures. Trauma-related hiatus widening may increase stress on ligaments, fascia and PFMs, ultimately allowing delayed prolapse. POP and LUTS often coexist, and LUTS are more prevalent with POP than without it; reviews consistently find more OAB symptoms and UUI with POP. Urinary symptoms may either improve or worsen following prolapse treatment. Severe POP may produce BOO symptoms or conceal SUI, which can appear after prolapse correction. Bowel and sexual symptoms can also accompany POP.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.2 Classification
document_sections.content: Since 1996, POP has been staged with Pelvic Organ Prolapse-Quantification (POP-Q), using nine measured points across anterior, posterior and apical compartments. Stages run from 0, no prolapse, through 4, complete compartment eversion. The hymenal remnant is the reference: maximum descent still 1 cm above it defines stage 1; descent between 1 cm above and 1 cm below it defines stage 2; and descent beyond 1 cm below it defines stage 3. The accompanying figures depict prolapse classification and POP-Q staging, including comparison with the earlier Baden–Walker system.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.3 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: POP is diagnosed clinically and staged with POP-Q. Prolapse remaining above the hymen should cause, at most, mild symptoms. If stage and symptoms disagree, consider measuring while standing rather than supine or later in the day; MRI assessments have shown substantial positional staging differences. Additional investigations chiefly address concurrent LUTS or bowel dysfunction; routine imaging is not advised. Prolapse reduction during examination or urodynamics can reveal occult SUI and inform discussion about concurrent anti-UI surgery. An observational comparison found SUI on at least one of five tests in 60/205 (29.2%) asymptomatic women; detection on individual tests rose from 4.4% without reduction to 22% with pessary reduction. In an RCT, twelve of 313 (3.7%) stress-continent women with stages 2–4 POP demonstrated urodynamic SUI without reduction. At 300 mL, reduction-test detection was 6% (5/88) with pessary, 16% (19/122) manually, 21% (21/98) with forceps, 20% (32/158) with swab and 30% (35/118) with speculum. Another trial found positive reduction cough tests in 33.5% (111/331); an observational study of 172 women detected occult SUI in 19% by office evaluation and 29% by urodynamics. Detection can reach 30%, without an agreed optimal method, and its clinical value is disputed. In one trial, postoperative SUI differed with preoperative test findings regardless of concomitant colposuspension: controls 58% vs. 38%, and Burch colposuspension 32% vs. 21%. In another, among women positive on a reduction cough test, UI at three months occurred in 29.6% after synthetic MUS and 71.9% after sham treatment; greater apparent benefit from MUS among test-positive women was present at three months but not twelve months. In an observational study without additional anti-UI surgery, 9% (16/172) developed de novo SUI and six underwent surgery; postoperative SUI occurred in 28% with versus 5% without demonstrable preoperative SUI. Urodynamics alone predicted one additional case, whereas office assessment detected SUI in all six subsequently treated women. A model testing twelve preoperative predictors found neither a positive reduction test by itself nor preoperative POP stage independently significant for de novo SUI.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.3.1 Summary of evidence and recommendation for detection of SUI in women with POP
document_sections.content: The evidence table rates at 2a both occult-SUI detection in ~30% of otherwise continent women after prolapse reduction and the likely increased postoperative SUI risk associated with occult SUI. Strong: Perform a POP reduction test in continent women to identify occult SUI and discuss advantages and disadvantages of adding anti-incontinence surgery during POP repair.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.3.2 Urodynamics in women with pelvic organ prolapse and LUTS (without stress urinary incontinence)
document_sections.content: The role of urodynamics for POP with LUTS other than SUI is uncertain. Detrusor measurements may inform risks of postoperative DO or retention due to DU. In an observational study of 1,503 women with preoperative POP-Q stage 3 or higher, maximum urethral closure pressure > 60 cm H2O, Qmax < 15 mL/s, Dmax > 20 cm H2O and PVR volume > 200 mL independently predicted postoperative DO. In another observational study (n = 49), preoperative DU defined by detrusor pressure at maximum flow < 10 cm H2O and Qmax < 12 mL/s objectively resolved in 47% after surgery, with normalised urodynamic findings. The 2019 NICE Guidelines recommend preoperative POP urodynamics only when symptomatic SUI is also present.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4 Disease management
document_sections.content: PFMT, pessaries, surgery and their combinations can address POP symptoms. The discussion focuses on urinary-symptom effects rather than all prolapse outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.1 Conservative management of pelvic organ prolapse
document_sections.content: The 2019 update to the 2013 NICE guidance judged conservative POP evidence low quality. Its review identified thirteen RCTs, seven reporting urinary-symptom change. An additional search found four RCTs adding PFMT to surgery and one comparing PFMT/Pilates with written lifestyle advice. Five studies compared PFMT with lifestyle advice, one PFMT with and without pessary, one PFMT against pessary, and five POP surgery with and without PFMT.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.1.1 Pelvic floor muscle training versus lifestyle advice
document_sections.content: In an RCT (n = 109), six-month ICIQ-UI-SF improvement was 2.40 points with PFMT and 0.2 points with lifestyle advice; baseline scores were 7.4 vs. 5.9, while follow-up scores of 4.8 vs. 5.2 did not significantly differ. Reports from another RCT assessed outcomes at three-, six- and twelve-month follow-up. At three months, UDI-6 improved significantly in both lifestyle-only (53 women) and lifestyle-plus-group-PFMT (56 women) groups, whereas UIQ-7 improvement was significantly greater in the lifestyle-only group. No between-group UDI-6 or UIQ-7 difference appeared at six months. By twelve months, 70% of lifestyle-only and 48% of combination participants had sought further treatment, leaving too few on original treatment for strong conclusions. In another RCT, 225 women with POP-Q stage 1–3 received individualised PFMT and 222 received lifestyle-leaflet advice. At six months the controls more often reported UI, straining and incomplete emptying, and had worse ICIQ-SF scores; these differences were absent at twelve months. During the twelve-month period, 50% of controls received extra care, including additional PFMT in 27%. At 24 months, a trial of 414 women with stage 1–3 POP, assigned 207 per group, found a better ICIQ-UI-SF score with PFMT/Pilates than lifestyle advice (mean difference –0.83), but no difference in any-UI reports or weekly pad use. In a PFMT-versus-PFMT-plus-pessary RCT, urinary questionnaire scores did not differ between groups at twelve months. The combination group improved from baseline on UIQ, but had more de novo SUI (48% vs. 22%) and more improvement of existing voiding difficulty (62.5% vs. 35.5%).

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.1.2 Pelvic floor muscle training versus pessary only
document_sections.content: An RCT comparing pessary treatment in 82 women with PFMT in 80 women with symptomatic POP found no significant UDI-6 difference at 24 months in either ITT or per protocol analyses.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.1.3 Surgery alone versus surgery with pelvic floor muscle training
document_sections.content: An assessor-blinded RCT found no twelve-month difference in UDI or IIQ change after POP surgery with versus without perioperative PFMT. A separate RCT of 57 women, 28 receiving surgery and 29 surgery plus PFMT, found within-group UDI-6 improvement at six months but no between-group difference. A 2x2 factorial trial comparing two operations and additional PFMT (n = 188) versus none (n = 186) found no UDI difference through 24 months or SUI difference in a further report. In a 2020 RCT, supervised perioperative PFMT in 48 women versus surgery alone in 40 yielded no UDI-6 difference at 40 or 90 days. ICI 2017 described level 1a evidence for reducing pelvic-floor symptoms with PFMT, some evidence for less bulging and some RCT evidence for improved POP stage. NICE advises considering > 16 weeks of supervised PFMT initially for symptomatic prolapse and considering a pessary alone or with PFMT. Expected benefits chiefly concern prolapse symptoms, not LUTS; available data do not support initiating conservative therapy for asymptomatic POP solely to treat UI or emptying difficulties.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.1.4 Pessary versus surgery alone
document_sections.content: A prospective cohort reported subjective improvement significantly more often after surgery than after pessary treatment.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.1.5 Summary of evidence and recommendation for the conservative treatment of pelvic organ prolapse and lower urinary tract symptoms
document_sections.content: The evidence table assigns 2a to LUTS improvement lasting up to 6 months with PFMT without pessary or surgery, and to the absence of additional PFMT benefit when pessary treatment or surgery is used. Strong: Tell women with POP not requiring a pessary or operation that PFMT might relieve LUTS. Strong: Do not offer preoperative PFMT to improve LUTS outcomes when a pessary or POP operation is indicated.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.2 Pelvic organ prolapse surgery and overactive bladder
document_sections.content: Few studies specifically evaluate OAB after POP surgery. A review of twelve studies excluding women with SUI found postoperative OAB improvement in all but one. In the authors' prospective analysis of 505 surgically treated women followed a mean 12.7 months, bothersome frequency fell from 36.6% to 14.6%, with de novo frequency in 6.1%; bothersome urgency fell from 36.8% to 12.9%, with de novo urgency in 5.0%; and UUI fell from 21.2% to 6.1%, with de novo symptoms in 5.3%. Another observational study of 87 women reported improvement in frequency of 75% and urgency of 83%; POP-Q stage did not appear to modify OAB outcomes in these studies. An observational study (n = 43) found 70–75% improvement in OAB/DO after posterior repair.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.3 Pelvic organ prolapse surgery and bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: BOO criteria depend on urodynamics. POP-related obstruction is categorised as anatomical BOO.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.4 Pelvic organ prolapse surgery and stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: This discussion compares surgical approaches for women with POP and symptomatic or reduction-detected SUI, and evaluates preventive anti-UI procedures when SUI is absent. It draws on a 2018 review of ten trials and a Cochrane review of nineteen trials (n = 2,717) that analysed women with symptomatic SUI, occult SUI or continence separately.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.4.1 Vaginal pelvic organ prolapse surgery in women with stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Two trials, with n = 185 and 134, compared concurrent MUS at vaginal POP repair against POP repair alone in women with preoperative SUI; the RR for postoperative SUI favoured combined surgery at 0.30. One trial also compared MUS at initial surgery against adding it at three months if SUI persisted. At twelve months postoperative UI did not differ (RR 0.41); among those without an initial MUS, 44% never required surgery and 29% were dry.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.4.2 Abdominal pelvic organ prolapse surgery in women with stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: An RCT of 47 women with POP and SUI found no postoperative SUI improvement from adding Burch colposuspension to abdominal prolapse surgery (RR: 1.38), including over five years. Another RCT of 113 women comparing MUS with Burch colposuspension added to sacro-colpopexy found less postoperative SUI with MUS at two years (RR 0.54).

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.5 Vaginal pelvic organ prolapse surgery in continent women
document_sections.content: In an RCT of 220 initially continent women, postoperative SUI occurred after vaginal POP repair alone in 46/113 (40.7%) and after repair plus MUS in 30/107 (28.0%); RR: 0.69.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.5.1 Abdominal pelvic organ prolapse surgery in continent women
document_sections.content: Two RCTs comparing sacro-colpopexy plus Burch colposuspension (n = 180) against sacro-colpopexy alone (n = 187) favoured prophylactic colposuspension for de novo SUI (RR: 0.69), although SUI developed in 34% versus 49%, respectively. In a trial followed for a mean 39.5 months, additional SUI surgery was required by only 1/31 women (3%) in both groups.

document_sections.heading: 4.7.4.5.2 Vaginal pelvic organ prolapse surgery in women with prolapse and occult stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Five RCTs compared vaginal POP repair alone in 194 women with repair plus MUS in 174 women who had occult SUI. Postoperative SUI favoured concurrent MUS (RR 0.38).
